A potentially seriously complicating factor for flow in crystalline rock is that the rock is deformable. Even small changes in the fracture openings cause large changes in permeability as the permeability is proportional to the aperture cubed. The rock deforms according to the rock stress field. Changes in the groundwater flow and changes in the temperature field will change the active stress acting on the rock which in turn will change the groundwater flow. Thus, the rock deformation, flow and heat transport are coupled processes. These couplings may be of great importance for the performance of a waste repository.   
The coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical effects may be important in many scales. For example, the stress changes introduced by excavating the repository and the canister deposition holes combined with the heat from the waste will af fect the permeability close to the repository. Furthermore, it is yet an unresolved matter if these changes may disturb the stability of the repository or cause more regional faulting.   
The strong coupling between flow and rock stress/deformation have been observed in many field experiments. Still existing hydromechanical models are basically research tools expressing quantitative behaviors. A practical problem with coupled hydro-mechanical models is that they are so complex that only very simplified examples can be studied. Furthermore, the underlying constitutive relations for joint deformation has not yet been validated. 

EVIDENCE:   The skinzone development is observed on the tunnel scale at e.g. Stripa (Gale, 1982) or SFR 86-07 (also URL). The stress impact on fracture permeability has been verified in numerous laboratory experiments (e.g. Witherspoon and others at LBL). 

EFFECT- MODEL:   The skinzone due to excavation needs to be taken into account when evaluating flow and transport measurements in and close to the excavated repository. The stress redistribution occurring after backfilling/resaturation (see 3.2.1) may affect the flow distribution in the rock and thus have implications on the benefit of applying a deposition procedure where potential canister holes with large flow are avoided. The result of the skinzone (permeability change) may be modelled with the "standard" flow/and migration models by appropriate changes of the permeability. However, evaluation of the development of the skinzone, if at all possible, require specially coupled hydro-mechanical models (e.g. ROCMAS Noorishad and Tsang, 1987).   
Modeling the skinzone development will be very difficult as the (generally unknown) undisturbed rock stress distribution is needed as input. Alternatively, rough estimates based on ''field experience" may be used. Skinzone development and hydraulic conductivity redistributions are basically near-zone phenomena and need no special attention in the far field modelling except for eventual changes in the source term.   
See also 4.2.7 Thermo-hydro-mechanical effects. 

REFERENCES: Witherspoon et. al.; 
Gale 1982; 
SFR 86-07; 
Noorishad and Tsang (ROCMAS), LBL, 1987.

pfep_description_raw:
PROCESS:   The water does not flow over the whole fracture plane. This fact is often noted by "channeling". However, within this term vastly different concepts on how flow occurs are possible.   
One concept of channeling is that each fracture plane consist of open and closed parts - for this there also is experimental evidence i.e. Abelin et al. (1987). This concept might only be viewed as an extension of the discrete fracture approach, at least if the closed part portion is not too large. There is little knowledge on how the fracture transmissivity is distributed on the fracture plane. It is clear that the flow distribution among the different fractures will depend very much on the shape of the open parts. To complicate matters further this shape depends upon the rock stress field. In fact, much basic research is needed to determine a proper way to attack this problem. Detailed mapping of tunnel or shaft walls, the use of statistical approach to hydraulic and fracture data in boreholes and tracer tests are some of the tools available to get improved knowledge of the channeling effect.   
Another concept of "channels" is "extreme channeling" where there only are a few paths where most of the water flows in the rock mass. These paths are either caused by real physical conduits "wormholes" in the rock mass or the com bined
The difference between "wormholes" and a poorly percolating network is that in the latter case the position and amounts of the important paths may change totally if the hydraulic boundary conditions are changed, whereas in the former case the flow is always confined to the "wormholes". The situation with a poorly percolating network would make it extremely difficult to characterize the flow and transport properties of the rock. Experiments performed on one scale then cannot be extrapolated to a larger scale. A poorly percolating fracture network could for example result if the transmissivity variance is large combined with large fracture size variance and a relatively low fracture density. 

EFFECT- MODEL:   Channeling will increase groundwater velocities but this is not the most impor tant effect. More important is that the fracture surface "per volume flowing water" available for sorption and matrix diffusion decreases. (This effect may also enhance the flow of oxidants to the deposition hole). The specific fracture surface available for sorption/matrix diffusion is included in the "standard" migration models but a well understood treatment of channeling is still lacking.   
In the near zone channeling will make the flow over some canister deposition holes much larger than the average flow (and v.v. much smaller at some holes). Channeling needs to be considered when evaluating the time distribution for canister failure and the when evaluating the source term (i.e. only a percentage of the canister holes will see the large flows). 

REFERENCES:   Abelin et.al., Stripa TR 87-21.

The difference between "wormholes" and a poorly percolating network is that in the latter case the position and amounts of the important paths may change totally if the hydraulic boundary conditions are changed, whereas in the former case the flow is always confined to the "wormholes". The situation with a poorly percolating network would make it extremely difficult to characterize the flow and transport properties of the rock. Experiments performed on one scale then cannot be extrapolated to a larger scale. A poorly percolating fracture network could for example result if the transmissivity variance is large combined with large fracture size variance and a relatively low fracture density.

More important is that the fracture surface "per volume flowing water" available for sorption and matrix diffusion decreases. (This effect may also enhance the flow of oxidants to the deposition hole). The specific fracture surface available for sorption/matrix diffusion is included in the "standard" migration models but a well understood treatment of channeling is still lacking.   
In the near zone channeling will make the flow over some canister deposition holes much larger than the average flow (and v.v. much smaller at some holes). Channeling needs to be considered when evaluating the time distribution for canister failure and the when evaluating the source term (i.e. only a percentage of the canister holes will see the large flows).

pfep_description_raw:
A potentially seriously complicating factor for flow in crystalline rock is that the rock is deformable. Even small changes in the fracture openings cause large changes in permeability as the permeability is proportional to the aperture cubed. The rock deforms according to the rock stress field. Changes in the groundwater flow and changes in the temperature field will change the active stress acting on the rock which in turn will change the groundwater flow. Thus, the rock deformation, flow and heat transport are coupled processes. These couplings may be of great importance for the performance of a waste repository.   
The coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical effects may be important in many scales. For example, the stress changes introduced by excavating the repository and the canister deposition holes combined with the heat from the waste will affect the permeability close to the repository. Furthermore, it is yet an unresolved matter if these changes may disturb the stability of the repository or cause more regional faulting.   
The strong coupling between flow and rock stress/deformation have been ob served in many field experiments. Still existing hydromechanical models are basi cally research tools expressing quantitative behaviors. A practical problem with coupled hydromechanical models is that they are so complex that only very sim plifled examples can be studied. Furthermore, the underlying constitutive rela tions for joint deformation has not yet been validated.   The validation exercises currently underway are related to block experiments with block sizes in the order of a few meters. Larger scale experiments are planned but the validation of the large scale effects are still in its infancy.   See also excavation backfilling effects on nearby rock (4.2.2.1) and ther mochemical effects (4.1.7). 

REFERENCES:   Noorishad and Tsang (ROCMAS) Users guide.

pfep_description_raw:
PROCESS:   Earthquakes occur in Sweden. They are usually small, magnitude 0-4, but there are historic examples with earthquakes up to magnitude 6 (1904 Oslo graben). There are also indications of even larger earthquakes occurring in connection with the last iceage due to an uneven distribution of the overburden (ice load). Magnitudes up to 8 and even 9 has been mentioned, but this is under dispute.   
Earthquakes in Sweden are generally generated by the build up of stresses in the rockmass, which are suddenly released. The mechanism behind this phenomena might be the ongoing plate movements (5.19) with a ridge push, or due to the ongoing land uplift (creep ) after the last glaciation (5.16) or a com bination of both. The stress is released by a movement along a preexisting fault or by a new fracture. 

EFFECT:   In the general case earthquakes do not create any substantial damage especially if it is an underground opening. There are examples of large earthquakes which had catastrophic impact on buildings on the surface but which weren't felt especially much in mines at depth (Japan, South America). This can be explained by the fact that the ground motions and interference waves at the surface are transmitted through buildings and amplified. At repository depth the waves propagate through the area without being amplified and without any damage.   
In the case with an earthquake activated fracture zone passing through the repository there could be movements along the fracture zone. This movement might damage a canister if the QA of canister emplacement is bad or if the process of earthquake generation creates an entirely new zone hitting one or a few canisters. The geometrical distribution of canister positions versus known fracture zones are important to consider in this case. (Considered in KBS-3)

pfep_description_raw:
PROCESS:   There is a continuous ongoing land uplift in Sweden. The maximum rate of uplift in northern Sweden is 9 mm per year, in Stockholm 5 mm and in Scania about 0 mm. Geological studies show that the greatest uplift was shortly after the retreat of the ice and has declined since then. The maximum total cumulative land uplift since deglaciation is estimated at about 850 m. The remaining future uplift is es timated to lie between 20 m and 200 m. The ongoing land uplift is mainly due to compression of the rockmass under the ice load during the last glaciation. This is a similar movement that the bedrock has undergone repeatedly in connection with previous glaciations. There is also proof of several uplifts in the earlier his tory during the formation and denudation of the basement more than 650 mil lion years ago. In the last case the mechanism has been associated with orogenies and ongoing crustal movements rather than 
by glaciation periods. 

EFFECT:   It is under discussion wether disturbances in the state of equilibrium of the crust due to iceloading would affect the repository at depth. In KBS 3 it was argued that it would not affect the repository at 500 m depth, it is only one more repeti tion of crustal movements that have already taken place before . There is an on going project, Stephansson et al, trying to model the impact of the load of an icesheet. The results will soon be published. It is believed that most of the move ments will take place in the major fracture zones, in which the repository will not be built.   
The work by Noorishad at LBL and also the above mentioned ongoing work by Stephansson show that minor cracks will also be affected by such movements, not necessarily by displacement, but by a variation of their opening. The result could be a modification of the permeability distribution in the rock mass. Ac cording to de Marsily this process should possibly be included in the central scenario since we have no way of showing that the present distribution of the fracture opening is the most probable one for the future. 

SCREENING:   Uplift is a presently ongoing process. However, the future development of uplift (and subsidence) is very dependent on the future climatic evolution which is un certain. Thus it is not practical to include uplift in the PROCESS SYSTEM).

pfep_description_raw:
PROCESS:   There are lot of evidences that Sweden has gone through several cycles of permafrost during the quarternary period (last 2 m.y.) At present, in the Spitzberg area, the permafrost depth is 450 m, and in Siberia, depths exceeding 1500 m have been reported. Although these latter examples are possibly permafrost of older ages than the last ice age. With todays present knowledge however it is not possible to exclude a deep permafrost situation in Sweden. It is therefore necessary to consider the potential of permafrost at repository depth as well as on the surface.   
As a gross generalization it is assumed that the limit of permafrost shows a strong relationship to the mean annual air temperature isotherm of -1 to -2 degrees C. The depth of frost penetration is affected by the topography and the thickness of the snow cover. The geothermal gradient is in general in Sweden today in crystalline rock about 3 degrees C per 100 m with some local variations. This is also a controlling factor, the lower limit to permafrost approaches an equilibrium depth, at which the temperature increase due to earth heat just off sets the amount by which the freezing point exceeds the mean surface tempera ture. 

EFFECT:   Possible potential effects of permafrost are for instance fracturing or opening of fractures because of water freezing; compression of backfill and opening of voids at melting; increasing water flow in the temperature gradient and potential rapid flow paths; accumulation (concentration) of gas and radionuclides below the lower surface of the permafrost frozen rockmass giving rise to a pulse of radionuclides when melting occurs.

pfep_description_raw:
PROCESS:   Gases from deeper geological layers might accumulate in the repository during permafrost, especially during the early phase when the nearby rock is still kept at higher temperatures. 

CAUSES:   Nitrogen and light hydrocarbons, notably methane, are known to penetrate from deep geological formations to the surface. 

EFFECTS:   Gas accumulation will lead to enforced outflow of groundwater from the re pository. This will take place at a very slow rate, and the consequence must be regarded as negligible. The influence of a gas cushion on the flow field might be of some importance, however.   
Clathrates are methane hydrates that occur as solids in certain conditions of temperature and pressure and are also associated with permafrost. They are found underground e.g. in the Spitzbergen, in sediment areas with methane production and in the seabed at greater depth. Their potential role can be in cluded within the general framework of gas production in the repository, its ef fect on migration, or on explosion in connection with radiolytic gases. As a result of the heating by the waste, existing clathrates could produce methane.   
Note that their presence is extremely difficult to detect since solid samples are sublimated when brought to room temperature and pressure. However, crystal line rocks are not known to contain large amounts of methane. However, for an intermediate level repository methane generation can be a problem and the potential formation of clathrates should be considered. This issue needs to be carefully considered and documented, but probably not included in the initial list of scenarios.

pfep_description_raw:
PROCESS:   Erosion of surface sediments (and crystalline bedrock) is a continuously ongoing process due to weathering. Erosion is balanced by deposition of eroded sedi ments at other localities. The material is redistributed by e.g. water flow. Due to frequent glaciation periods in Sweden the sediment cover is relatively thin, as the surface of the rock is eroded to the greatest extent during glaciation periods.  (formation of eskers etc). Calculations (KBS-3) showed that in the normally type of flat terrain that characterizes most of Sweden, the cumulative erosion of the crystalline basement caused by the glaciers has normally been limited to a few tens of meters. In a hilly terrain the erosion might be deeper. 

EFFECT:   Affect groundwater recharge/discharge and thus gw flow (i.e affects release) and geosphere transport. However, the impact on (the distribution) of the ground water recharge is minor relative to the general uncertainty of the (distribution of) the groundwater recharge. The (sure) occurrence of sediment erosion should be considered when estimating the recharge/discharge uncertainty but may otherwise be screened out.   
Groundwater recharge/discharge should perhaps be entered as a special phenomenon into which one may lump 5.26 (this phen.), human induced actions on g.w. recharge (5.27), change in sealevel (5.31), river meandering 6.9.

PROCESS:   During the past earth history there are many evidences for repeated glaciation periods. Glacial and interglacial periods have followed each other. Numerous hypotheses have been put forward in order to account for the appearance of ice ages in the geological past. It is however acknowledged as stated by Bjelm (1989) that the ultimate cause of the Pleistocene glacial and interglacial cycles are the Milankovitch orbital forcing parameters. These involve the three cycles of earth/sun geometry that controls the distribution of solar radiation on earth, the tilt (obliquity) of the earth's axis, the eccentricity of the earth's orbit around the sun, and the precession of the equinoxes. These are continuously ongoing processes.   
There are no reasons which exclude that these processes will not happen also in the future, though human induced effects like the "greenhouse effect" might have an impact on the rate and on the starting point of the next glaciation period. As a fact there are scientists arguing that we already have left the "true" inter - glacial conditions behind us and that we have entered the glacial part of such a cycle. Full glacial conditions may perhaps according to them lie 40,000  80,000 years ahead of us or even longer. Today there is a general consensus that within the next one million years Sweden will most probably be affected by one or more new glaciation periods. 

CONSEQUENCE:   During full glacial conditions in a region like Scandinavia the weight of the in land ice sheet (3000 m ice thickness) depresses the earth's surface by several hundreds of metres, or perhaps even thousand metres. This affects the regional stress field, fracture zones, induces movements along old and perhaps new frac tures. The movements might be associated with seismic events or not. The above mentioned processes will also affect the groundwater flow at depth and at the surface. It may also cause extreme groundwater heads at he ice edge, change the position of the inflow and outflow areas and cause sea level changes.

DESCRIPTION:   Colloids are particles in the size range between 1 and 100 nm. They might sorb or otherwise include radionuclides in the groundwater system. 

CAUSES:   Colloids are always present in deep groundwaters; measured concentrations are generally less than 1 mg/l. They are of both inorganic and organic origin. Possible sources of specific significance for a deep geological repository in crystalline rock are the presence of gradients in groundwater composition leading to precipitation (e.g. as a result of changes in redox potential and pH), and erosion (dispersion) of clay minerals. Under extreme external conditions (e.g. glaciations, faulting) transients in colloid concentration might occur. 

EFFECTS:   Depending on composition and physico-chemical characteristics (e.g. size distribution, surface potential, etc.) colloids are transported more or less with the same velocity as the groundwater. Reversible sorption of radionuclides on particles in the larger size range is of less importance, and this probably also holds for colloids in the smallest size range (the formation of such colloids should be reversible and sorption of them considerable). "Irreversible" sorption on and transport with colloids in the intermediate range might be of some importance for certain radionuclides. Until this problem has been further studied these statements are to be regarded as speculations, however.

PROCESS:   More or less regardless of the level of detail used in the description of the flow field there will always remain velocity variations that cannot be described explicitly in an advection term. The spreading of radionuclides by means of diffusion and these unresolved velocity variations could generally be denoted by the term dispersion. Dispersion is especially important in connection with radio nuclide transport (KBS-3). Even a small fraction of early arriving nuclides will carry a considerable amount of radioactivity as the time for radioactive decay has been very limited for these nuclides.   
Obviously, the actual definition of dispersion is directly related to the used definition of the advection. In some instances it is possible to relate the dispersion to a given statistical structure of the permeability field (see e.g. Gelhar and Axness, 1983 or Neuman et.al. 1987). However, the great uncertainty with regard to the spatial structure of crystalline rocks also implies great uncertainty on the dispersion.   
For extreme channeling dispersion cannot be described as a Fickian process (see e.g. Rasmuson WRR 8, 1247, 1986) not even for one-dimensional flow. It has been suggested (in KBS-3) that channeling could be described with a constant Peclet number implying that the dispersivity will increase with travel distance. However, transport with extreme channeling is not at all dispersive, it is skewed to the fast flow paths. Using a constant Peclet number is correct only for the first two moments of a breakthrough curve whereas higher order moments will differ. Again the portion of nuclides that will arrive in the very fast channels will carry most of the radioactivity due to their limited time for radioactive decay.   
Dispersion in a two or three dimensional flow field of a strongly heterogeneous spatial structure is even more complicated. In particular Tsang (1989) notes that it is impossible to make accurate predictions of tracer arrivals at a given point in space and time. Multiple point or areal averages are needed. However, the actual formulation of appropriate measures of this kind is still a re search problem. 

SCREENING:   Dispersion is a process that needs to be included in the PROCESS SYSTEM.

DESCRIPTION:   In an assessment of the behaviour of radionuclides the presence of stable and/or naturally occurring isotopes of the same elements must be taken into account. For transport paths through the geosphere and biosphere to man, mixing or dilution of the radioactive species from the waste with species of the same element from other sources will lead to a reduction of the radiological consequences. The following viewpoints mainly concern the processes in the geosphere. 

MODELLING:   The presence of several isotopes of the same element are included in models that describe e.g. dissolution and precipitation reactions in the nearfield. However, these effects are not limited to isotopes of the same element. Coprecipitation of similar elements is a wellknown phenomenon that might lead to significant reduction of the release to the geosphere. Similar elements of this kind are the trivalent actinides and lanthanides.   
Another important aspect is the naturally occurring decay series. For example, Swedish granitic bedrocks are often saturated with respect to uranium and thorium. This means that in calculation of the outflow of radionuclides to the biosphere there should be no contribution from the spent fuel to the dose consequences for these radionuclides above the natural background.

project_title: SKI SITE-94 Deep Repository Performance Assessment Project
host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Ongoing chemical reactions between groundwater and rock- and fracture minerals lead to more or less continuous changes of the solid phases along the flow paths from a repository. Thus, not only weathering of rock minerals take place, but also healing of existing and newly formed fractures.

Natural and human induced perturbations of groundwater chemistry will affect alteration/weathering of rock and fracture minerals. Especially in the near-field rock, changes in water chemistry due to degradation of materials in technical barriers and tunnel reinforcements may cause weathering and changes of the fracture properties. In addition, the early temperature gradient in the near-field rock may cause increased weathering of silicate minerals and a subsequent precipitation of silica (potentially as colloids) downstream the repository. Precipitation of calcite which have a lower solubility at higher temperatures may decrease the fracture aperture or even lead to fracture healing. 

Alteration/weathering of rock and fracture minerals may lead to changes in fracture and pore properties which influences groundwater flow and nuclide retardation processes such as sorption and matrix diffusion. Alteration/weathering may also liberate nuclides already sorbed on the minerals. On the other hand, weathering may also result in inclusion of nuclides in weathering products making them inaccessible to the flowing groundwater. Rock deformation due to stress changes from i.e. thermal load or glaciations may also open or close fractures.

Influenced by:
Alteration/weathering of rock and fracture minerals is influenced by minerals composition and the groundwater chemistry. In addition, the temperature and the stress field may have an impact.

Affects:
Alteration/weathering will affect the mineral composition and the physical characteristics of fractures and pores. It may also affect the water chemistry and the generation of colloids.

Modelling aspects:
Potential changes of mineral stability can be calculated by thermochemical equilibrium models, but may require consideration of kinetic effects. One such model is EQ3/6 which also has some abilities to treat kinetics.

project_title: SKI SITE-94 Deep Repository Performance Assessment Project
host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Mineral surfaces are usually negatively charged in contact with water. Because of the negative electric field anions are repelled from the surface. As a consequence, the movement of anions in clays and rock matrices are restricted to the largest pores or fractures. This would result in a lower diffusion flux of anionic radionuclide species in the bentonite buffer and backfill as compared to cationic species. Potentially it would also mean a lower diffusion flux of anionic species into pores and micro-fractures in the rock matrix. 

Experiments with diffusion of anionic species in bentonite have shown that the diffusion is dependent on the density of the bentonite, the electrolyte concentration in the porewater and the charge of the anionic species. At high bentonite densities and low electrolyte concentrations the pore volume accessible to anionic species, the effective porosity, is smaller than at lower densities and higher electrolyte concentrations.

Influenced by:
Anion exclusion is dependent on the characteristics of the pores in the solid material, the ionic strength of the solution and the charge of the diffusing species.

Affects:
Anion exclusion affects the diffusive mass transport of species in solution.

Modelling aspects:
Should be considered in the selection of diffusivity values.

project_title: SKI SITE-94 Deep Repository Performance Assessment Project
host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
As a consequence of water uptake the bentonite buffer will swell to fill up the void between the canister and the rock in the deposition hole. Swelling into cracks intersecting the deposition holes and into the tunnels, which are backfilled with bentonite/sand with a lower swelling pressure, is also possible.

The extent of swelling will influence the hydraulic properties of the bentonite buffer and the swelling pressure. Consequently, an additional swelling into cracks intersecting the deposition holes and into the tunnels will result in higher hydraulic conductivity and lower swelling pressure compared to swelling restricted to the deposition holes.

The swelling pressure will impact the canister and surrounding rock. The canister should be designed to withstand the bentonite swelling pressure. However, the build-up of corrosion products which are more voluminous than the canister material will result in a compression of the bentonite buffer and an increase in swelling pressure.

Swelling of bentonite into a failed canister may have to be considered. This could lead to a reduction in hydraulic and transport resistance in the buffer.

Uneven swelling can occur, but probably represents a transient state (resaturation phase). Deficiences in material structure, cementing etc could cause steady-state imperfections. Uneven swelling could cause preferential pathways or even flow instead of diffusion. Its effect on canister integrity needs to be evaluated.

Influenced by:
The mineralogy and density of the bentonite buffer, and the volume available for buffer expansion will affect the extent of swelling once resaturation of the buffer is initiated.

Affects:
Swelling will affect backfill properties which are important for water and gas transport through the backfill and for radionuclide transport and release. The swelling pressure may also affect the stress field in the nearby rock, and may mechanically impact the canister. Swelling into fractures in the nearby rock will affect the apertures of these fractures.

Modelling aspects:

pfep_description_raw:
General:
If the mechanical supporting properties of the bentonite buffer or tunnel backfill decrease, the mechanical stability of the rock adjacent to deposition holes and tunnels is affected.Loss of mechanical stability may cause movements of rock blocks, and in extreme cases collapse of a deposition hole or a tunnel section.

Influenced by:
The potential for rock blocks caving in is dependent on the swelling ability and swelling pressure of the buffer/backfill. In addition, properties of the near-field rock such as fractures, joints, weaknesses, planes and stress field etc detemines which rock blocks that cave in.

Affects:
Movements of the rock surrounding deposition holes and tunnels may mechanically impact the bentonite buffer, tunnel backfill and canister. In addition it will change the hydraulic properties of the rock.

Modelling aspects:

host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the changes in concentration of radionuclides in the spent fuel components after deposition.

The radionuclide inventory at time of deposition is defined by the initial fuel composition, the conditions in the reactor and the decay time subsequent to discharge of the fuel from the reactor. The inventory of long-lived radionuclides is a function of fuel burn-up. The inventory of long-lived fission products is approximately proportional to the burn-up, whereas the actinides follow other functions of the burn-up.

Most of the radionuclides are incorporated in the matrix of the spent fuel. However, measurements indicate that fractions of fission and activation products are present in cracks in the uranium dioxide matrix and in the gap between fuel and cladding as well as in grain boundaries. Such elements are: I, Cs, Tc, Sb, Mo and possibly Sr. The fraction of the total inventory of I and Cs present in cracks and in the gap is estimated to be less than 10%, and probably of the order of 1%.

Radioactive isotopes of some elements in the metallic components may have to be considered. Examples of such elements are C, Ni, Nb and possibly Zr. 

After deposition, radioactive decay will change the radionuclide inventory. The inventory will also change if the spent fuel inside the canister becomes critical. Criticality will initiate chain reactions and fission products will be formed. An increase in the fission product inventory will influence the subsequent release of these from the fuel.

An analysis of criticality carried out in the KBS-2 study showed that the amount of long-lived radiotoxic nuclides created as a consequence of plutonium criticality is small compared to the already existing inventory in the canister.

Influenced by:
Radioactive decay will affect the radionuclide inventory. In addition, the inventory may change if the spent fuel becomes critical.

Affects:
Radionuclide abundances and distribution in the fuel, grain boundaries and metal parts after canister failure will influence the total release of radionuclides from the fuel.

Modelling aspects:

canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Interactions with components in the groundwater, chemical reactions with dissolved species from canister corrosion and concrete leaching and thermal load may chemically alter the buffer/backfill material and thereby lead to changes in physical and chemical properties. The effects of thermal load are covered in the FEP “Thermal degradation of buffer/backfill material”.

Replacement of sodium in the bentonite by calcium in the water by ion-exchange will lead to a decrease in plasticity and swelling ability of a sodium-based bentonite. Calcium in the water may together with carbonate dissolved from the bentonite form precipitates of calcite. The possibility of this process is highest during the high temperature period since the solubility of calcite decreases with increasing temperature. Precipitation of calcite, cementation, may lead to a blocking of pores in the buffer/backfill and to a reduction in elastic properties.

Copper and iron dissolved during the corrosion of the canisters may interact with the bentonite in the buffer by ion-exchange where sodium is replaced by copper or iron. These processes occur in competition with sodium-calcium exchange, and are expected to have a similar effect on the physical properties of the bentonite buffer as the sodium-calcium exchange. In addition, copper and iron may precipitate in the buffer leading to reduced porosity, but also to a reduction in elastic properties of the buffer.

If the water in contact with the bentonite buffer/backfill is affected by concrete leaching, hydroxide ions in the water may interact with smectite forming zeolites and hydrosilicates which will reduce the elastic properties of the buffer. However, smectite has a high pH-buffering capacity.

Precipitation in the buffer/backfill of elements leached from the spent fuel will reduce the porosity of the buffer and may also cause cementation and reduction in plasticity.

Chemical degradation could also be caused by material deficiences or by unexpected chemical composition of the groundwater.

The ion-exchange properties of bentonite and impurities such as sulphides, sulphates, organic compounds, carbonates, and Fe(II), will influence the chemical composition of the groundwater. This will in turn have impact on the aggressivity of the groundwater on the corroson of the canister. The ion-exchange properties may also be beneficial and have a positive impact in cases where the groundwater chemistry deviates from the standard composition.

Influenced by:
The composition of the water in the buffer/backfill, e.g. concentrtion of calcium, carbonate, potassium, iron, copper, pH etc, will influence chemical alteration of the bentonite buffer/backfill.

Affects:
The result of chemical alteration could be a reduction of swelling capability leading to increased hydraulic conductivity, or cementation and reduction in plasticity which increases the risk for channeling effects. Precipitation in the pores could result in a reduction of the permeability of the material. Chemical alteration will also affect the composition of the water in the buffer/backfill, and the mineralogy of the buffer/backfill.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Coagulation or flocculation is the process by which dispersed clay particles begin to stick together in suspensions. The flocculation may take place due to the addition of a few percent of salt to the clay suspension. The flocculation gives rise to aggregates of clay particles. Large aggregates are influenced by gravity forces and will settle to a bottom sediment.

Flocculation is only expected to take place in a dilute clay-water system (e.g. gel, solution or suspension). Flocculation is mainly favoured by high ion concentrations and by high cation valences.

Although flocculation may change the properties of a bentonite-water system, the buffering capacity in the originally dense bentonite is expected to be damaged mainly by the dilution of the system and not by the subsequent flocculation. In fact, in order to avoid that bentonite particles are dispersed from the buffer into the fractures, it is necessary that the bentonite in the buffer has a sufficient capacity for coagulation (the concentration of coagulating ions exceed the CCC (Critical Coagulation Concentration)).

Influenced by:
Coagulation of clay particles in the buffer/backfill is dependent on the density of the buffer/backfill and the ionic strength of the buffer/backfill porewater.

Affects:
Coagulation of dispersed clay particles will affect the sedimentation of clay particles and thus limit the erosion of the buffer/backfill.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Colloids are particles in the size range between 1 and 100 nm. They may sorb or otherwise include radionuclides in the groundwater.

Colloids are always present in deep groundwaters; measured concentrations are generally less than 1 mg/l. They are of both organic and inorganic origin. Possible sources of specific significance for a deep geological repository in crystalline rock are the presence of gradients in groundwater composition leading to precipitation (e.g. as a result of changes in redox potential and pH) and erosion (dispersion) of clay minerals. Under extreme external conditions (e.g. glaciations, faulting) transients in colloid concentration might occur.

Depending on composition and physico-chemical characteristics (e.g. size distribution, surface potential etc) colloids are transported more or less with the same velocity as the groundwater. Reversible sorption of radionuclides on particles in the larger size range is of less importance, and probably also for colloids in the smallest size range (the formation of such colloids should be reversible and sorption of them considerable). “Irreversible sorption” on and transport with colloids in the intermediate range might be of some importance for certain radionuclides. Until this problem has been further studied these statements are to be regarded as speculations, however.

Influenced by:
The water composition (e.g. pH, ionic strength), the presence of interfaces between different water compositions, and microbial activity may influence colloid generation and stability in the near-field and far-field rock. In addition, chemical alteration of flow paths may generate colloidal fractions of secondary fracture minerals, and faulting may mechanically liberate colloidal fractions of rock minerals. In the near-field rock, degradation of reinforcement and grouting materials may act as colloid sources and so may the bentonite buffer/backfill. The transport of colloids in the rock is affected by the fracture/pore characteristics (filtering effects) and the magnitude of the groundwater flow.

Affects:
Colloid generation and transport may affect the transport of radionuclides from the repository.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
The bentonite buffer/backfill may contain, or produce, particles small enough to follow the water in colloidal form, especially in case of non-filled cavities. Colloidal fractions could be formed as a consequence of erosion of the buffer/backfill. In addition, microbes in the buffer/backfill or substances produced by microbes may form aggregates which may act as mobile species.

Colloids generated in the buffer/backfill may act as carriers for radionuclides and thereby affect the radionuclide transport from the repository. However, the filtering capacity of the buffer/backfill may be strong enough to restrict colloid transport through the buffer/backfill. In such cases, colloid generation at the interface buffer/backfill and near-field rock is most important.

Influenced by:
Erosion and microbial activity in the buffer/backfill, as well as the composition of the water in the buffer/backfill will affect colloid generation and stability. The presence of interfaces between different water compositions, e.g. a redox front, may also generate colloids.

Affects:
A buffer/backfill acting as a colloid source will affect the transport in the near-field rock of colloids and radionuclides attached to the colloids.

Colloid generation inside the canister may affect the radionuclide release from the canister. If the colloids/particles are able to escape through the failed canister, they may increase the nuclide release. If they are not mobile, they will decrease the release from the canister.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to general corrosion, localised corrosion (pitting), crevice corrosion, galvanic corrosion, stress corrosion, etc. of the copper canister.

Copper is thermodynamically stable in pure water, but may corrode by the action of certain dissolved species in groundwater. Such species are oxygen, chloride, sulphide and sulphate. In the presence of oxygen, protective layers of copper oxides is formed on the copper surface, preventing any further general corrosion. If the water also contains high chloride concentrations, the oxidised copper may form charged chloride complexes that appears in solution. Under such conditions it is possible that no solid, protective layer is formed on the copper surface, which then could be exposed to general corrosion.

In an oxygen-free environment copper is corroded by sulphides and sulphates forming cuprous sulphides. Corrosion by direct sulphate attack is kinetically hindered for temperatures below 100°C, and the extent of such corrosion will also be limited by the amount of available ferrous iron. However, sulphate may be reduced to sulphide by microorganisms provided that a carbon source is available.

Localised corrosion could occur in the presence of oxygen due to differences in microchemistry at the copper surface. Anions like chloride, sulphate and nitrate can initiate and propagate local corrosion. In an oxygen-free environment containing dissolved, reduced sulphur species the growth of copper sulphide on the copper surface might take place at specific locations to form outgrowths, “whiskers”, using copper from underneath the base of the whisker. The reason for this is the high mobility of copper in the copper sulphide formed. 

Estimates assuming general corrosion indicates life-times considerably higher than 1 My for a canister wall thickness of 100 mm. Passivation of parts of the metal surface as well as inhomogeneities in the surrounding bentonite buffer could cause localised (pitting) corrosion. In KBS-3 the corrosion rate for localised corrosion was assumed to be 5 to 25 times higher than the average corrosion rate. In Project-90, a pitting factor of 5 was assumed.

Stress corrosion of copper may occur in the presence of nitric compounds, ammonia and chloride.

Galvanic corrosion may occur due to temperature differences on the canister surface.

After failure of the steel canister aggressive components in the waste (iodine and bromide and possibly also Se and Te) may corrode copper.

Corrosion may lead to failure of the copper canister and subsequent water intrusion and corrosion of the inner stel vessel. It will also form corrosion products which due to swelling mechanically may impact the canister and the surrounding bentonite buffer.

Influenced by:
The composition of the water in contact with the copper canister in terms of concentration of corrosive agents and corrosion products, pH and Eh will affect the corrosion mechanism and the corrosion rate. Electrochemical gradients in the canister and in the surrounding buffer may also have implications on the corrosion mechanism and rate. The temperature will influence the corrosion rate and mechanical impact on the canister may cause stress corrosion.

Affects:
Corrosion of the copper canister will influence the physical and chemical characteristics of the canister and the composition of the water in the surrounding buffer and also inside the canister after failure of the copper canister. Solid corrosion products formed may occupy a larger volume than the metal exposed to corrosion which means that the corrosion mechanism and rate affect the degree of volume expansion.

ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert,

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the corrosion of metal components of the fuel such as zirkaloy cladding (and fuel boxes), and spacers, springs, grids etc of stainless steel and inconel after canister failure.

After water intrusion in the inner steel canister the metal components may be subjected to hydrogen evolving corrosion. The presence of oxide or hydroxide layers may act as a passivating layer thereby reducing the corrosion rate. However, the stability of the passivating layer may be time-limited. In addition, a build-up of a hydrogen pressure inside the canister may suppress the corrosion rate. The temperature inside the canister and the water composition will affect the corrosion rate and the type of corrosion products formed. Species which may influence the corrosion of steel are carbonate, chloride, sulphate and nitrate.

Iodine induced stress corrosion cracking of cladding and crevice corrosion of spacers/cladding interface may also take place.

Influenced by:
The composition of the water in contact with the metal components in terms of the concentration of corrosive agents, corrosion products, pH, Eh etc, and the temperature may affect the corrosion mechanism and rate. Electrochemical gradients between different metals may also have implications on the corrosion mechanism and rate.The hydrogen pressure inside the canister may influence the rate of hydrogen evolving corrosion, and mechanical impact on the canister may cause stress corrosion.

Affects:
Corrosion of metal parts in the waste will liberate radionuclides deposited on the metal surfaces (CRUD) as well as activation products induced in the metal components. In addition, corrosion of the zircaloy cladding may increase the contact area between intruding water and fuel matrix, increasing the release rate of nuclides in the fuel and the extent of radiolysis. The corrosion of metal parts may also contribute to the hydrogen generation in the canister. Dissolved corrosion products may influence the water chemistry in the canister, e.g. concentration of multivalent metal ions and redox potential.

project_title: SKI SITE-94 Deep Repository Performance Assessment Project
host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to the corrosion of the outer surface of the steel vessel after failure and water penetration through the copper canister, and corrosion of the inner surface of the steel vessel after failure and water penetartion through the steel vessel. It includes general corrosion, local corrosion (pitting), stress corrosion, internal corrosion caused by components in the fuel, galvanic corrosion due to the presence of copper, crevice corrosion etc.

Steel surfaces in contact with water will be subjected to corrosion. If oxygen is present it will cause oxidation and dissolution of iron from the steel and the formation of iron oxides. Hydrogen evolving corrosion will occur in the absence of oxygen. The build-up of a hydrogen pressure is likely to suppress the corrosion rate.

The presence of oxide or hydroxide layers may act as a passivating layer thereby reducing the corrosion rate. However, the stability of the passivating layer may be time-limited.The temperature inside the canister and the water composition will affect the corrosion rate and the type of corrosion products formed. Species which may influence the corrosion of steel are carbonate, chloride, sulphate, sulphide and nitrate. Carbonates may have a catalytic effect on steel corrosion by acting as proton-donators. In oxidising environments, chloride can act as an initiator for localised corrosion, and in anaerobic systems passivating oxide layers are less stable in the presence of chloride. Sulphate may act as an oxidising agent in anaerobic environments, but is not readily reduced. However, sulphate may be reduced to sulphide by microbial activity, provided that a carbon source is available, causing an oxidation  and dissolution of iron. In similarity to sulphate and sulphide, nitrate may be reduced by carbon steel in anaerobic solutions.

Aggressive components in the fuel (iodine, bromide and possibly also Se and Te) may cause corrosion. The effect can be estimated from the content of such components in the fuel.

The presence of copper could influence the corrosion rate of the steel since the cathodic, water reduction reaction could take place also on the copper surface. A coupling of roughly equal areas of the two metals would lead to a doubling of the steel corrosion rate in the gap between copper canister and steel vessel. The effect on the interior steel surfaces is probably smaller.
 
Corrosion attack on the outside of the steel vessel will eventually lead to failure of the steel vessel. Formed corrosion products may due to their larger volume enlarge the defect in the copper canister.

Influenced by:
The composition of the water in contact with the steel vessel in terms of the concentration of corrosive agents, corrosion products, pH, Eh etc, and the temperature may affect the corrosion mechanism and rate. Electrochemical gradients in the canister may also have implications on the corrosion mechanism and rate.The hydrogen pressure inside the canister may influence the rate of hydrogen evolving corrosion, and mechanical impact on the canister may cause stress corrosion.

Affects:
Corrosion of the steel vessel will influence the physical and chemical characteristics of the canister and the composition of the water in the canister and surrounding buffer. Solid corrosion products formed may occupy a larger volume than the metal exposed to corrosion which means that the corrosion mechanism and rate affect the degree of volume expansion, and thus the mechanical impact on the canister. The corrosion mechanism and rate will affect the amounts of gas generated and the gas pressure in the canister.

Corrosion continuing after failure of the steel vessel affect the amount of water in contact with the fuel and the transport characteristics inside the copper canister which are of importance to the release of nuclides from the fuel and from the canister.

host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the corrosion of metal components of the fuel, such as spacers, springs, grids etc of stainless steel and inconel, and corrosion of the steel vessel prior to water penetration into the copper canister.

Prior to water intrusion into the copper canister and inner steel canister, the metals may react with oxygen in the air in the steel canister and in the gap between steel and copper canister forming solid, protective layers of oxides or hydroxides on the metal surfaces. After the oxygen is consumed a high relative humidity of the air may cause hydrogen evolving corrosion of the metal surfaces exposed to the water. Alternatively, the metal components may be subjected to corrosion by nitrous and nitric acids which may be formed by radiolysis of the water in the air. In addition, the metal components may corrode due to reaction with ammonia formed by radiolysis of a mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen inside the canister. However, ammonia is not generated unless hydrogen is formed either by corrosion or by radiolytic decomposition of the water initially present in the air.

By filling the canister with an inert gas like He or Ar before sealing, the initial amount of air is reduced. This reduces the fraction of the radiation absorbed by nitrogen, oxygen and water and thereby also the rate of conversion to nitric acid.

Corrosion prior to wetting will probably be localised to surfaces where water vapour may condens, i.e. the coldest parts. Since the initial water content in the steel vessel and in the gap between the steel vessel and the copper canister is small, local attack prior to wetting will probably not by itself lead to cracking of the steel vessel, but the mechanical properties of the vessel may change.

Influenced by:
Corrosion of the metal parts in the canister and of the canister materials before canister failure is influenced by the presence of oxygen, nitric acid formed by radiolysis of moist air and by condensed water vapour.

Affects:
Corrosion prior to canister failure will affect the chemical and physical properties of the components exposed to corrosion. this may have implications for the mechanical stability of the canister and for the corrosion and radionuclide release processes occuring after canister failure.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Creeping of rock mass occur in connection with excavation due to stress changes. These changes create an unstable situation in the rock mass close to the repository. However, this effect is probably of minor importance.

The ongoing plate motion induces creep in the rock to a certain extent. This creates rock stresses that are released through continuous or discontinuous movements (by sudden stress releases e.g. earthquakes). The latter may be the end effect of creep. Creeping of rock mass is a continuously ongoing process. Creep should only be related to already formed discontinuities.

Creep will change the rock properties and thereby groundwater flow through fractures. If channelling exists, slow ongoing movements can change position of channeling flow. It may also affect the buffer and backfill materials mechanically.

Influenced by:
Rock creep is affected by stress changes in the rock.

Affects:
Rock creep will affect fracture density and apertures in the rock, and may also cause stress changes in the rock. Another consequence of rock creep could be a mechanical impact on the buffer and canister, and on the tunnel backfill.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
If voids inside or outside of the canisters are present, and the canisters are exposed to internal pressure and/or external forces, the canister material may creep into these voids. If tension stresses are formed in the material during manufacturing, these stresses might be reliefed by creeping of the material.

Creep may lead to deformation of the canister, and potentially also creep failure, provided that tensile forces are present in the material. Coppers ductility for creep are yet not known to full extent but can be limited to deformations to a few percent. Especially the welding zone is sensitive for creep since this small area is subject to heavy heat changes during manufacturing of the canister.

Influenced by:
Creep of the copper and steel canister are influenced by mechanical impact on the canister caused by internal or external forces. The temperature may also affect creep of the canister materials.

Affects:
Creep of the canister may lead to deformation of the canister and reduction in the mechanical strength of the canister.

host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)

copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Spent fuel contains fissile isotopes, principally Pu-239 and U-235. If fuel is accumulated in an uncontrolled manner a chain rection may start and the fuel becomes critical. Whether criticality can occur depends on the concentration of fissile isotopes, the amount and geometry of the accumulated fuel and the availability of neutron moderating material, e.g. water.

To avoid an unfavourable geometry and thereby minimise the criticality risk, spacers are used to separate the fuel elements when placed in the canisters. The initial geometry may, however, change if the zirkaloy cladding is degraded to such an extent that the fuel pellets can accumulate in the bottom of the canister. The amount of water in contact with the accumulated fuel is dependent on the properties of the failed canister in terms of amount of filling material and corrosion products.

Plutonium criticality would call for selective dissolution and out-transport of uranium before most of the Pu has decayed to U-235, i.e. within approximately 100 000 years after disposal. The enrichment of the uranium initially present in the spent fuel is low, but in-growth from decay of Pu-239 will increase the fraction of U-235 to a level where  criticality theoretically is possible. However, the critical mass of uranium is large, 4 400 kg.

Influenced by:
Accumulation of fuel pellets, e.g. due to degradation of zirkaloy cladding, or selective leaching of urnaium over plutonium will affect the possibility of obtaining a critical mass. The amount of water entering the canister will also affect the possibility of the spent fuel to become critical.

Affects:
Criticality would impact the radionuclide inventory and thermal behaviour of the repository.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Saline water is often present at repository depth and at larger depths. Changes in groundwater salinity will influence chemical equilibria, and salinity gradients may be of importance for groundwater flow.

Saline water can be both of recent marine origin or it might occur as a result of release of salt from the rock itself. Intrusion of saline water in significant amounts could occur during the resaturation phase, and in connection with prolonged glaciations and the subsequent subsidence.

The intrusion of saline water will affect the groundwater chemistry in the geosphere and in the repository. Some chemical elements form soluble complexes with chloride which may influence the solubility and sorption of radionuclides. High salinity may also affect the stability of buffer materials as well as the stability of colloids. In addition, the formation of sharp interfaces between saline and fresh groundwaters should be considered in terms of effects on both geochemical processes and groundwater flow.

Influenced by:
Intrusion of saline water is influenced by the origin of the saline water and the groundwater flow.

Affects:
Saline water intrusion implies changing density gradients and changing groundwater flow. Location of discharge areas may alter. In addition, the water chemitry may be affected, and sharp interfaces between saline and fresh water may be established.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the degradation and potential change in chemical and physical properties of the spent fuel and cladding after canister emplacement. Destruction of the fuel structure and cladding may increase the fuel surface exposed to water penetrating a failed canister. This will affect both the extent of radiolysis and the release of radionuclides from the spent fuel. Extensive degradation of the cladding could result in an accumulation of fuel pellets in the canister. The possibility that such accumulation of fuel pellets results in a critical mass should be avoided by an appropriate canister design.

Influenced by:
The fuel could be altered by high-energy alpha particles and by transmutation. Local pressure build-up of helium from radioactive decay and hydrogen from radiolysis could cause cracking/fragmentation of the fuel and cladding. Furthermore, the integrity of the cladding could be compromised by corrosion and by gamma and neutron flux from decaying radionuclides in the fuel.

Affects:
Cracking and fragmentation of the fuel may create paths through which I and Cs could migrate from the fuel matrix to the surface. In addition, cracking and fragmentation of the fuel could increase the contact area between fuel and intruding water thereby affecting the release of radionuclides from grain boundaries and the dissolution of radionuclides in the fuel matrix as well as the amount of water exposed to radiolysis.

Modelling aspects:

pfep_name_mapping_raw: Degradation of rock reinforcement and grout
pfep_name_profep_raw: Degradation of rock reinforcement and grout
pfep_name: Degradation of rock reinforcement and grout
pfep_description_raw:
General:
During excavation, the rock around the tunnel is reinforced and inflow of water is sealed off by grouting in order to establish a secure environment during the operation phase. In the long-term perspective one does not rely on rock reinforcements and grout. The question is instead to minimise foreign material which could endanger the function of the barriers (rock mass, bentonite etc.).

Grout and reinforcement materials could be concrete (shotcrete) and steel. Leaching of concrete will increase the concentration of calcium and hydroxide ions in the water. These ions may react with magnesium and carbonate in the water to form precipitates of calcite and brucite in fractures and pores in the rock or in the buffer/backfill, but also in the concrete material itself. Increased concentration of calcium may also affect the properties of the buffer/backfill by ion-exchange with sodium.

Concrete may react with sulphate in the water to form the swelling mineral ettringite and with chloride in the water to form calcium chloro aluminate hydrates. If these reactions occur the concentration of sulphate and chloride in the intruding groundwater may be lowered.

Corrosion of steel material used as reinforcement may lead to hydrogen formation and solid corrosion products which may lead to blocking of pores/fractures in the adjacent backfill material and rock.

Influenced by:
The degradation of rock reinforcements and grout is affected by the groundwater chemistry, the temperature and the stress in the rock.

Affects:
Degradation of rock reinforcements and grout affects the water chemistry in the rock (dissolved species and potentially also amount of colloids), as well as the mechanical properties and permeability of the rock. Corrosion of steel reinforcements may generate gas.

Modelling aspects:

copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
This FEP refers to diffusion in clay and diffusion in water-filled fractures in the rock.

Diffusion as a fundamental transport process will certainly not require any comments. On the other hand, the underlying mechanisms must be understood so that the beneficial and/or detrimental effects of diffusion processes can be judged and so that laboratory measurements can be interpreted and the results used to model the in situ diffusion process.

When using laboratory measured sorption coefficients, Kd-values, to estimate diffusion of different elements in samples of bentonite clay and granitic rock, it has been observed that certain cations like Cs+ and Sr2+ moves faster than expected. This phenomena has been referred to as “surface diffusion”, and it has been necessary to take the effect into account when calculating diffusion rates to be used in performance assessment.

The mechanisms for the hitherto observed cases of “surface diffusion” is not yet fully understood. However, it seems unlikely that the observed phenomenon actually involves movement of ions or molecules that are really sorbed upon mineral surfaces. A more plausible explanation seems to be that cations which can take part in an ion exchange process are not “sorbed” at any specific sites at the mineral surface - they occupy the charged layer in the vicinity of the surface and are thus still highly mobile. The ion mobility in this layer is in fact lower than in ordinary water due to its higher viscosity. Also, the state of surface (or inter-layer) water depends on the clay density, e.g. as described by the water sorption isotherm (which directly gives the swelling pressure). In order to more fully understand this mechanism the interpretation of diffusion data must also take into account the dependence of observed (“apparent”) distribution coefficient on e.g. ionic strength, the state of surface water and free water porosity. A multiphase model might be developed and tested.

Influenced by:
The pore (fracture) characteristics, the water content and the water composition (ionic strength) affect the diffusive flux of species in bentonite and rock materials. The ionic strength of the water affects the characteristics of the electric double layer adjacent to the mineral surfaces which in turn have implications both for anion exclusion and surface diffusion effects on the diffusive mass transport.

Affects:
Diffusion affects the water chemistry in the different barriers and the mass transport of radionuclides from the repository.

Modelling aspects:
In order to perform a logical analysis of the behaviour of certain barriers development, e.g. during chemical and physical degradation, it is necessary to use a model that more in detail describes all aspects of diffusion - including “surface diffusion” and effects of anion exclusion. Alternatively, diffusion parameters for the instationary phase should be evaluated from instationary experiments and diffusion parameters for the stationary phase from experiments under stationary conditions. In this way indirect determinations of the diffusivity under stationary conditions using questionable values of the Kd are avoided.

pfep_name_mapping_raw: Diffusion in and through failed canister
pfep_name_profep_raw: Diffusion in and through failed canister
pfep_name: Diffusion in and through failed canister
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to the diffusion inside the canister and out through the failed canister of elements dissolved from the fuel and other dissolved species in the water inside the canister, as well as the indiffusion of dissolved species from the water in the bentonite buffer surrounding the canister.

This process will influence the release of radionuclides from the fuel as well as affect the water chemistry in the failed canister and in the surrounding bentonite buffer. The flux of dissolved species in and out from the canister by diffusion is influenced by the physical properties of the failed canister such as internal void volume and size of hole/breach.

The driving force for this transport mechanism is a concentration gradient and the release of elements from the fuel and the water chemistry in the canister and in the surrounding bentonite will therefore also influence the diffusion flux. In addition, the diffusivity is temperature dependent.

Influenced by:
The diffusive mass transport inside and out from the canister is influenced by the concentration gradients, the physical properties of the canister and the temperature.

Affects:
Diffusion will affect the release rate of radionuclides from the canister as well as the water chemistry in the canister and in the surrounding buffer.

Modelling aspects:

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to the potential lowering of the density of the buffer and backfill.

An extensive swelling of the bentonite buffer into surrounding cavities, such as tunnels and cracks, could result in a lowering of the density of the buffer. Swelling of the buffer into voids in the canister after canister failure may also result in a lowering of the density of the buffer. Erosion of the buffer and the backfill where bentonite particles are carried away by flowing groundwater is another process which may lead to dilution of the buffer and backfill.

Dilution will change the hydraulic and transport properties of the buffer and backfill in terms of increasing the hydraulic conductivity. An extensive dilution may also lead to inhomogeneities in the material causing preferential pathways for water and nuclide transport. In addition, the ability of the buffer to mechanically protect the canister may be decreased.

Influenced by:
Dilution of the buffer/backfill is influenced by the volume available for expansion and by the extent of erosion of the buffer backfill.

Affects:
A reduction in density of the buffer/backfill will affect the hydraulic and mechanical properties of the buffer backfill.

Modelling aspects:

pfep_description_raw:
General:
More or less regardless of the level of detail used in the description of the flow field there will always remain velocity variations that cannot be described explicitly in an advection term. The spreading of radionuclides by means of diffusion and these unresolved velocity variations could generally be denoted by the term dispersion.

Influenced by:
Dispersion is affected by the water velocity distribution and by mixing between flowpaths.

Affects:
Dispersion affects the distribution in solute travel times.

Modelling aspects:
Obviously, the actual definition of dispersion is directly related to the used definition of the advection. In some instances it is possible to relate the dispersion to a given statistical structure of the permeability field. However, the great uncertainty with regard to the spatial structure of crystalline rocks also implies great uncertainty on the dispersion. Description of large scale dispersion is thus best handled by detailed hydrogeological models such as discrete fracture network models or stochastic continuum models.

For extreme channeling, dispersion cannot be described as a Fickian process, not even for one-dimensional flow. It has been suggested (in KBS-3) that channeling could be decribed with a constant Peclet number implying that the dispersivity will increase with travel distance. However, transport with extreme channeling is not at all dispersive, it is skewed to the fast flow paths. Using a constant Peclet number is correct only for the first two moments of a breakthrough curve whereas higher order moments will differ.

In performance assessments radionuclide migration is usually modelled with sets of one dimensional streamtubes. In such models the dispersion term is usually of less importance than the ratio between flow wetted surface and darcy velocity.

pfep_name: Distribution and release of nuclides from the geosphere
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to the transport of radionuclides in the geosphere and the release of radionuclides from the geosphere to the biosphere. The nuclide transport and release is influenced by the the release from the near-field and the retardation in the geosphere.

Prior to estimating the flux of nuclides to the biosphere, the knowledge of the distribution (concentration) of nuclides in the entire geosphere is needed, e.g. for intrusion scenarios. 

Influenced by:
The radionuclide transport and release from the geosphere may be influenced by:
- the radionuclide release from the near-field rock,
- groundwater flow and dispersion in the far-field rock,
- diffusion, matrix diffusion, sorption/desorption, and precipitation/dissolution of radionuclides in the far-field rock,
- radioactive decay,
- gas flow and transport in the far-field rock,
- colloid generation and transport in the far-field rock,
- electrochemical gradients (Telluric currents) in the geosphere (far-field rock) which may affect the distribution and release of charged nuclides by electro-osmosis or electro-phoresis,

Affects:
The release of radionuclides from the far-field rock affects the subsequent transport of radionuclides in the biosphere. The distribution of radionuclides in the far-field rock may affect the consequences of intrusion scenarios.

Modelling aspects:

General:
Refers to the phenomenon under which the small changes of the gravitational field due to celestial movements (sun and moon) cause pressure variations in the groundwater flow systems. 

Tidal pressure variations may cause a pulsating exchange of water between fractures and the rock matrix. A substance transported by the fracture flow system would be sequentially pumped into and flushed out of the matrix during a tidal cycle. However, due to the irreversibility of hydrodynamic dispersion, some tracer would be retained in the matrix.

Tidal pressure variations may also occur within the plane of a fracture due to lateral variations in fracture stiffness. The corresponding pressure gradients may enhance especially lateral dispersion.

Influenced by:
Earth tides are influenced by the celestial movements.

Affects:
Earth tides could influence groundwater flow and matrix diffusion (pumping effect).

project_title: SKI SITE-94 Deep Repository Performance Assessment Project
host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Electrochemical gradients may be established in the canister after failure due to the presence of different metals in canister and waste (copper, steel, zirkaloy). Electrochemical effects may also arise from different local micro-environments (e.g. Eh, pH) on the surface of the same metal barrier.

Natural currents occurring in the ground, known as “telluric currents”, may also create electrochemical gradients. The major source of telluric currents is related to the solar activity, which creates ionospheric currents around the earth, in relation to its magnetic field. These currents are random, and cover a large range of frequencies. The frequencies below 1 Hz have a penetration depth which exceeds the repository depth and therefore they need to be considered. Telluric currents also follow the solar activity (with the 11 year cycle) and have the same origin a the “polar lights”.

At repository and since crystalline rocks are mostly resistors, the flow of the electric currents will take place in the water conducting fractures, and will be “channelised” by the conducting argillaceous material introduced into the repository as buffer and backfill. They will also use the long copper canisters as preferential pathways. It is thus necessary to study their role in corrosion studies, e.g. pit corrosion, since the circulation of the current in the water conducting fractures will concentrate them to restricted areas of the canister, where they may increase the corrosion rate and pitting factors; this effect may be one reason why the pitting factor of metal is a function of the size of the object (a small coin does not have the same pitting factor as a large bronze cannon).

It is also of interest to investigate the possible changes of these solar ionospheric currents in the future, e.g. if they have other cycles than the 11-year one, or what can happen when the magnetic pole of the earth vanishes and becomes inverted (a phenomenon that occurred several times in the past and is used as a geological clock; the next magnetic pole inversion is predicted to occur in approximately 200 000 years, i.e. within the time frame of a repository performance assessment).

If these currents are quantified, their potential impact on corrosion rates and transport enhancement by electro-osmosis (dissolved species) or electro-phoresis (particulates) could be assessed by a preliminary calculation, to see if they should be included in the scenarios.

Influenced by:
The establishment of electrochemical gradients in the canister is influenced by the presence of different metals and by the presence of different local micro-environments (e.g. Eh, pH) on the surface of the same metal barrier. The distribution of water and differences/inhomogeneities in mineralogic distribution as well as the water chemistry affect electrochemical gradients in the buffer/backfill and the rock.

Affects:
Electrochemical gradients may influence corrosion of the canister materials and the zirkaloy cladding and affect the mobility of charged radionuclide species (by electro-osmosis) and particulates (by electrophoresis) in the barriers.

host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
