copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Solid material in buffer and backfill is carried away by flowing groundwater. This process should be distinguished from chemical dissolution, which of course can occur simultaneously.

Release of particulates in the “normal” situation is very unlikely. For normal groundwater compositions this may only occur for very high flowrates. Flowrate criteria may be available. High flowrates may be caused by events such as earthquakes, glaciations etc, most of which are of a transient nature. The effect of temperature may be important.

Another cause for release of solid clay particles seems to be connected to change in water chemistry that gives abnormally low salt content (ionic strength); distilled water gives suspensions of bentonite. Criteria for groundwater can be developed.

Preceding or simultaneous chemical alteration of the clay might of course influence the situation.

Erosion might impair the barrier in question. Redistribution of eroded material into fractures in the nearby rock may change the properties of the fractures. In addition, the eroding clay may act as an “engineered” source of colloids.

Influenced by:
Erosion of the buffer/backfill is influenced by the goundwater flow in the rock surrounding the buffer/backfill, and by the extent of coagulation of bentonite particles in the buffer/backfill.

Affects:
Erosion may locally “dilute” the buffer/backfill and may liberate of colloidal particles which could be transported by groundwater flow in the rock.

host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Excavating a repository in hard crystalline rock implies that there will be a volume of the rock that will be affected by the excavation, operation and sealing operations. The rock mass will be disturbed, it will be altered in an immediate and possibly time dependent way due to the excavation process (e.g. drilling, blasting) and by the stress redistribution resulting from removal of constraint round the system. This may result in new fractures, reactivation of healed fractures or displacements on preceeding fractures. This also modifies the hydraulic conditions in the surrounding of the excavated rock mass. The impact of excavation damage will possibly create a zone of enhanced radial or longitudinal hydraulic conductivity. This zone could provide a preferential pathway for radionuclide migration to the prevailing system of groundwater flow. This zone of disturbance has to be taken into account when sealing the different parts of the repository. Also the introduction of air (and decreased pressure possibly resulting in degassing) may alter the groundwater flow in the vicinity of the tunnel.

The extent of rock disturbance depends on the excavation methods used. The highest amount of damage is expected in the floor of a tunnel excavated with the drill and blast technique. If blasting is used, gas will be generated.

Influenced by:
The excavation method will affect the effects of excavation on the nearby rock.

Affects:
The excavation will affect the stress situation in the surrounding rock and the properties of the rock, e.g. fracture density and apertures.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Faulting may occur due to sudden major changes in the stress situation, e.g. earthquakes etc, and due to slow motions (creep) in the rock mass, e.g. orogenic events, loading-unloading of an ice-load, and plate motions. The result of the release of stress may be the formation of a fracture, and if movement occurs along the fracture, a fault. A more likely event is movement along already existing fractures and faults.

Faulting may alter the rock permeability in the rock mass and alter or short-circuit the flow paths and flow distributions close to the repository and create new pathways through the repository. New or regenerated faults may enhance the groundwater flow, destabilise and damage engineered barriers, thus decreasing the transport times for potentially released radionuclides. 

It has also been shown that fractures due to ice loads may be affected not always by displacement along the fracture, but through a variation of the opening of the fracture. The result in that case would be a modification of the permeability distribution in the rock mass.

Existing faults may also act as hydraulic squeeze pumps when exposed by forces of an earthquake or a moving ice-sheet. Such a mechanism could introduce oxidising waters into the repository area and/or propel radionuclide migration from a repository.

Influenced by:
Stress changes in the rock could lead to faulting.

Affects:
Faulting affects the mechanical stability of the rock and the fracture density and fracture apertures. Faulting might also mechanically liberate particles/colloids which can be transported by moving groundwater.

Modelling aspects:
The displacement and movements of already existing faults/fractures can be analysed with mechanical discrete fracture models. To study the formation of new faults/fractures, a rock mechanical model incorporating rock failure models and criteria could be used to pinpoint location and geometry of newly formed faults/fractures.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Flow through the buffer/backfill may occur as a consequence of changes in the hydraulic properties due to chemical and physical degradation. In addition, gas generation may create pressure gradients which will cause water to flow through the materials and so will differences in temperature. Preferential flowpaths could be created as a result of cementation and fracturing of the material and various chemical and physical degradation processes could lead to reduction of the overall resistance to flow. Flow could also occur as a consequence of initial deficiences in the material.

Flow through the buffer/backfill will enhance the exchange of dissolved species between the water in the near-field rock and the water in the buffer/backfill. This may increase the chemical degradation rate of the buffer/backfill. Preferential pathways in the materials may locally expose the copper canister to corrosive agents thereby inducing localised corrosion. After canister failure, flow through the buffer will increase the transport rate of dissolved radionuclides and other non-radioactive elements from the canister interior. 

Influenced by:
The hydraulic properties, gas generation and flow, and the temperature and hydraulic gradients in the buffer/backfill will influence water flow through the buffer/backfill.

Affects:
Flow through the buffer/backfill may affect the water chemistry and the transport and release of radionuclides from the buffer/backfill. Initially after repository closure, flow through the backfill may affect the resaturation of the bentonite buffer, and flow through the backfill may also affect the dispersion of radionuclides transported by the water flowing in the backfill.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the dissolution and conversion of the uranium oxide matrix when water penetrating the canister comes in contact with the fuel surface. As a consequence uranium will be dissolved and elements incorporated in the fuel matrix will be liberated. 

If the water coming in contact with the fuel matrix is free of oxidants the rate of uranium dissolution is governed by the rate of uranium transport away from the fuel surface and the solubility of UO2 in the water adjacent to the fuel surface.

If the water in contact with the fuel contains oxidants, e.g. from radiolysis, oxidation of the uranium dioxide may occur. How far this oxidation proceeds depends on the amount of oxidants available. An oxidation to U4O9 or U3O7 can take place without changing the crystal structure of the fuel matrix. This 
will probably mean that the rate of fuel dissolution still is determined by the transport of uranium away from the surface and the solubility of the oxide in the water adjacent to the fuel surface.

An oxidation of the fuel to a higher oxidation stage, such as U3O8, UO3 or some other U(VI) compound, may disrupt the crystal structure of the fuel. This will probably not change the mechanism for uranium dissolution. However, the liberation of elements incorporated in the fuel is probably determined by the rate of fuel conversion instead of being determined by the dissolution of uranium.

Influenced by:
The chemistry of the water coming in contact with the fuel surface and the temperature in the canister will influence the dissolution/conversion of the fuel matrix. In addition, sorption of uranium onto canister corrosion products and filling materials in the canister as well as release of uranium from the canister will affect the concentration of uranium close to the fuel surface and thus also the fuel dissolution/conversion rate.

Affects:
Dissolution/conversion of the fuel matrix will affect the liberation of uranium and elements incorporated in the fuel matrix. Fuel conversion may affect the  available surface area at the water-fuel interface and thereby the accumulation of alpha-sources. In addition, oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions of the UO2 matrix will affect the redox conditions in the canister.

Modelling aspects:
Predictions of the dissolution of spent uranium fuel could be done by a chemical kinetics modelling approach, assuming surface-reaction control and explicitely accounting for formation of alteration/secondary phases and feedback from the evolving composition of the coexisting solution. This approach permits the integration of fuel dissolution with other near-field processes (e.g. diffusional transport, sorption) to model early, transient dissolution behaviour. However, the long-term, steady-state dissolution rate is constrained to be derived from an empirical fit of shorter-term laboratory data. Accordingly, the predictive capability of such detailed, kinetic models for long-term fuel dissolution analysis is problematical. However, the approach clarifies the importance of formation of alteration phases at the surface of the fuel. These phases control the subsequent concentration of most radionuclides released from the fuel.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the partial, but rapid release of some soluble elements (e.g. I, Cs) present in cracks in the fuel and in the gap between fuel and cladding after canister failure. It also concerns the release of elements potentially present in grain boundaries in the fuel matrix (e.g. Cs, I, Tc, Sb, Mo, Sr). The grain boundary release is slower than the release from gap and cracks in the fuel, but faster than the release of radionuclides incorporated in the fuel matrix.

Experiments have shown selective leaching of Cs, Sb, Tc and Mo from spent fuel under reducing conditions. This has been interpreted as an indication that these elements are present in inclusions, cracks or fissures in the fuel or in grain boundaries.

The cumulative release of Cs and I to groundwater is of the same order as the fission gas release from the fuel (about 1% in the SKB programme reference fuel).

Influenced by:
The gap and grain boundary release is influenced by the chemical and physical properties of the fuel and the distribution of radionuclides at the time of deposition, as well as by additional alteration of the fuel structure after deposition.

Affects:
Enhanced release of fractions of some radionuclides compared to the release by dissolution of the fuel matrix.

copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the escape through failed copper canister of hydrogen gas formed in the gap between copper canister and steel vessel as well as the escape of gas from the interior of the steel vessel after failure.

Gas will leave the failed canister and accumulate in any voids present between the canister and the surrounding bentonite buffer. Major gas escape will, however, probably not take place until the internal over-pressure exceeds the “critical pressure” for opening up gas channels in the surrounding bentonite buffer. This pressure is in average equal to the hydrostatic pressure plus an additional pressure which is in the range 60 to 90% of the buffer swelling pressure. If this critical pressure is not reached, gas may leave in dissolved form by diffusion or water exchange. Gas escape will lower the internal pressure allowing water to enter the failed canister when the internal pressure has decreased below the surrounding hydrostatic pressure.

Influenced by:
The internal gas pressure and the extent of gas flow and transport through the surrounding bentonite buffer will affect the gas escape from the canister.

Affects:
Gas escape from the canister will affect gas flow and transport through the surrounding bentonite buffer. Escape of gaseous radionuclides will contribute to the total release of nuclides from the canister.

host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Gas flow in bentonite occurs when the gas pressure exceeds the threshold value required to open up gas channels in the material. Experiments have shown that this threshold value approximately is corresponding to the hydraulic pressure plus 50-90% of the swelling pressure for a material with high clay content and density and related to the capillary tension for a material with low clay content. As long as the gas pressure is maintained above the threshold value gas is flowing through the material. If the pressure decreases below the threshold value the channels are closed and no gas flow takes place until the gas pressure once again is raised above the threshold value.

Gas dissolved in the water in the buffer/backfill is transported by diffusion and flowing water. The relation between gas flow and transport of dissolved gas depends on the amounts of gas released from the canister and the gas generation rate in the buffer/backfill.

After canister failure, gas flow and transport through the bentonite will affect the amounts of gas and the gas pressure in the failed canister. This would in turn have implications on water intrusion in the canister and the dissolution of radionuclides from the fuel.

Influenced by:
Gas flow and transport in the buffer/backfill is influenced by the gas generation rate in the buffer/backfill, and the properties of the buffer/backfill such as swelling pressure and pore characteristics which affects the threshold pressure for gas flow, the permeability to gas and the diffusivity of dissolved gas. In addition, gas flow and transport in the buffer is affected by the gas release from the canister and the gas flow and transport through the surrounding rock and the tunnel backfill. Gas flow in the tunnel backfill is affected by gas flow and transport through the bentonite buffer and in the surrounding rock.

Affects:
Gas flow and transport will affect the gas release and the gas pressure in the failed canister. In addition, water movement and the degree of saturation of the buffer backfill could be affected, and gas dissolved in the water could influence the water chemistry in the buffer/backfill. Furthemore, gas flow and transport in buffer/backfill will affect the subsequent gas flow and transport in the surrounding rock, including radionuclides in gaseous phase.

General:
Gas released from the buffer and backfill and gas generated in the near-field rock will flow through fracture systems in the near-field rock and in the geosphere. Gas may dissolve in the groundwater and be transported by the moving water, but as the pressure decreases in the rising groundwater flow gas may again form. If the gas carries radionuclides in gaseous state, this is a fast transport mechanism through the geosphere barrier for these nuclides.

Influenced by:
Gas flow and transport in the rock is affected by the gas release from the bentonite buffer and the tunnel backfill, and by gas generation in the rock. In addition, the fracture characteristics and the groundwater flow in the rock will affect the gas flow and transport.

Affects:
Gas flow and transport may affect the saturation conditions and groundwater flow in the rock as well as the groundwater chemistry. Furthermore, the gas flow and transport through buffer/backfill is affected, and the release of gaseous radionuclides to the biosphere.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the generation of gas inside the canister. The fuel itself contains radionuclides in gaseous form which may be released and accumulated in the canister. In addition, several other processes may generate gas inside the canister. 

Helium is formed by alpha decay of radionuclides in the fuel. This gas generation process has to be considered from the time of canister emplacement.

Hydrogen is generated by anaerobic corrosion of the inner steel canister and of the metal parts of the fuel. In contact with water free from oxygen, iron is dissolved from the steel and hydrogen is formed by reduction of water. The rate with which hydrogen is formed is dependent on the kinetics and stoechiometry of the reaction between iron and water. This gas generation process requires the presence of water and is therefore mainly of importance after failure of the outer copper canister. However, anaerobic corrosion and hydrogen generation may take place prior to canister failure if the relative humidity of the air inside the canister rise to 100% at ambient temperature. 

Radiolytic decomposition of water by alpha and beta irradiation results in the formation of hydrogen and oxidants such as hydrogen peroxide. The hydrogen generation rate is dependent on the radiolytic yield and will decrease with time due to decay. Alpha and beta radiation only affects water in direct contact with the fuel, which means that water has to penetrate both the outer copper canister and the inner steel canister before hydrogen formation due to alpha and beta radiolysis is initiated. Hydrogen generation by radiolysis prior to water intrusion may occur if the relative humidity of the air in the canister reach 100%.

Microbial decomposition of organic material may lead to the formation of carbon dioxide, methane and hydrogen.

Radiolysis of moist air in the canister can take place prior to water intrusion in the canister. This would lead to the formation of corrosive gases such as nitrous and nitric acids and ammonia.

Gas generation inside the canister is influenced by alpha decay in the fuel
(helium generation), anaerobic corrosion of steel canister and metal components of the fuel, and radiolytic decomposition of moist air and water.
Microbial degradation of organics is another gas source provided that microbes can survive in the environment inside the canister.

Gas generation inside the canister will affect the gas pressure in the canister. Local gas pressure build-up in cracks and pores in the fuel matrix and in the gap between fuel and cladding may cause cracking/fragmentation of the fuel and cladding, therby affecting the structure of the fuel elements. Dissolution of gas generated in the canister may affect the water chemistry in the canister. Formation of corrosive gases may initiate corrosion of the canister materials prior to water intrusion.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
The world's climate will for the next 100,000 years be featured by periods of glaciations, as it has been over similar periods for the past million years. This statement is based on research performed during the past 20 years which has shown that glaciations have occurred periodically over the last 900,000 years. Evidence indicate that the time of occurrence is triggered by small periodic changes in the earth's orbit around the sun (the latter governed by the so-called Milankovitch orbital parameters). These changes result in changes in the solar radiation which reaches the earth. These periodic changes are possible to calculate which imply that also future glaciations are possible to predict. Full glaciation is expected to occur some 20,000-80,000 years from now.

During full glacial conditions in a region like Scandinavia the weight of the inland ice sheet (3000 m ice thickness) depresses the earth’s surface by several hundreds of metres, or perhaps even thousand metres. This affects the regional stress field, which in turn may induce movements along old fractures and fracture zones.  The movements might be associated with seismic events or not. Even formation of new fractures and faults may occur.  Tensional forces and/or shearing may increase the aperture and thus the permeability of fractures and fracture zones/faults.

Glaciation will have large impact on the magnitude of principle stresses, but only minor effects on stress orientations. The ice will also close near vertical and horizontal fracture zones. 

The ice will constitute a shielding barrier layer which will bind most of the precipitation, thus limiting recharge and flow through the  (most probably permafrosted) bedrock, melt water being discharged at the base of the ice driven by the slope of the ice. On the other hand, a glacier lake on the ice sheet providing a high hydraulic head, possibly in direct hydraulic contact with the base of the ice, or particularly, excessive recharge at the rim of the ice sheet may provide direct recharge of oxidizing water to considerable depths in conductive fracture zones. If the basal transmissivity of the till/bedrock below the ice is low, water pressures may rise to levels equalling the ice pressure inducing the formation of major conduits in the subglacial material. If the permeability at and beyond the rim of the ice is low, e.g. due to permafrost, the water pressures may again build up resulting in hydrofracturing of the ice or the bedrock. As the ice sheet proceeds, these induced fractures may increase in aperture and depth extent due to freezing of subglacial meltwater.

In addition, the glaciation will bind large volumes of water in the ice sheet which will result in global lowering of the mean sea level. A Fennoscandian ice sheet extending to the Stockholm-Helsinki region will result in a lowering of the sea level with c. 85 m. However, when the ice sheet covers the region the downwarping of the crust due to the ice load results in crustal positions below sea level. Immediately following a deglaciation, before isostatic uplift commence, the sea level in the Stockholm-Helsinki may be some 100 m higher than the present highest shoreline.

The topography of the land surface will be reshaped and restructured. Considering the already flattened topography in Sweden, the erosional effect will probably be minimal.

Influenced by:
Climate changes

Affects:
The ice load affects the regional stress field, which in turn may affect the characteristics of fractures and fracture zones, fracture densities and  the groundwater flow at depth and at the surface. It may also cause extreme groundwater heads at the ice edge, change the position of the inflow and outflow areas and cause sea level changes.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to the groundwater chemistry in the geosphere (far-field rock) as well as changes in groundwater composition. The groundwater chemistry is dependent on the rock mineralogy through rock-water interactions and on other processes occuring in the groundwater, but also on interactions with other waters e.g. near-field waters, surface waters and saline waters.

The groundwater chemistry is important for the long-term stability of the engineered barriers and the spent fuel and for the migration of radionuclides in the far-field rock. Important aspects of the water chemistry in this sense are e.g. redox conditions, salinity, pH, complexing agents and corrosive agents. Redox conditions are strongly dependent on the redox capacity of the rock which generally is determined by the presence of Fe(II) in the rock matrix. The salinity of the groundwaters usually increases with increasing depth. In crystalline rocks, weathering of rock minerals will buffer the pH of the groundwater to be weakly alkaline. 

Humic and fulvic acids are complexing agents which are present in groundwaters. These form strong complexes, especially with trivalent radionuclides. In saline waters, chloride complexes can be formed, e.g. with neptunium. Other important complexing agents are carbonate, phosphate and sulphate. Carbonate forms strong complexes with uranium and americium, and sulphate may form complexes with plutonium.The formation of radionuclide complexes will affect the solubility and sorptivity of the radionuclides.

Corrosive agents naturally present in groundwaters are e.g. sulphides, chloride and carbonate. The measured concentrations of total sulphide is in general below 1 mg/l.

Influenced by:
The temperature, the mineralogy of the rock and fracture filling materials and alteration/weathering of these minerals as well as the chemistry of recharging surface waters, intruding deep (saline) waters and near-field waters will affect the groundwater composition in the far-field rock. The groundwater flow will also affect the groundwater chemistry by affecting the degree of mixing of different waters. Gas generation and transport and microbial activity in the far-field rock are other processes that influence the groundwater chemistry.

Affects:
The groundwater chemistry in the geosphere (far-field rock) will affect the water chemistry in the near-field rock, alteration/weathering of rock minerals, microbial activity and the generation and stability of colloids in the water. It will also affect sorption and precipitation/dissolution of radionuclides in the far-field rock.

Modelling aspects:
Thermodynamic models and coupled chemistry and transport models could be used for simulations of the evolution of groundwater chemistry. However, many of the reactions between rock minerals and groundwater are determined by the kinetics of the reactions, which means that thermodynamic models might give misleading results.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to the magnitude, distribution and direction of the groundwater flow in the near-field and far-field rock.The groundwater flow may be altered locally around the repository due to changes in the barriers or the nearby rock, in the far-field due to changes in the rock and globally due to changes in the groundwater recharge. The groundwater flow may also be affected by gas generation and flow and by gradients in water salinity and vice versa.

The water flow will also be affected by variations in temperature, thermal buoyancy, since both the water density and the viscosity depends on the temperature. In reverse, the groundwater flow affects the temperature field as the flowing water will transport the heat through advection. However, heat is also transported through conduction in both the water and the solid phase. In very low permeable media heat conduction is the dominant heat transport mechanism. In general, the temperature effects on groundwater flow are relatively well understood. However, special attention to the problem may be required in relation to coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical effects.

The flow of water is not evenly distributed in the rock. It is confined to the fractures. In addition the water does not flow over the whole fracture plane. This fact is often noted "channelling". However, within this term vastly different concepts on how flow occurs are possible.

One concept of channelling is that each fracture plane consists of open and closed parts - for this there is also experimental evidence. This concept might only be viewed as an extension of the discrete fracture approach, at least if the closed part portion is not too large. There is little knowledge on how the fracture transmissivity is distributed on the fracture plane. It is clear that the flow distribution among the different fractures will depend very much on the shape of the open parts. To complicate matters further this shape depends upon the rock stress field, the strength of the rock, and the asperity distribution and strength of the fractures. There exist a need to establish the geometry and statistics of such channels, which existence is already confirmed by the shape of breakthrough curves of certain tracer experiments. Statistical analysis of fracture and hydraulic conductivity data, resin imprints of natural fractures are possible tools to increase the understanding of the channelling effect. Detailed mapping of inflows on tunnel and shaft walls have also been suggested. However, it is questionable whether these observations are relevant for the bedrock beyond the disturbed rock zone, but simply show the perturbation of flow by the disturbed zone.

Another concept of “channels” is “extreme channelling" where there are only a few paths where most of the water flows in the rock mass. These paths may be considered and modelled as real physical conduits, “worm holes”, in the rock mass. Other means of obtaining extreme channelling are through a poorly percolating fracture network model or a poorly percolating stochastic continuum model and a given set of boundary conditions. Geostatistically, channelling will emerge in a model when the correlation scale of the material property is equal to the flow domain and its variance is high. A poorly percolating fracture network could be the result of a large fracture size and a relatively low fracture density. 

The difference between “worm holes” and a poorly percolating network  or stochastic continuum is that in the latter two cases the position and amounts of the important paths may change totally if the hydraulic boundary conditions are changed, whereas in the former case the flow is always confined to the “worm holes”. The situation with a poorly percolating network would make it extremely difficult to characterise the flow and transport properties of the rock. Experiments performed on one scale then cannot be extrapolated to a larger scale. 

The uneven flow distribution implies that  groundwater velocities varies considerably in space. This in turn affects the retention properties (ratio between flow wetted surface and flow) considerably.

In the near-field, channelling will make the flow over some canister deposition holes much larger than the average flow (and v.v. much smaller at some holes).

Influenced by:
Properties of the rock, such as fracture frequencies, orientations, connectivity, apertures etc, will affect the groundwater flow, and so will gradients in temperature and salinity and gas flow in the rock. The hydraulic properties of the bentonite buffer and the tunnel backfill will influence groundwater flow in the near-field rock, and groundwater flow in the far-field rock is influenced by earth tides and groundwater discharge/recharge (topography, climate and sea-level changes).

Affects:
Groundwater flow affects the transport and dispersion of radionuclides, dissolved as colloids and as dissolved gas, as well as the exchange of other dissolved species in the water and mixing of different waters. The distribution of the groundwater flow affects radionuclide retardation by determining the amount of rock surfaces accessible to matrix diffusion and sorption. Furthermore, groundwater flow affects the rock stresses, the temperature and gas flow and transport in the rock. The groundwater flow in the near-field rock will affect the resaturation of the bentonite buffer and the tunnel backfill and the water flow in them, and may cause erosion of these materials.

The situation with a poorly percolating network would make it extremely difficult to characterise the flow and transport properties of the rock. Experiments performed on one scale then cannot be extrapolated to a larger scale. 

The uneven flow distribution implies that  groundwater velocities varies considerably in space. This in turn affects the retention properties (ratio between flow wetted surface and flow) considerably.

In the near-field, channelling will make the flow over some canister deposition holes much larger than the average flow (and v.v. much smaller at some holes).

Influenced by:
Properties of the rock, such as fracture frequencies, orientations, connectivity, apertures etc, will affect the groundwater flow, and so will gradients in temperature and salinity and gas flow in the rock. The hydraulic properties of the bentonite buffer and the tunnel backfill will influence groundwater flow in the near-field rock, and groundwater flow in the far-field rock is influenced by earth tides and groundwater discharge/recharge (topography, climate and sea-level changes).

Affects:
Groundwater flow affects the transport and dispersion of radionuclides, dissolved as colloids and as dissolved gas, as well as the exchange of other dissolved species in the water and mixing of different waters. The distribution of the groundwater flow affects radionuclide retardation by determining the amount of rock surfaces accessible to matrix diffusion and sorption. Furthermore, groundwater flow affects the rock stresses, the temperature and gas flow and transport in the rock. The groundwater flow in the near-field rock will affect the resaturation of the bentonite buffer and the tunnel backfill and the water flow in them, and may cause erosion of these materials.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to sorption/desorption and coprecipitation/dissolution of elements released from the fuel with solids formed by corrosion of metals in the canister.

It is well known that hydrous ferric hydroxide has a scavenging effect leading to coprecipitation of various aqueous substances despite their expected higher solubility. The general mechanism can be described as a sequence where ferric hydroxide is formed from a solution of ferrous iron and precipitates as a flocculent solid, onto which various solutes are adsorbed. The adsorbed substances may later form solid solutions with the carrier substance whereby a permanent immobilisation can be expected. The adsorbed substances may also be physically embedded as a result of further precipitation of carrier substance. It is, however, important to demonstrate that the embedded substances are not expelled from the solid material if some kind of transformation, recrystallisation, of the carrier substance occurs. In addition, mobile colloidal fractions of the corrosion products may be formed.

Sorption and coprecipitation of a wide range of elements (both redox-active and redox-inert) with iron minerals have been observed around a natural redox front at the Osamu Utsumi uranium mine in the Pocos de Caldas region in Brazil. Enrichment of elements ranging from a factor of 10 to about 300 was found both in ferric oxyhydroxides on the oxidising side and in pyrite on the reducing side. McKinley et al. (1992) compared the ratio for the net inventory of some elements in vitrified HLW to the Fe which will be present in the canister corrosion products with the trace element to Fe ratio observed in Pocos de Caldas. They found that the near-field ratios were significantly less than the Pocos de Caldas observations (except for Cs for which the ratios were comparable). They concluded that this implies that coprecipitation with iron corrosion products or secondary iron minerals formed by redox buffering reactions would be quite capable of immobilising the whole inventory of most safety relevant nuclides.

Influenced by:
The physical and chemical properties of the corrosion products, and the water chemistry and temperature in the canister affect sorption/coprecipitation with corrosion products.

Affects:
The uptake of uranium by sorption/coprecipitation can strongly affect the fuel dissolution rate. Sorption/coprecipitation will lead to retardation of elements released from the fuel and thereby affect the release of radionuclides from the canister. Subsequent desorption/dissolution may liberate nuclides and enhance the release. In addition, sorption on colloidal fractions may influence the release.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the gas pressure inside the steel vessel prior to and after failure of the steel vessel, as well as the gas pressure in the void between steel vessel and copper canister prior to and after failure of the copper canister. It also includes local pressure build-up in cracks in the fuel and in the void between fuel and cladding.

Prior to failure of the steel vessel, generation of helium may lead to a pressure increase in cracks in the fuel and in the gap between fuel and cladding which may cause further cracking of the fuel and cladding. Helium generation and potential hydrogen formation inside the steel vessel prior to failure will lead to a pressure increase with time which is dependent on the gas generation rate and the void inside the steel vessel.

After failure of the steel vessel generation of hydrogen may lead to pressure increase in the vessel if gas accumulates in the vessel. Accumulation of gas will occur if the gas cannot escape from the vessel or if the gas generation rate is faster than the rate with which gas leaves the vessel. If the pressure increases above the surrounding hydrostatic pressure a displacement of water from the interior of the vessel may take place.

Prior to failure of the copper canister, gas formation by radiolysis and/or corrosion due to the presence of air with high relative humidity in the void between copper and steel canister may lead to a pressure increase.

After failure of the copper canister, hydrogen formation will lead to a pressure increase in the void as long as gas accumulates in the void. A pressure increase will affect the inflow of water to the void and may also displace water from the void if the pressure increases above the surrounding hydrostatic pressure.

A fluctuation in internal pressure will probably take place with a pressure increase during periods of gas accumulation, and a decrease in pressure as a result of gas escape or decrease in gas generation rate. A decrease in gas generation rate will, for example, occur as a result of displacement of water.

Influenced by:
The gas generation inside the canister and gas escape from the canister will influence the internal gas pressure.

Affects:
The internal gas pressure will affect the inflow/outflow of water and thereby processes like canister corrosion, fuel dissolution and radionuclide release from the canister. A high internal pressure may mechanically impact the canister. Build-up of hydrogen pressure may influence the hydrogen evolving corrosion rates and radiolytic yields. Furthermore, the gas escape from the canister will be affected by the internal gas pressure.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Matrix diffusion is the process by which nuclides and other species in the water flowing in the rock fissures migrates into the porous rock by diffusion. Matrix diffusion is a very efficient retarding mechanism, especially for strongly sorbed radionuclides due to the increase in rock surface accessible to sorption. It is governed by the characteristics of fracture fillings and the rock mass (porosity and mineralogy). In addition, the water chemistry may be of importance for matrix diffusion of anionic species, anion exclusion effects.

Here, matrix diffusion also refers to the diffusional transport of nuclides and other species from water flowing in larger pores or fissures in the buffer/backfill into stagnant water in small pores and microfissures in the buffer/backfill.

Influenced by:
Matrix diffusion is affected by the pore and fracture characteristics and the structure of the flow field which determines the surface area of the fracture accessible to matrix diffusion. In addition, the temperature and the water chemistry may affect matrix diffusion.

Affects:
Matrix diffusion affects the transport and release of radionuclides from the different repository barriers.

Modelling aspects:
Matrix diffusion requires a special model, but it is not very difficult to account for. One problem though, is to get a measure of the flow wetted surface, i.e. the amount of fracture surfaces in contact with water containing radionuclides. Since this parameter is dependent on the structure of the flow field in the fractured rock, it is not a simple geometrical property that can be directly measured from rock samples. Instead, it must be evaluated by tracer experiments in the field.

In principle, matrix diffusion should be treated likewise both in the far field and in the rock close to the canisters.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Mechanical impact on the canister is caused by internal and external forces such as internal gas pressure, forces caused by swelling corrosion products, bentonite swelling pressure and rock movements. If the mechanical impact exceeds the mechanical strength of the canister it may crack or breach. Mechanical impact may also with time enlarge the size of an initial damage. Furthermore, mechanical impact may initiate stress corrosion of the canister material. 

Mechanical impact could affect the life-time of the canister and the characteristics of the failed canister with time, which are important entities for the release of radionuclides from the canister. However, the canister are designed to withstand an evenly distributed external pressure of 10 MPa from the surrounding bentonite and rock. 

Influenced by:
External forces such as the swelling pressure of bentonite, rock creep and faulting in near-field rock, and cave in may mechanically impact the canister. The mechanical properties of the bentonite will affect the mechanical impact by the surrounding rock. In addition, volume increase of canister corrosion products and build-up of internal gas pressure may mechanically impact the canister.

Affects:
Mechanical impact on the canister may reduce its mechanical strength, affect canister corrosion (stress corrosion), affect canister creep, affect the canister position in the bentonite buffer, and may crack or breach the canister. Mechanical impact may also affect the shape of an intact canister and a failed canister.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Microorganisms can be brought into the repository by man or may occur naturally in the groundwater. Anaerobic bacteria are the most likely species in deep groundwaters, e.g. methanogenic bacteria and sulphate reducers.

Microbial activity requires access to water and certain nutrients. In addition, the chemical environment is important, where optimal conditions for most microorganisms are a pH close to neutral, a temperature of 25 - 30°C and absence of bio-toxic substances such as heavy metals. However, microbes can adapt to quite extreme conditions. The only true environmental limitations for subterranean bacteria seem to be temperature (< 110°C), water availability and the supply of utilisable energy sources.

Microbial activity is likely both in the near-field and far-field of a high-level waste repository, but the nutrient availability will generally be very low in the near-field as compared to the biosphere. The activity in the far-field is likely to depend on the supply of nutrients from the surrounding waters and host rock.

Microbial activity may lead to the formation of corrosive agents such as sulphide and organic acids. Organic acids may also act as complexing agents for many metal ions, but they are usually only intermediate products which are further decomposed to carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane. Other substances produced by the microbes or the microbes themselves can be imaged to take up radionuclides by sorption or complex formation. These aggregates may act as mobile species of radionuclides which would otherwise have a low solubility or a strong tendency to sorb on the mineral surfaces. Bacteria driven geochemical reactions can also at least in principle cause generation of colloids, e.g. ironhydroxide particles by oxidation of iron. Bacteria in a heterotrophic environment have themself a tendency to live sorbed on mineral surfaces. This may in fact add to the uptake of radionuclides on mineral surfaces, but it also introduces an uncertainty vis-à-vis laboratory sorption measurements and the fact that dead bacteria or decomposition products of them may become released to the water phase.

Influenced by:
Microbial activity is influenced by temperature, water activity and nutrients (energy sources). Furthermore, pH and radiation might influence microbial activity. 

Affects:
Microbial activity may lead to the formation of corrosive agents, complexing agents and gas. By taking part in redox reactions they will influence the redox conditions. Microbes may also take up radionuclides and thereby acting as mobile carriers if suspended in the water phase and as a trap for radionuclides if attached to mineral surfaces.

Bacteria in a heterotrophic environment have themself a tendency to live sorbed on mineral surfaces. This may in fact add to the uptake of radionuclides on mineral surfaces, but it also introduces an uncertainty vis-à-vis laboratory sorption measurements and the fact that dead bacteria or decomposition products of them may become released to the water phase.

Microbial activity is influenced by temperature, water activity and nutrients (energy sources). Furthermore, pH and radiation might influence microbial activity.

Microbial activity may lead to the formation of corrosive agents, complexing agents and gas. By taking part in redox reactions they will influence the redox conditions. ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
There are lot of evidences that Sweden has gone through several cycles for permafrost during the Quarternary period (last 2 m.y.). At present, in the Spitzbergen area, the permafrost depth is approximately 450 m, and in Siberia, depths exceeding 1500 m have been reported. These latter examples are though possibly permafrost occurrences of older ages than the last ice age. With the  knowledge of today, it is not possible to exclude a deep permafrost situation in Sweden. It is therefore necessary to consider the potential of permafrost at repository depth, as well as on the surface.

As a gross generalization it is assumed that the limit of permafrost shows a strong correlation with the mean annual air temperature isotherm of -1 to -2 degrees C. The depth of permafrost penetration is affected by the topography and the thickness of the snow cover. The geothermal gradient in Swedish crystalline rock is in general about 3 degrees C per 100 m, with some local variations. This gradient is also a controlling factor since it detemines the maximum depth to which permafrost reaches.

The permafrost would in itself be associated with glaciation which constitutes a natural barrier shield of recharge to the bedrock, thus decreasing groundwater flow. The permafrost enhances this shielding effect for the duration of the glacial cycle. After retreat of the ice tongue, the permafrost will continue to facilitate an increased surface run-off until sufficient melting will allow rechrge/discharge of water.

The development of permafrost may entail changes in the hydrochemical situation, i.e. formation of very saline groundwaters, particularily at the base of the permafrosted region, which may affect radionuclide transport. 

Influenced by:
Climate changes

Affects:
Possible potential effects of permafrost are for instance fracturing or opening of fractures because of water freezing; compression of backfill and opening of voids at melting; increasing water flow in the temperature gradient and potential rapid flow paths; changes in the hydrochemical situation, i.e. formation of very saline groundwaters; accumulation (concentration) of gas and radionuclides below the lower surface of the permafrost frozen rockmass giving rise to a pulse of radionuclides when melting occurs.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to the precipitation and dissolution of elements previously released from the fuel. This may occur as a consequence of changes in water chemistry. A change to a more reducing environment away from the fuel surface will cause precipitation of uranium and other redox sensitive elements which have a lower solubility under reducing conditions. A dissolution of the precipitated elements may occur if the redox conditions shifts from reducing to oxidising. Other factors that may cause precipitation and dissolution away from the fuel surface is a change in temperature or in the concentration of ions and complexes that affects the speciation of the elements.

The localisation and potential movement of the interface between oxidising and reducing conditions, the redox front, is dependent on the formation of oxidants by radiolysis in relation to the amount of reduced species in the water in the canister. As long as corrosion of steel occurs, a continuous supply of reduced iron is maintained. Other reduced species may be present in the water entering the canister. Redox reactions leading to reprecipitation of uranium and other redox sensitive elements will consume reducing species, such as Fe(II), and may thereby influence the redox conditions in the canister. 

Radionuclides initially precipitated as microcrystalline or amorphous phases may recrystallise as coarser crystals, a process which is thermodynamically favorable, and leads to lower solubility of the radionuclides. Radionuclides present in trace quantities in the spent fuel will probably be incorporated (coprecipitated) as trace components in solid solution within alteration phases, such as alumino-silicates, carbonates, sulphates, phosphates, and sulphides.  In addition, radioelements may be coprecipitated with some carrier substance, e.g. hydrous oxides of iron, and may later be either released into solution, or enter into a solid solution if the carrier substance recrystallises to another crystalline structure. The use of cementitious materials, e.g. for reinforcement of the rock, adds the possible effects of recrystallisation of cement gels in the long term which may influence the groundwater chemistry in the vicinity of the caverns.

Influenced by:
Precipitation/dissolution of elements released from the fuel is influenced by changes in redox conditions, temperature, or concentration of ions and complexes in the water which influences the speciation of the elements.

Affects:
Precipitation/dissolution of elements released from the fuel affects the transport and release of radionuclides from the different barriers. In addition it may affect the water chemistry, and radiation from precipitated radionuclides might affect water (radiolysis) and barrier materials.

host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)

copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the hydrological, chemical, mechanical, thermal and gas transport properties of the bentonite buffer. As a result of degradation of the buffer these properties will change with time. The main functions of the buffer are to act as a hydraulic barrier and to mechanically protect the canister. Therefore, the buffer should have a good swelling ability ensuring a low hydraulic conductivity and good elastic properties and self-healing capacity in order to be resistant to mechanical impact. In addition, a high sorption capacity will have positive effects by delaying the transport of radionuclides escaping from a failed canister.

A reduction in, or even loss of, swelling ability and plasticity may be caused by chemical degradation by ion-exchange, precipitation causing cementation of the buffer, conversion to illite, formation of zeolites and hydrosilicates. A high salinity of the porewater will also reduce the swelling ability of the clay. The consequences could be a reduced mechanical and hydraulic resistance and possibly creation of preferential flowpaths in the buffer.

Parts of the buffer may be unsaturated as a consequece of gas generation and transport. This will affect water flow and transport of radionuclides in the water phase in the buffer.

If the buffer is partly saturated it may swell unevenly if the water supply is limited and unevenly distribuated. The saturation also depends upon the heat generation in the canister.

A reduction in buffer density, dilution, due to swelling into surrounding cavities and into failed canister and due to erosion of the buffer may reduce the hydraulic resistance of the buffer.

Irradiation of the bentonite by decaying radionuclides, dissolved or precipitated, may affect the mineralogy of the bentonite.

Chemical degradation by ion-exchange prior to canister failure will reduce the cation exchange capacity of the buffer available for radionuclides released from a failed canister. Changes in the composition of the buffer, such as conversion to illite, zeolites or hydrous mica may also change the surface characteristics of the buffer thereby affecting sorption.

Changes in the properties of the bentonite buffer may reduce the capacity of the buffer to protect the canister against mechanical impact, as well as increase the water flow and thereby also the radionuclide transport through the buffer, especially if preferential flow paths are created.

Influenced by:
The properties of the buffer may be influenced by:
- chemical and thermal alteration of buffer materials,
- swelling of buffer into the backfill, intersecting fractures, failed canister
- mechanical impact on the buffer,
- irradiation by decaying radionuclides,
- dilution, coagulation and sedimentation of buffer materials,
- gas generation and flow in the buffer,
- movements of the canister in the buffer,
- sorption of species in the porewater causing saturation of sorption sites.

Affects:
The buffer properties may affect:
- the swelling ability of the buffer,
- the resistance against mechanical impact on buffer and canister,
- the potential for canister movement in the buffer,
- the magnitude and distribution (preferential pathways) of water flow through the buffer,
- migration of radionuclides in the buffer in terms of sorption, diffusion, matrix diffusion and anion exclusion,
- gas flow and transport through the buffer,
- groundwater flow in the nearby rock,
- the extent of buffer swelling into the backfill,
- the transport of colloids/particles in the buffer (filtering capacity),
- the stress field in the surrounding rock,
- the water chemistry in the buffer.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Refers to the chemical and physical (transport) properties of the failed steel vessel and copper canister. It includes the size and location of the initial failure, changes in failure characteristics with time due to corrosion or mechanical impact, amount of corrosion products as a function of time and amount and characteristics of the filling material.

The size and location of the hole/breach in the copper canister will influence the inflow and outflow of water in the gap between copper canister and steel vessel. The size and location of the hole/breach in the steel vessel will influence the inflow/outflow of water in the steel vessel. The size influences the resistance to flow and the location influences the amount of water that will be displaced from the canister interior by gas. The size of the hole/breach is also influencing the release of radionuclides by diffusion from the canister.

The possibility of healing of the hole/breach by corrosion products should be considered. 

The amount of corrosion products in the canister will increase with time thereby increasing the potential radionuclide retardation capacity by sorption/coprecipitation and reducing the void volume accessible to water in the canister.

The amount and characteristics of the canister filling material will influence the void volume accessible to water and will also constitute a potential sorption capacity to elements dissolved from the fuel.

The physical properties of the failed canister may also influence the escape of gas.

Influenced by:
The properties of the failed canister may be influenced by:
- the mode of failure,
- corrosion of the canister materials and metal components of the fuel,
- mechanical impact,

Affects:
The properties of the failed canister may affect:
- the water inflow/outflow in the canister,
- the nature and effectiveness of interactions with corrosion products,
- sorption on filling materials,
- gas escape and build-up of internal gas pressure,
- diffusion inside and out from the canister,
- the potential for buffer expanding into the canister

General:
Refers to the hydrological, mineralogical, mechanical, thermal and gas transport properties of the near-field rock which are of importance to the stability of engineered barriers and radionuclide transport in the rock. Due to various processes and events, these properties will change with time. 

Changes in the stress field in the near-field rock during excavation of the repository may result in the formation of new fractures, reactivation of healed fractures or displacements on pre-existing fractures.

The swelling pressure of bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill may change the stress field in the adjacent rock causing an increase in fracture apertures.

The initial high temperature in the near-field rock and subsequent decrease in thermal load will cause stress changes and displacements in the rock mass which will affect the fracture apertures in the near-field rock.

The groundwater flow may change the stress field with deformations of the rock as a consequence.

Changes in the stress field caused by degradation of the bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill may result in subsidence and cave in which will change the fracture system in the near-field rock.

Swelling of bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill into intersecting fractures and cracks may seal these fractures at the interface buffer/backfill and rock. In addition, erosion of buffer/backfill and subsequent sedimentation in fractures in adjacent rock may have a sealing effect.

Dissolution and precipitation of fracture mineral may increase and decrease the fracture apertures as well as change the mineral composition of the surfaces.

Resaturation of the rock after repository closure and gas generation and gas transport in the rock will influence the water saturation conditions in the near-field rock.

- excavation of the repository,
- resaturation of the rock, the buffer and the backfill,
- buffer and backfill expansion into intersecting fractures,
- fracturing, faulting, cave in and rock creep,
- alteration/weathering of rock and fracture minerals,
- gas flow and transport in the rock,
- sorption causing saturation of sorption sites,
- degradation of rock reinforcements and grout,

- the magnitude, distribution and direction of groundwater flow in the rock,
- migration of radionuclides in terms of sorption, diffusion, matrix diffusion, anion exclusion,
- colloid generation and transport,
- gas flow and transport,

host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
Concerns the hydrological, chemical, mechanical, thermal and gas transport properties of the bentonite/sand material used as tunnel backfill. As a result of degradation of the material these properties may change with time.

The main functions of the backfill material are to prevent rock cave in and to re-establish the hydraulic conditions in the rock. In addition, a high hydraulic resistance in the backfill and high sorption capacity of the backfill material will delay the transport of radionuclides migrating upwards from the canister and bentonite buffer into the tunnel backfill. 

A reduction in, or even loss of, swelling ability and plasticity of the bentonite may be caused by chemical degradation by ion-exchange, precipitation causing cementation of the bentonite, conversion to illite, formation of zeolites and hydrosilicates. A high salinity of the porewater will also reduce the swelling ability of the bentonite. The consequences could be a reduced mechanical and hydraulic resistance and possibly creation of preferential flowpaths in the tunnel backfill.

Parts of the backfill may be unsaturated as a consequece of gas generation and transport. This will affect water flow and transport of radionuclides in the water phase in the backfill.

A reduction in backfill density, dilution, due to swelling into intersecting fractures/cracks and due to erosion of the backfill may reduce the hydraulic resistance of the tunnel backfill.

Irradiation of the backfill materials by decaying radionuclides, dissolved or precipitated, may change the mineralogy of the backfill materials.

Changes in the properties of the tunnel backfill may reduce the capacity of the backfill to prevent rock cave in, as well as increase the water flow through the backfill. This may influence the degradation of the bentonite buffer and also the radionuclide transport, especially if preferential flow paths are created.

Influenced by:
The properties of the tunnel backfill may be influenced by:
- chemical and thermal alteration of backfill materials,
- swelling of buffer into the backfill,
- swelling of backfill into intersecting fractures,
- mechanical impact on the backfill,
- irradiation by decaying radionuclides,
- dilution, coagulation and sedimentation of backfill materials,
- gas generation and flow in the tunnel backfill

Affects:
The properties of the tunnel backfill will affect:
- the swelling ability of the backfill,
- the resistance of the backfill against mechanical impact,
- the magnitude and distribution (preferential pathways) of flow through the backfill,
- migration of radionuclides in the backfill in terms of sorption, diffusion, matrix diffusion and anion exclusion,
- gas flow and transport through the backfill,
- groundwater flow in the nearby rock,
- the extent of buffer swelling into the backfill,
- the transport of colloids/particles in the backfill (filtering capacity),
- the stress field in the surrounding rock,
- the water chemistry in the backfill

General:
The radioactive decay of the fuel in the repository is well known. It changes the initial radionuclide content in the fuel with time and generates heat. The type of radiation generated by the decay depends on the radionuclide, and the penetration distance of the radiation depends on the type of radiation, its energy and the surrounding medium.

Influenced by:
The inventory of radionuclides in the fuel.

Affects:
Radioactive decay will change the inventory of radionuclides in the fuel, and the heat generation will affect the temperature in the canister. Radiation from decaying nuclides may cause radiolysis of water and gas in the canister and in the buffer outside the canister. Radiation from decaying radionuclides in the fuel may also affect the chemical properties and structure of the fuel, the canister properties, and the mineralogy and structure of the buffer.

Modelling aspects:
Radioactive decay is included in the fuel model which keeps track of the timely isotope inventory in the fuel matrix. Whether or not the model corrects the inventory for amounts of different isotopes that have left the fuel by dissolution is not known. Even the heat generated by radioactive decay is modelled.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Alpha, beta , gamma and neutron irradiation of water leads to the formation of highly reactive excited and ionised species which in turn can undergo various reactions. In pure water the final products are hydrogen and oxidants, mainly hydrogen-peroxide with a yield determined by the radiation doses absorbed by the water.

The presence of different species in the water may influence the formation of hydrogen and oxidants. Multivalent metal ions, such as iron, may act as scavengers for hydrated electrons thereby reducing the radiolytic yield of hydrogen and oxidants. In addition,the formed oxidants may react with dissolved iron(II) which will decrease the net yield of oxidants.

Alpha and beta radiolysis, occurring up to 0.03 mm from the fuel pellets, will be of importance after failure of the inner steel canister, when intruding water gets in close contact with the fuel matrix. The contact area between fuel and water determines the amount of water being radiolytically decomposed.

Gamma and neutron radiation penetrating the canister walls may cause radiolysis of the water just outside the steel or copper canister.

In KBS-3 it is shown that the impact of radiolysis on chemistry is negligible outside an intact copper canister with a reasonable thickness.

Influenced by:
Radiolysis is influenced by the type and energy of the absorbed radiation and by the amount of water available and the chemistry of this water. Radiolysis in the canister may also be influenced by the hydrogen pressure.

Affects:
Radiolysis will affect the water chemistry and the formation of hydrogen.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
The redox front could refer to three different possible redox fronts:
1)	The change of water chemistry when oxidising surface water enters the 	far field and at the redox front changes to reducing conditions.
2)	The transient after closing the storage, when the near-field resumes the 	natural reducing conditions.
3)	The possible establishment of oxidising conditions, due to radiolysis in 	the close vicinity of the fuel, and the change to oxidising conditions 	further out in the near-field.

The effect of the first point (natural phenomenon) should be well known and taken into account in base case scenario. Alternative scenario could be caused e.g. by human induced changes of surface water chemistry.

The second point should have negligible impact, as the transient will have ceased long before canister failure.

The third point should be taken into account as a base case assumption. When a canister is breached, the radiolysis of water may create an oxidising environment close to the fuel. The uranium solubility in an oxidising environment is higher than in a reducing environment. These conditions will create a uranium concentration gradient, which promote fast uranium transport from the fuel surface. Dissolved oxidised uranium is expected to react with reduced compounds, e.g. ferrous iron. The amounts of reduced compounds inside the canister, in the bentonite porewater and in the groundwater will then affect the establishment and propagation of a redox front.

Influenced by:
The establishment and propagation of a redox front is affected by the water chemistry in terms of the relative amount of oxidising and reducing species.

Affects:
The establishment and propagation of a redox front will affect the precipitation/dissolution of redox sensitive elements. Colloids may be formed at the redox front, and the location of the redox front may then affect the location of colloid formation.

canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
During the resaturation (and sealing) of the repository flow directions are different and the hydraulic conductivity is different due to, for example, partially saturated fractures. Furthermore, (or especially) the groundwater chemistry is very different (oxidising conditions etc.).

During operation of the repository atmospheric pressure will prevail in the repository and fractures in the nearby rock are partially drained. At repository closure pumping is stopped and resaturation of the repository starts. Local flow directions will gradually change from  (radially) converging flow towards the underground openings to flow directions more aligned with the original flow field. 

As long as atmospheric pressure prevail in the repository, the hydraulic head is determined by the location and depth of the repository, drawdown effects. The successive emplacement of buffer in the deposition holes and of backfill in used tunnels will lead to resaturation of parts of the repository already during operation.

It is likely that two-phase flow conditions initially will pertain in the rock zone disturbed by the excavation of the repository. Unsaturation and invasion of gas bubbles temporarily change the physics of the disturbed rock zone. During resaturation, the possible two-phase flow effects in the disturbed rock zone and in the nearby rock will dissipate, to finally disappear at fully developed saturation.

During the resaturation process, the groundwater chemical conditions will shift from oxidising in the nearby rock to successively reattain reducing conditions. It is likely that oxygen will be trapped dusring resaturation. This oxygen will be consumed by oxidising Fe(II) to ferric minerals.

Influenced by:
Resaturation of the near-field rock is influenced by the groundwater flow and the properties of the bentonite buffer and the tunnel backfill.

Affects:
Resaturation of the near-field rock will affect the groundwater flow in the near-field rock. It may also affect the water chemistry in the near-field rock and the displacement of entrapped air.

canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
The bentonite buffer in the deposition holes will take up water from the surrounding rock resulting in a swelling of the material. After water saturation and swelling the bentonite will have a low hydraulic conductivity and a high swelling pressure which leads to homogenisation and self-healing of the material.

The time to reach full saturation of the bentonite depends on the initial water content of the bentonite, the groundwater flow into the deposition zone from the adjacent rock and also to some extent on the heat generated by the fuel inside the canister.

During the saturation phase, a higher temperature in the buffer in the vicinity of the canister may result in evaporation of incoming groundwater with subsequent precipitation of elements in the water. These precipitates may cause some cementation of the buffer material which may lead to reduced swelling ability of the clay, but also to a decrease in hydraulic conductivity. Evaporation and precipitation will not occur in an initially water saturated bentonite.

An uneven resaturation may lead to uneven swelling of the buffer.

Influenced by:
The groundwater flow in the near-field rock and in the tunnel backfill as well as the temperature in the bentonite buffer may affect the saturation process.

Affects:
Resaturation of the buffer will affect the swelling of the buffer and the chemistry of the porewater. In addition, the saturation process may affect the temperature in the buffer and also the degree of water saturation in the nearby rock.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
The change in sea level is coupled to changes in the world climate. Presently, there are indications that we are experiencing a transition towards a warmer period due to the "greenhouse effect" induced by an increased CO2 content in the atmosphere due to combustion of hydrocarbons.  A global warming will result in a mean sea level rise due to release of the larger volumes of water stored in glaciers and polar areas. Other researchers claim that we are facing a transition towards a colder climate. A global transition towards a colder climate and even a glaciation will result in a global mean sea-level lowering due to increased binding of water in glaciers and ice sheets.

The possible rise in sea level due to changes in climate (eustatic changes) is in Scandinavia to some extent balanced by a corresponding uplift of the earth's crust following glaciation. The rise in groundwater level due to warmer climate is caused by both thermal expansion and the addition of freshwater from melting polar ice caps.

It has been estimated that during the last ice age the sea level of the oceans dropped about 120 m. The exposed seabottom suffered extensive erosion especially close to the ice rim during the inter glacial periods (warmer periods). Figures mentioned to the amount of sealevel rise varies, 80 m has been mentioned.

Estimated future sea-level rise magnitudes extrapolated to Sweden imply a successive loss of land in the southern parts. This would reduce topographically induced hydraulic gradients in coastal areas, thus reducing groundwater flow. In addition, saline water may intrude into the far-field and repository regions.

A lowering of the sea level would entail an increase in the topographically induced hydraulic gradient. In addition, in a coastal environment, the successive loss of the marine biosphere would mean a loss of its  diluting capability. Instead the discharge would take placee in newly developed streams and lakes.

Influenced by:
Natural and human induced climate changes.

Affects:
Hydraulic gradients and water chemistry.

Modelling aspects:
Far field: Change in hydrological boundary conditions.
Near field: Potential change in flow.
Biosphere: Change in recipient. This is especially important if the repository is situated close to the sea, where it is foreseen major changes in the recipient situation.

Sedimentation is the process where large particles (on a molecular scale) in a suspension settles due to the gravity forces and form a sediment. After the sedimentation the suspension consists of the sediment and a clear, particle-free supernatant liquid.

It should, however, be pointed out that sedimentation of water-transported buffer material may play a significant role in the sealing of rock fissures.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Sorption is the collective term for adsorption of particles (molecules, ions, colloids) on outer or inner surfaces of solids. The forces responsible for sorption range from “physical” interactions (v d Waals’ forces) to the formation of “chemical” bonds. Sorption retards the transient diffusion of radionuclides through buffer and backfill and the advective transport in the nearby rock and the far-field. The effect is well established and included in the migration models. Sorption is element specific and depends both on radionuclide speciation (valency state, hydrolysis, complexation) and the solid phase composition and surface characteristics. At true thermodynamic equilibrium these two sets of conditions are linked together.

Sorption could be reversible or irreversible. If sorption is reversible the sorbed species will be desorbed and mobilised if the concentration of the species in the water decreases. Species which are irreversible sorbed will to a large extent remain fixed to the solid surface even if the concentration in the water decreases.

For sorption on colloids, irreversibility may radically increase the transport velocity of radionuclides.

Sorption will affect the transport and release of sorbing radionuclides from the different repository barriers. Sorption may also affect the sorption capacity of the barriers through saturation of sorption sites.

Modelling aspects:
In most transport calculations sorption is accounted for by the simplistic method of letting the retardation be determined by constant distribution coefficients (Kd). project_title: SKI SITE-94 Deep Repository Performance Assessment Project
host_rock: crystalline basement in Sweden (based on geological data from the Äspö site)
ebs_concept:
copper canister with steel insert, 
canisters in vertical boreholes with bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill
pfep_description_raw:
General:
The crystalline bedrock deforms according to the acting stress field and its inherent strength. Changes in the groundwater flow and changes in the temperature field will change the active stress acting on the rock which in turn will change the fracture properties and thereby the groundwater flow. Thus, the rock deformation, flow and heat transport are coupled processes. These couplings may be of great importance for the performance of a waste repository.

The coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical effects may be important in many scales. For example, the stress changes introduced by excavating the repository and the canister deposition holes combined with the heat from the spent fuel will affect the permeability close to the repository. 

Other causes to stress changes in the rock are the swelling pressure of bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill and the ice-load during glaciation.

Influenced by:
The stress field in the rock is influenced by the host rock properties and structure and changes in these entities, the swelling pressure of bentonite buffer and tunnel backfill, the temperature, the groundwater flow and by the ice-load during glaciation.

Affects:
Stress changes may result in deformation of the rock thereby changing the fracture properties which are of importance to groundwater flow and nuclide transport. Deformation of the rock adjacent to canister deposition holes and tunnels may cause rock movements thereby affecting the stability of the bentonite buffer and the tunnel backfill and possibly also the canister.

Modelling aspects:
There is a continuous development of modelling tools based on available thermo-hydro-mechanical constitutive models. Presently there exists a large number of computer codes that provide means to assess the effects of thermo-mechanical response. The omission of the hydraulic coupling with the rock mechanics is a limitation, which is brought to the attention in current research and development work such as the DECOVALEX study.

pfep_description_raw:
General:
Surface waters will determine the groundwater conditions in the upper most part of the rock, but can also enter deeper down in the geosphere by the existence or the formation of highly permeable fracture zones caused by tectonic movements or due to other changes in the stress field in the rock. The intrusion of surface waters may also be a result of glaciation or may be caused by human activities e.g. injection of water for energy extraction.

The character of the surface water is depending on the soil cover where it infiltrates. Human actions may also affect the groundwater chemistry, e.g. by acidic rain, increased atmospheric carbon dioxide content, complexing agents in the surface waters. 

The composition of the surface waters will affect the groundwater chemistry in the geosphere e.g. content of organics, complexing agents and redox conditions. Sharp interfaces between the different waters might also be formed resulting in favourable conditions for colloid formation.

Influenced by:
Changes in infiltration areas and human activities may affect the surface water chemistry. Sea-level changes causing intrusion of sea-water may influence the surface water chemistry, and low temperature during permafrost may also affect the surface water chemistry. During glaciations, recharge of fresh oxygenated water may affect the surface water chemistry.

Affects:
The surface water chemistry may affect the groundwater chemistry.

Modelling aspects:
