project_title: Nagra Scenario Development for Kristallin-I
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel
host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:
thick steel containers, 
in-tunnel emplacement with bentonite buffer
pfep_description_raw:
Many of the processes occurring within the engineered barriers are temperature dependent.  In particular, to assure the required properties of the bentonite, it is desirable that a significant thickness of bentonite does not experience temperatures above 100 ˚C.  Model results for the thermal evolution of the repository in Project Gewähr 1985 (NGB 85-04; NTB 85-54) showed sensitivity to the assumptions made concerning the resaturation of the bentonite; several different calculations were carried out based on the variable bentonite porewater content, the existence or not of air gaps within the bentonite and the thermal properties of such air gaps.  The results of these calculations have been confirmed as part of a joint project with the Obayashi Corporation of Japan (OBAYASHI 1993a); the more recent calculations also investigate alternative tunnel spacings and uncertainties concerning the thermal properties of the bentonite buffer.  Assuming conservative values for the thermal conductivity and heat capacity of the bentonite, a porewater content which varies as a function of temperature between 7% at 30 ˚C and 0% at  150 ˚C, an ambient rock temperature of 55 ˚C and a reference tunnel separation of 40 m (the reference tunnel separation in Project Gewähr 1985), a maximum temperature of 150 ˚C would be reached at the canister-bentonite interface, but less than half the thickness of bentonite would experience temperatures above 100 ˚C; moreover, the period of elevated temperatures would be rather short (less than 50 years).  The assumption of a reduced emplacement tunnel spacing of 20 m leads to a similar temperature evolution.  More realistic assumptions on thermal properties (higher thermal conductivity and heat capacity) give significantly lower temperatures in the bentonite.

In summary, after reaching a temperature maximum within the first ten years, the temperature gradient decays away over the next few hundred years, so that at the time of possible canister failure (T ≥ 1000 years) ambient geothermal conditions would be reached. 

The FEP is important in engineered barrier design but not in safety assessment calculations.

pfep_description_raw:
After emplacement, groundwater will slowly penetrate the bentonite, which will swell and seal gaps between the blocks, at the bentonite-host rock interface and at the bentonite-canister interface, so that a homogenous mass is formed (see, for example, NTB 87-25).  The time taken for bentonite to saturate depends on the hydraulic and thermal properties of both the bentonite and the surrounding rock.  This coupled problem is difficult to solve because of the effects of the thermal pulse from the waste and perturbation of the host rock caused by tunnel construction.  Modelling studies indicate that saturation times may range from less than 100 years to greater than 1000 years (NTB 86-27). 

In safety assessment calculations, the resaturation time is conservatively neglected (assumed to be instantaneous) in estimating the canister lifetime (delay in saturation could delay the onset of canister corrosion).

pfep_description_raw:
The saturation of the bentonite (see FEP 3.3) creates a swelling pressure on the host rock and waste canister.  It is planned to emplace the bentonite in the form of precompacted blocks with a dry density of 1650 to 1750 kg m-3, in order to provide a swelling pressure in the order of 4 to 18 MPa (KBS TR 80-13; KBS TR 83-46).  This is so that the combined bentonite swelling pressure plus hydrostatic pressure (~ 10 MPa) will not exceed the lithostatic pressure (~ 30 MPa), so that any fracturing of surrounding rock will be avoided.

The FEP is implicitly included in assumed low hydraulic conductivity of bentonite.

host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:

pfep_description_raw: If the bentonite is to be effective as a safety barrier, retarding solute transport and preventing the movement of colloids, it must continue to completely surround the steel canister over a long period of time.  If the canister were able to sink through the bentonite under gravity, then the effectiveness of the bentonite barrier could be lost. Calculations of canister sinking have been carried out in which it is assumed that the bentonite is fully saturated, the clay is modelled using conventional soil-mechanical creep-strain equations (MITCHELL et al. 1968) and data are taken from short-term compression tests on bentonite (BÖRGESSON et al. 1988).  Results indicate a maximum sinking of 1 to 5 mm in 10 000 years, with a rate of sinking that decreases with time (WHITTLE & ARISTORENAS 1991).  This amount of canister displacement is negligible for safety assessment.  A 20% sinking of a canister has been calculated to have negligible effect on total radionuclide release from the buffer (McKINLEY et al. 1992b).  However, confirmation that the creep-strain equations are applicable over the very long periods required for repository safety assessment is lacking and, if future work does not rule out significant canister sinking, then design modifications, e.g. incorporation of a sand-rich layer around the canister or use of stone supports beneath the canister, could be considered to avoid the effect.

pfep_description_raw:
The bentonite porewater chemistry is buffered by ion exchange reactions, mineral equilibria and dissolution of some mineral components of the bentonite.  Key features are mildly alkaline pH (~8.5) and reducing conditions (due to canister corrosion products/Fe(II) minerals in bentonite).  These should be buffered to relatively constant values on a timescale of ~106 years (c.f. Sellin et al. 1991, p111-129).

For the Kristallin-I safety assessment, a range of bentonite porewaters has been defined using an empirical model of groundwater reaction with bentonite that assumes both ion exchange (based on the model of WANNER 1986) and saturation equilibria with mineral phases.  Two groundwaters having a wide range of compositions were selected - one representative of less saline and one of more saline groundwaters.  Eh values of the resulting bentonite porewaters are defined by canister corrosion products, assuming thermodynamic equilibrium between magnetite-hematite or magnetite-goethite (NTB 93-45).

Several models, with significantly different conceptual bases, can equally well simulate experimental bentonite porewater chemistry data and hence such models must be interpreted with caution.  In parallel, therefore, independent estimates have been made by GRAUER (1993) to establish expected constraints on key parameters such as pH and carbonate concentration.  The Eh and pH range (Eh = 1367 to -396 mV and pH = 8.5 to 9.0) which is used in the selection of elemental solubility limits, is consistent with both the modelling and literature studies.

The FEP is included by considereation of porewater chemistry in selection of solubility limits, see FEP 3.18.

waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel
host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:

in-tunnel emplacement with bentonite buffer
pfep_description_raw:
Alteration of bentonite minerals (if it occurred) could lead to reduction of bentonite swelling properties and/or plasticity.  Short-term (thermal) and long-term processes must be considered.

(a)	Short-term processes

The calculated temperature at the canister-bentonite interface, though slightly dependent on the model assumptions, peaks at about 150 ˚C and then drops to below 100 ˚C after 50 years (OBAYASHI 1993a).  The temperature at the rock wall depends less on model assumptions and, assuming a reference 40 m tunnel spacing, reaches a maximum of about 75 ˚C.  Up to a third of the thickness of the bentonite is exposed to temperatures in excess of 100 ˚C for a period of a few tens of years.  In this zone, the interlayer water of unsaturated montmorillonite is easily expelled. At 105 ˚C, a layer of water remains intact, but, between 130 and 150 ˚C, all the water is removed (PUSCH & KARNLAND 1990).  However, such dehydration is reversible.  Shrinkage cracks can form if the bentonite dries out, but it has been shown that these cracks heal in the presence of water (OSCARSON et al. 1990).  Only if the cation-exchange capacity of the montmorillonite is saturated with potassium ions does drying-out at 110 ˚C lead to irreversible layer collapse.  Saturation with potassium can, however, be ruled out by the low rate of supply of this element, and the temperature, which is maintained at around 100 ˚C for only few decades, is insufficient for significant illitisation.  This is supported by investigations of natural smectites which were exposed to higher temperatures (NTB 83-12; NTB 85-60; Pusch & Karnland 1988).

pfep_description_raw:
(b)	Long-term processes

The long-term stability of bentonite at repository temperature has been evaluated by review of the literature (NTB 86-12E; NTB 88-24E; Appendix C in NEA 1993).  The most likely possible alteration process appears to be the transformation of montmorillonite to illite, which would reduce the swelling potential and the cation-exchange capacity of the buffer.  Alteration to chlorite occurs only in waters with high magnesium concentrations, which are not found in the crystalline basement of Northern Switzerland.

Two conditions have to be fulfilled simultaneously for illite to form from montmorillonite, namely (i) an increase in the (tetrahedral) layer charge of the clay; and (ii) replacement of the interlayer ions by potassium ions.  The transition from montmorillonite to illite occurs naturally via intermediate stages of illite and montmorillonite interlayers.  Increasing the layer charge alone does not affect the swelling capability, which is lost only if the interlayer ions are exchanged for potassium.

For the hypothetical case that supply of potassium ions to the repository controls illite formation, the extent of alteration can be estimated from the potassium supply from the groundwater and the cation exchange capacity of the bentonite.  For Project Gewähr 1985 conditions, total conversion of montmorillonite to illite was calculated to take longer than 10 million years (~7x107 years based on calculations in NGB 85-09 and ~4x107, as calculated in NTB 84-48).  This was for an assumed groundwater flowrate of 0.7 litres per canister per year and a potassium concentration in groundwater of 1.15 mM.  For Kristallin-I, the reference water (Area West) contains 0.22 mM K+ (see Table 3.5.2, NTB 84-32), while the reference flowrate through the repository is 3 m3 y-1, equivalent to 1.1 litres per canister per year (see Table 3.7.2, NTB 93-22).  In the Reference Case, therefore, montmorillonite to illite conversion times longer than 108 years are indicated.  Even for the most conservative groundwater flowrates, two orders of magnitude higher than the Reference-Case value, and assuming that all potassium in groundwater is taken up in the alteration process, a montmorillonite "lifetime" of greater than one million years can still be justified.

Natural analogue investigations of montmorillonite-rich clay sediments are a useful tool for assessing the long-term stability of these materials. For example, the clays in the Gulf of Mexico have been studied in considerable depth in connection with oil exploration. These sediments have been deposited continuously over a 200 million year period. Studies of drill cores indicate that, even in old sediments (30 million years), significant illitisation occurs only at temperatures in excess of 80 ˚C. Independent of geological age, the maximum illite component is in the order of 80%. The temperature required for illitisation to begin is between 60 and 90 ˚C and alteration to 70 to 80% illite occurs in the temperature range 90 to 140 ˚C (FREED & PEACOR 1989). Evaluation of the large number of investigations carried out on natural analogues leads to the conclusion that, with a long-term temperature within the bentonite close to that of the host rock (55 ˚C), there will be no drastic change in swelling capability, hydraulic conductivity or cation exchange capacity of the bentonite in time periods well in excess of one million years. The formation of mixed illite-montmorillonite layers during the course of time cannot be ruled out, but complete illitisation can be.

Finally, although the alteration to illite may reduce the swelling capacity and cation-exchange capacity of the buffer, illite has many of the favourable properties required of a buffer material, i.e. low permeability and microporous structure that will prevent colloid transport. Illite has also been considered as a potential buffer material (BROOKINS 1984).

pfep_description_raw:
There are indications that the interaction of water vapour with bentonite can cause cementation, with relatively rapid loss of swelling capacity (the "Couture effect"; see COUTURE 1985).  This has been interpreted in terms of silica cementation (NTB 89-03; Pusch & Karnland 1988; Pusch & Karnland 1990).  However, such cementation is weak and does not have significant effects in highly compacted bentonite (SHARLAND 1991).

A set of hydrothermal field tests on the resaturation of compacted clay, conducted for up to 4 years at a maximum 170-180 ˚C and a gradient of 13 ˚C cm-1 (PUSCH et al. 1992) showed that there was considerable cementation of the clay, causing brittleness and loss of expansivity but only within a few centimetres of the steel surface of the heat source.  It thus seems probable that any cementation that occurs is limited to the zone immediately around the canister, leaving a thick annulus of unaffected bentonite.  Even if the loss of swelling is more extensive, it should be noted that, following water vapour treatment the swelling capacity of bentonite is reduced but is not completely lost (COUTURE 1985).  For the emplacement densities considered, the remnant (intercrystalline) swelling is sufficient to ensure that the bentonite has an adequately low permeability (NTB 88-24E).

pfep_description_raw:
Corrosion of the steel canister under anaerobic conditions produces magnetite.  There is very little information on potential interactions between this corrosion product and the bentonite and the thermodynamic data required for making a reliable evaluation are lacking.  However, experiments with iron- and magnetite-bentonite mixtures at 80 ˚C show, after 27 and 29 weeks respectively, that there is no adverse change in the bentonite properties. 

Potential interactions between magnetite and montmorillonite have been discussed in detail on the basis of chemical and crystal-chemistry data.  The most likely of these reactions leads to the formation of new iron silicate phases; the formation of chamosite, greenalite or nontronite is considered likely and these reaction products have only a limited swelling capability.  However, given the quantity ratios in the repository, a complete reaction of this type could alter only a limited amount of the montmorillonite.

pfep_description_raw:
Long-term corrosion experiments in which hydrogen evolution is measured indicate low rates of evolution, which justify the assumption of a long-term hydrogen generation rate in the range 0.02 to 0.2 moles m-2 y-1 (see FEP 2.16).  Since the possible rate of loss of hydrogen by aqueous diffusion at the canister surface is estimated at about 0.2 moles y-1 per canister (0.02 moles m-2 y-1; ANDREWS 1993), it is uncertain whether or not a gas phase will form.  However, if a gas phase does form around the canister surface, this is itself likely to reduce the rate of corrosion and the rate of production of further hydrogen.  If future studies reveal that the rate of hydrogen generation will exceed the rate at which hydrogen can diffuse from the surface, it may be necessary to consider special design features, such as the incorporation of a sand capillary-breaking layer (NTB 85-35) to provide additional buffer volume and surface area for hydrogen dissolution.

At low gas pressures, the gas permeability of the bentonite is low but a 100 times increase in permeability occurs at around 30 to 70% of swelling pressure, the low gas permeability being restored when gas pressure is relieved.  This is interpreted as escape of gas by "channelling" through connected pore spaces.  Experimental evidence (e.g. DeCANNIERE et al. 1993) indicates that, when gas pressures are applied across clay plugs, only a tiny fraction of the pore space is evacuated prior to gas breakthrough; indeed, it is often impossible to detect the gas flowpaths except by X-ray tomography.  Recent modelling studies (e.g. GRINDROD et al. 1994) are able to reproduce this behaviour and indicate that gas can overcome the capillary forces and hydrostatic pressure to pass through larger connected capillary pores of typically 10 nm, which is consistent with the estimate of minimum effective diameter of connected porosity in the bentonite buffer (NTB 88-26).  Thus it is likely that no significant physical disturbance of the clay is involved and no degradation of the bentonite hydraulic properties or colloid retention properties is expected due to the passage of the gas.

pfep_description_raw:
Assuming any gas tranport is negligible (see FEP 3.17), the low permeability of the saturated bentonite (see FEP 3.8) ensures that radionuclides migrate through the buffer by aqueous diffusion only.  In addition, they may be sorbed/retarded (see FEP 3.10);  colloid transport is precluded (see FEP 3.11)

The diffusion of radionuclides in compacted bentonite is described by an element-specific apparent diffusion constant.  The apparent diffusion constant is usually expressed as the quotient of a pore diffusion constant and a retention factor. The pore diffusion constant takes account of radionuclide retardation due to the tortuosity and constrictivity of the pore space and of processes such as ion exclusion.  An effective diffusion constant (the product of the pore diffusion constant and the porosity) within the saturated bentonite at 55 C of 6.3x10-3 m2 y-1 (2x10-10 m2 s-1) and a porosity of 0.38 are assumed, as in Project Gewähr 1985.  The retention factor includes retardation due to chemical interaction (sorption) of the radionuclide with the mineral surfaces in the bentonite.

Apparent diffusion constants for compacted bentonite are primarily functions of the composition of the pore solution, its redox state and the physical properties of the pore space.  These factors are taken into account when selecting the element-specific diffusion constants for Kristallin-I safety analysis (NTB 93-06).  In cases where measurements have been carried out under conditions appropriate to Kristallin-I, direct use is made of apparent diffusion constants.  Sorption constants are calculated from the apparent diffusion constants (and the assumed pore diffusion constant ) and compared with sorption constants determined directly in batch experiments.  The values of sorption constants selected for the safety analysis are always the lesser of the values obtained by the two methods.

For the Kristallin-I safety analysis both a "realistic-conservative" and a "conservative" value of sorption constants is selected for each safety-relevant chemical element.  The "realistic-conservative" value is appropriate for sorption under the reference conditions specified after canister failure and is a value which can be realistically supported from the available data.  For the corresponding "conservative" sorption constant, the scatter of values measured under reference conditions, as well as some feasible perturbations of the reference conditions that are likely to have the maximum effect on the sorption behaviour of that element, are considered.

Assuming any gas tranport is negligible (see FEP 3.17), the low permeability of the saturated bentonite (see FEP 3.8) ensures that radionuclides migrate through the buffer by aqueous diffusion only.  In addition, they may be sorbed/retarded (see FEP 3.10);  colloid transport is precluded (see FEP 3.11)

The diffusion of radionuclides in compacted bentonite is described by an element-specific apparent diffusion constant.  The apparent diffusion constant is usually expressed as the quotient of a pore diffusion constant and a retention factor. The pore diffusion constant takes account of radionuclide retardation due to the tortuosity and constrictivity of the pore space and of processes such as ion exclusion.  An effective diffusion constant (the product of the pore diffusion constant and the porosity) within the saturated bentonite at 55 C of 6.3x10-3 m2 y-1 (2x10-10 m2 s-1) and a porosity of 0.38 are assumed, as in Project Gewähr 1985.  The retention factor includes retardation due to chemical interaction (sorption) of the radionuclide with the mineral surfaces in the bentonite.

Apparent diffusion constants for compacted bentonite are primarily functions of the composition of the pore solution, its redox state and the physical properties of the pore space.  These factors are taken into account when selecting the element-specific diffusion constants for Kristallin-I safety analysis (NTB 93-06).  In cases where measurements have been carried out under conditions appropriate to Kristallin-I, direct use is made of apparent diffusion constants.  Sorption constants are calculated from the apparent diffusion constants (and the assumed pore diffusion constant ) and compared with sorption constants determined directly in batch experiments.  The values of sorption constants selected for the safety analysis are always the lesser of the values obtained by the two methods.

For the Kristallin-I safety analysis both a "realistic-conservative" and a "conservative" value of sorption constants is selected for each safety-relevant chemical element.  The "realistic-conservative" value is appropriate for sorption under the reference conditions specified after canister failure and is a value which can be realistically supported from the available data.  For the corresponding "conservative" sorption constant, the scatter of values measured under reference conditions, as well as some feasible perturbations of the reference conditions that are likely to have the maximum effect on the sorption behaviour of that element, are considered.

in-tunnel emplacement with bentonite buffer
pfep_description_raw:
Even in the harsh conditions expected in the engineered barriers of a HLW repository, microbiological activity cannot be precluded (NTB 85-43).  Microbiological activity, with the associated production of organic complexants, could reduce the effectiveness of the engineered barriers by increasing near-field solubilities and decreasing sorption (see also the discussion of the microbially mediated corrosion of the canister by sulphides - FEP 2.5).  However, the maximum extent of such activity is constrained by the low rates of supply of some key elements and low availability of usable energy for microbial growth in this extremely oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) environment.  The relative simplicity of the disposal system allows these constraints to be quantified from the rates of nutrient supply and the maximum rate of supply of chemical energy from redox reactions. 

The maximum steady-state biomass production calculated for Kristallin-I repository conditions is 10-5 kg (dry) y-1 per waste package (McKINLEY & HAGENLOCHER 1993).  In the worst possible case, this high biomass production would be balanced by a similar rate of production of organic by-products, available for complexation. This source of organic carbon would be large when compared to the rate of supply from groundwater (10-8 kg y-1 per waste package). Furthermore, assuming an average molecular weight of 103 daltons - corresponding to a typical size of siderophores, which are extremely strong specific complexants for some radionuclides (BIRCH & BACHOFEN 1990; BRAINARD et al. 1992), these organic by-products would be mobile in the bentonite pores. However, even the pessimistic assumption that all organics complex solely with actinides would only approximately double the maximum release rate, since the production rate (10-5 moles y-1) is roughly equivalent to the total, solubility-limited release rate of actinides to the bentonite.  Such an increase is insignificant compared to other uncertainties involved in the estimation of solubility limits. 

Natural analogue studies link microbial populations at redox fronts with trapping of trace elements, which suggests that the net effect of microbiological activity in such an environment will be catalysis of redox reactions and the formation of secondary minerals, thus tending to reduce radionuclide releases (e.g. NTB 89-17).  Considering the above, the net consequences of microbial activity in terms of complexant production can be safely neglected.

pfep_description_raw:
Radionuclides in aqueous solution in the buffer will be constrained by elemental solubility limits (which will be function of porewater chemistry, see FEP 3.9).

The low solubility of many key radionuclides is an important constraint limiting their concentrations and hence their rate of diffusion through the bentonite.  Because of the limitations of current models and databases for quantifying solubility limits, a number of simplifications are made in deriving a solubility database:
	 –  Solubility limits are defined for a water chemistry which would correspond to bentonite porewater with redox conditions buffered by canister corrosion products.  Although based on the reference bentonite porewater compositions (pH range 8.5 to 9.0), uncertainties in groundwater composition are also taken into account.
	 –  A chemical thermodynamic model is used to assess solubility limits for a range of pure mineral phases which could potentially form under the expected conditions.
 	–  The output of the thermodynamic model is reviewed in terms of literature data on the formation of identified minerals and measured concentrations of the element of interest in relevant natural and laboratory systems.
	 –  The likelihood of formation of pure phases is assessed in terms of the relative inventories of elements with similar chemical properties in the waste.
	 –  Bearing in mind the intention to err on the site of conservatism in the derivation of parameters values (i.e. overprediction of solubility limits), expert judgement is used to select elemental solubility limits which are defensible as "realistic-conservative" and "conservative" values.  The procedure and results of this selection procedure are documented in NTB 94-08.

host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:

pfep_description_raw:
Radiation can cause disassociation of molecules, e.g. water, leading to change in chemical conditions and gas production.  Prior to canister failure this effect must be negligible due to the shielding provided by the massive steel container (c.f. FEP 2.11).

The progress of an oxidising front from a cracked canister into the bentonite has been calculated for a pessimistic case in which the following assumptions are made: (1) a high value for the rate of production of radiolytic oxidant, which does not decrease with time, is assumed; (2) the products of alpha radiolysis are hydrogen, which is chemically inert and lost from the near field, and oxygen, which is reactive;  (3) the inner surfaces of the canister and the hypothetical crack are coated with a non-reactive layer, e.g. Fe2O3;  (4) the oxidant is consumed only by reaction with aqueous Fe(II) in bentonite porewater, originating from groundwater.  For the expected concentrations of Fe(II), 10-6 to 10-7 M, only very limited penetration of the oxidation front into the bentonite is predicted, and, even for very low Fe(II) concentrations in porewater, 10-8 M, the redox front does not penetrate more than halfway into the buffer (McKINLEY et al. 1992b).

Realistically, the oxidation potential of the steel canister and corrosion products will ensure reducing conditions and there is no need to consider the case of oxidising conditions in the near field in assessment calculations.

pfep_description_raw:
During tunnel and shaft construction, some stress relief, leading to dilation of joints and fractures, is expected in an axial zone of up to one diameter width surrounding the tunnels and shafts; this is termed the excavation-disturbed zone (EDZ).  The characteristics and long-term importance of this zone are uncertain.  It is possible that the swelling pressure of the bentonite may restore dilation of open joints, so that the long-term effect is negligible.  On the other hand, the zone may remain as a higher-permeability zone and hence act as a preferential path for both water flow and radionuclide transport.

The existence of an EDZ is conservatively assumed in near field model boundary conditions.

During repository construction and operation the EDZ will partially desaturate and the local hydrological regime may be disturbed.

After backfilling, groundwater re-enters host rock zones which were partially desaturated during the operational phase.  The hydrology of the EDZ fissure system and local host rock stabilises.  This process has been studied at the Grimsel Test Site (NTB 93-10) where it was concluded that there is no irreversible effect occurring due to the desaturation, and that host rock resaturation occurs within a few years.

In assessment models, it is assumed that resaturation is immediate.

pfep_description_raw:
After resaturation, water flow through the EDZ depends on the contrast in hydraulic conductivity between the EDZ and the host rock and absolute conductivity of the EDZ.  It also depends on the relationship between the hydraulic gradient and the tunnel layout/orientation (c.f. NTB 88-26 Figure 3).

In Kristallin-I calculations, water flow past the repository place is assumed to be uniformly distributed.  A discontinous EDZ and variations in host rock permability could produce a distribution of water flows leading to reduced releases from some canisters, but increased releases from others.  A worst case situation is scoped by the zero concentration outer boundary parameter variation.

pfep_description_raw:
The TRU (long-lived intermediate-level or ‘transuranic’ waste) silos contain large quantities of cementitious backfill and structural material, as well as small quantities of organic material within the disposed wastes.  Over time, the interactions of groundwater with the silos will lead to a plume of cementitious species, which is expected to alter the mineralogy of water-conducting features in its path.

In the Kristallin-I reference design, the TRU silos are sited in a separate block of low-permeability crystalline basement.  They are thus separated from any HLW emplacement panels by a major fault zone that may be either non-conductive (acting as a barrier to groundwater flow) or water-conducting (acting as a source of dilution). In the Kristallin-I assessment, it is assumed that the TRU silos could be sited so that there would be no hydrological or hydrochemical effect on the HLW panels.  The relative siting of the TRU silos and HLW panels is a subject that will require further consideration on a site-specific basis.

project_title: Nagra Scenario Development for Kristallin-I
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel
host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:

pfep_description_raw:
At closure, massive concrete tunnel seals and bentonite-concrete rock grouting will be emplaced to hydraulically isolate the individual HLW panels and TRU silos from each other and from higher permeability zones in the host rock.  Similarly seals will be emplaced in the shafts and investigation boreholes.

Shaft and tunnel seals may consist of short sections of the access tunnels and shafts filled with a low-permeability material (e.g. compacted bentonite blocks) and contained, on either side, by thick plugs (e.g. concrete).  Bentonite can be altered by alkaline solutions (cement porewater).  However, only a limited thickness of bentonite adjacent to the concrete plugs is expected to be affected, due to the limited extent of diffusion of such solutions into the bentonite.

The practicality and effectiveness of seals for boreholes, shafts and tunnels has been investigated. The seals are expected to provide complete hydraulic isolation of the repository panels, so that the only route for radionuclide transport is by movement through the undisturbed low-permeability host rock.

The case of ineffective shaft and tunnel seals, although not expected, is represented by two alternative models within an alternative scenario.

waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel
host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:

pfep_description_raw:
The crystalline low permeability domain (LPD) consists of volume(s) of crystalline rock, generally at depths greater than 400-600m below the upper surface of the crystalline basement, whose average effective hydraulic conductivity is small (generally less than 10-10 m s-1).

The hydraulic properties of the crystalline basement are controlled by the properties of the small-scale water-conducting features which dissect it.  In Area West, the transmissivity and density of these features, and therefore of the hydraulic conductivity of the rock through which they pass, decreases at depths greater than 400-600 m below the upper surface of the crystalline basement.  The transmissivities measured within this lower rock unit vary little within Area West and the unit is termed the low-permeability domain (LPD).  In Area East, the existence of the LPD is uncertain; substantially higher transmissivities are measured in both the upper and lower units than in Area West, although data are limited to a single borehole and thus may be unrepresentative of Area East as a whole.

For groundwater flow modelling, the LPD of Area West is assigned a hydraulic conductivity of 10-3 m y-1.  Two alternative hypotheses are adopted in the case of Area East: one in which a hydraulic conductivity of 0.3 m y-1 is assigned, based on the (limited) data for the area, and a second in which the hydraulic conductivity is assumed to be equal that of Area West.  The former hypothesis (the more conservative) is adopted in radionuclide transport calculations.

project_title: Nagra Scenario Development for Kristallin-I
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel
host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:
thick steel containers,

pfep_description_raw:
Groundwater flow in the crystalline basement is controlled by the hydrogeological framework, which is the combination of structural features and units of which the LPD is one, and the driving forces which are dominated by topographic effects, i.e. recharge in outcropping regions of higher elevation.  The Black Forest is expected to be the principal recharge area for groundwater in the crystalline rocks of Northern Switzerland.  On the basis of local-scale groundwater flow modelling, within blocks of the LPD, narrow marginal zones occur along side the MWCF within which flow is directed towards the adjoining faults.  Away from the marginal zones, flow may carry radionuclides either upwards to the overlying HPD, or laterally to a down-gradient MWCF, depending on the spacing assumed for the MWCF.

For the modelling of radionuclide transport, groundwater flow is assumed to be confined to open channels within the water-conducting features of the LPD.  The rate of flow within the channels, and hence the advection velocity for radionuclides, is determined from hydrogeological modelling, in which, for outcrop areas of crystalline rocks such as the Southern Black Forest, prescribed constant heads are assigned that approximate the topography and provide the principal driving force for flow.  Alternative assumptions are considered regarding the direction of flow (see FEP 5.4).  Uncertainty in groundwater flow is taken into account by parameter variations.

pfep_description_raw:
Radionuclides would be transported from the bentonite-host rock interface along a variety of pathways, depending on their point of release and on the pattern of groundwater flow.  Radionuclides would migrate through the LPD of Area West, or the lower unit of Area East, and would exit either at the interface with a major water-conducting fault (MWCF) or, in the case of Area West, at the interface with the overlying higher-permeability domain (HPD).  A feature of the current repository design is that no emplacement tunnel, at any point on its surface, is closer that 100 m either to a MWCF or to the lower boundary of the HPD.  Hence, the minimum distance from any part of the emplacement tunnel system to any of these more permeable features is 100 m.

Modelling of transport through the LPD (Area West) or the lower unit (Area East) requires the specification of a single, representative, one-dimensional flow path from the repository to a feature of higher permeability.  For both Area West and Area East, the Reference-Case flow path length is set to 200 m, irrespective of whether the representative flow path is principally horizontal, exiting at a MWCF, or principally vertical, exiting at the HPD.  This distance corresponds to the product of the minimum direct flow path length (100 m) and the ratio of actual flowpath length to direct flowpath length (2).  In Area West, a range from 1.2 to approximately 3 has been calculated for this ratio on the basis of groundwater-flow modelling; a value of 2 is adopted as a reference value, with a conservative parameter variation of 1.  A reference value of 2 is also assumed to be applicable to Area East.

Path length of 200m is adopted as the reference value in assessment modelling.  Transport direct to the HPD is adopted as the Reference Model Assumption; transport to a MWCF and thence to the HPD is considered as an alternative model assumption.

project_title: Nagra Scenario Development for Kristallin-I
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel
host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:

in-tunnel emplacement with bentonite buffer
pfep_description_raw:
Solubility limits appropriate to the groundwater chemistry are not expected to be exceeded (see FEP 5.16) and so radionuclides in the LPD would exist either in solution in pores within the rock or sorbed onto solid surfaces.  In pores through which groundwater flow occurs, predominantly the open channels of the small-scale water-conducting features (see FEP 5.2), radionuclides in solution would be transported by advection. Interconnections between channels with different properties, and variability in those properties along individual channels, would give rise to mechanical dispersion.  Radionuclides would also diffuse from this flow porosity into adjacent pores where the groundwater is stagnant (see FEP 5.6).  This matrix diffusion would result in a retardation of advective transport.  Radionuclides would sorb onto the surfaces of the channels and the matrix pores, leading to further retardation, and onto groundwater colloids (see FEP 5.15), leading either to enhanced or diminished retardation, depending on the mobility and stability of the colloids.  The degree of sorption is influenced by mineralogy and groundwater chemistry.

The channels within the small-scale water-conducting features are modelled by a conduit of simple geometry (constant cross-section along its length), which follows the one-dimensional representative flow path (see FEP 5.4).  The model conduit is either parallel-walled or tubular, depending on the dimensions assumed for the channels.  In the Reference Case, where the channels are assumed to be predominantly broad and widely spaced, a parallel-walled model conduit is considered to be more appropriate. pfep_description_raw:
Radionuclides can migrate from the flow porosity (i.e. the open channels of small-scale water-conducting features) into the static water of the pores of the adjacent wallrock by molecular diffusion.  This process is known as matrix diffusion.  The rate of diffusion through the wallrock pores is a function of pore geometry (constrictivity and tortuosity), the surface properties of the pores (charge) and the size and charge of the diffusing species.  There is uncertainty in the extent of connected porosity in the wallrock, which determines the maximum depth to which radionuclides can diffuse.  A lower limit of 1 cm has been derived on the basis of natural analogue studies.  However, it is likely that the entire fracture infill and the altered zone of wallrock immediately adjacent to the channels (see FEP 5.2) is accessible by diffusion, and possibly also the unaltered wallrock at greater distances from the channels.

Diffusion is modelled using a diffusion constant based on a survey of experimental results for comparable crystalline rocks.  The constant is assumed to be nuclide-independent.   “Realistic-conservative” and “conservative” values are defined.  Matrix diffusion is restricted to one spatial dimension, directed normally to the surface of the parallel-walled or tubular conduit. Matrix diffusion is, in the model, confined to a spatially-limited region of connected porosity surrounding the conduit.  In this region, the transport properties (i.e. diffusion constant, porosity, sorption parameters) are uniform.  Because of uncertainty as to whether the unaltered wallrock, as well as altered wallrock and fracture infill, is accessible by matrix diffusion, alternative model assumptions are applied in determining the extent of the modelled region.  The Reference Model Assumption is that only altered wallrock and fracture infill are accessible.  An alternative assumption is that unaltered wallrock is also accessible. A conservative parameter variation, in which only 1 cm of altered wallrock is assumed to be accessible, is also considered.  The fracture infill, altered wallrock and unaltered wallrock differ in their porosities. In assigning a single porosity value to the modelled region, which may contain all three rock types, a low (conservative) porosity is used.

pfep_description_raw:
The groundwater chemistry is controlled by a range of factors, including the rock mineralogy, recharge conditions and residence time.  For repository performance, the most important chemical parameters are the ionic strength, the pH and the Eh.  On the basis of a regional synthesis of groundwater chemistry, the predominant groundwater of the LPD of Area West is of the Na-SO4-(Cl-HCO3) type, with about 1 g l-1 total dissolved solids, a pH of 7.66 and an Eh of -0.18m volts.  This is taken as a reference water for Area West.  A reference water for Area East has also been defined, although on the basis of limited data.  This is of the Na-HCO3-SO4-(Cl) type with 0.5 g l-1 dissolved solids, a pH of 7.68 and an Eh of - 0.03 volts.  The groundwater chemistry determines radionuclide speciation.  This, together with the mineralogy of pore surfaces, influences sorption (see FEP 5.9).

The groundwater chemistry of the LPD is assumed to be unperturbed by the presence of the repository.  In particular, radionuclides will be released in trace concentrations and bentonite porewater will not influence groundwater composition downstream of the repository.   The groundwater chemistry is taken into account in the selection of sorption parameter values.

pfep_description_raw:
The interaction of dissolved radionuclides with rock surfaces, excluding precipitation, is termed sorption. Radionuclides can sorb on the surfaces of open channels within water-conducting features and also on the surfaces of pores accessible by matrix diffusion (i.e. pore surfaces within fracture infill and wallrock).  The degree to which radionuclides sorb on pore surfaces depends on the elemental concentration (i.e. the concentration of the element of which the radionuclide under consideration is an isotope) and on the properties of the rock-water system under consideration - in particular, the mineralogy and the groundwater chemistry.  For the LPD of the crystalline basement, data is available on the mineralogies for the component parts of the different types of water-conducting features (see FEP 5.7) and on the chemical composition, pH and Eh of the groundwaters of Area West and Area East (see FEP 5.8).  For a particular rock-water system, radionuclide partitioning between the sorbed phase and the aqueous phase can be determined experimentally.  For Kristallin-I, measurements on LPD samples are complemented with an appraisal of the wider sorption literature, including measurements on pure minerals.  In this case, sorption within the LPD is determined by adding contributions from the constituent minerals, weighted according to their relative abundances.

The concentration of radionuclides sorbed onto the surfaces of open channels is assumed to be small with respect to that sorbed onto matrix pore surfaces and is neglected in assessment calculations.  Sorption on matrix pore surfaces is assumed to be both completely reversible and rapid with respect to the transport times of radionuclides through the LPD.  The assumption that sorption is reversible and rapid is consistent with the sorption database used (data comes mainly from relatively short-term experiments, in which the sorption processes operative are those with rapid kinetics).  It is possible that, on longer timescales, other sorption processes, especially irreversible sorption processes, might become important.  However, the effect of these would be to further retard radionuclide release and they can, therefore, be conservatively neglected in the modelling of transport.  In the Reference Model Assumptions, sorption is represented by a concentration-independent distribution coefficient, i.e. linear sorption is assumed, quantified by a sorption constant Kd, equal to the equilibrium radionuclide concentration in the sorbed phase, divided by the concentration in the aqueous phase.  “Realistic-conservative” and “conservative” Kd values are defined for each safety-relevant element.  The effect of differences in mineralogy between different rock types (fracture infill, altered and unaltered wallrock within different types of water-conducting features) has been found to be small and Kd values which are independent of rock type are used in assessment calculations.  Although the partitioning of many elements in natural rock-water systems between the sorbed and aqueous phases is known to show some concentration dependence, of the elements with safety-relevant isotopes, only caesium has been studied sufficiently to justify sorption also being represented by a non-linear isotherm (see FEP 5.10).

pfep_description_raw:
In general, the partitioning of radionuclides between sorbed and aqueous phases is dependent on elemental concentration (i.e. the concentration of the element of which the radionuclide under consideration is an isotope). Where such dependency exists, sorption is said to be non-linear.  Sorption is quantified by a relationship termed an isotherm, which may be linear or non-linear.  There are several forms on non-linear isotherm, including the Freundlich and Langmuir isotherms.

Although many of the safety-relevant radionuclides may be better characterised by a non-linear isotherm, rather than a linear isotherm (i.e. a Kd value), a suitable database is available only for caesium.  Sorption of caesium is described in Kristallin-I by a Freundlich isotherm.  In the Reference Case, the exponent of the Freundlich isotherm is set to unity (in which case the Freundlich isotherm reduces to a linear isotherm) and a Kd value for the resulting linear isotherm is selected conservatively, such that the amount of sorption calculated using this Kd is always less than with the full Freundlich isotherm.  This enables the reference geosphere transport code for Kristallin-I (RANCHMD) to be employed.  In a parameter variation, the full Freundlich isotherm (with an exponent of 0.7) is used.  This requires the use of an extended geosphere transport code (RANCHMDNL).

pfep_description_raw:
Saline waters are found in the sedimentary units overlying the crystalline basement, in the Permo-Carboniferous Trough and, at a small number of sampling points, in the crystalline basement itself.   Hydrochemical and isotopic evidence suggests that the composition of most groundwater in the crystalline basement is a product of chemical evolution of water entirely within crystalline rock and that the intrusion of saline water from the surrounding sediments is minimal.  Most saline waters within the crystalline basement occur in zones of restricted circulation and great age.  However, some saline waters, in particular those observed to the north of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough, could have arisen as a result of limited intrusion from the sediments of the Trough. 

Since, on the basis of hydrochemical and isotopic evidence, there is very little intrusion of saline groundwater from the Permo-Carboniferous Trough into the adjacent crystalline basement, the southern boundary of the regional-scale groundwater flow model is assigned a no-flow boundary condition.  With regard to groundwater chemistry, reference groundwaters have been defined for both Area West (1 g l-1 total dissolved solids) and Area East (0.5 g l-1) on the basis of a regional synthesis of data.  These reference groundwaters form the basis of calculations of sorption parameters for geosphere transport modelling.  The occurrence of a small number of samples of higher salinity (5 to 13 g l-1) is neglected.  However, it is possible that at least part of a repository in Area West could be affected by small amounts of the more saline waters.

The possibility of intrusion of saline groundwater, e.g. from the Permo-Carboniferous Trough, should be considered as a factor in siting and in site-specific assessments.

pfep_description_raw:
The distribution of temperature within the crystalline basement is expected to be correlated with a distribution of groundwater density.  Variations in density provide a driving force for groundwater flow.  The geothermal anomaly observed in Central Northern Switzerland (see FEP 5.13) is believed to reflect the overprinting of conductive heat transport by convective heat transport, resulting from the density-driven flow of deep groundwaters along fault systems.  The fault systems in question lie along the northern and southern boundaries of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough; these correlate, as a first approximation, with the two maxima of the anomaly.

Density variations due to temperature (or salinity) are not considered in the domain within which groundwater flow is modelled in Kristallin-I.  However, the density-driven upwelling of groundwater, which is believed to occur in the fault systems lying along the northern margin of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough (the southern boundary of the regional-scale model), is included as a non-zero flux boundary condition along a small part (500 m) of the bottom of the regional-scale model, at its southern limit.  The Darcy flux hypothesised to help explain the geothermal anomaly is 2 x 10-10 m s-1, which corresponds (for a hydraulic conductivity within the fault systems of 10-7 m s-1) to a vertical (upward) gradient of 0.002.  This variant does not produce significantly different flow regime.

pfep_description_raw:
The temperature field within the crystalline basement is determined by (i) the large-scale geological and petrophysical properties of the rock (e.g. radiogenic heat production, thermal conductivity) and (ii) by the hydrogeological properties of the rock (in particular, the hydraulic conductivity), which provide a means by which convective heat transport via fluid phases can occur.  This can be either free convection (i.e. thermally-driven circulation of deep groundwaters) or forced convection, in areas where groundwater circulation is maintained by marked hydraulic gradients.  Temperature data from deep boreholes, together with data on thermal properties of the rock, enable the temperature field, the geothermal gradient and the heat-flux field to be mapped. The vertical geothermal gradient is depth-dependent and has therefore been calculated for two depth intervals:
  •  gradient for the interval 0 - 500 m:  40 - 45 ˚C km-1;
  •  gradient for the interval 750 - 1700 m:  35 - 40 ˚C km-1.

On this basis, the ambient rock temperature at repository depth (1050 - 1200 m) is expected to be about 55 ˚C. There is a geothermal anomaly in Central Northern Switzerland, with two maxima: one to the north of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough (160 mW m-2)  and the other approximately above its southern margin (170 mW m-2), coinciding with the main overthrust of the folded Jura.  This is explained by convective heat fluxes in the form of upwelling deep groundwaters.

Temperature gradients may drive groundwater flow; this is neglected in groundwater flow modelling for Kristallin-I, see FEP 5.12. Temperature is also a factor in determining groundwater speciation, and hence the sorption parameters for geosphere transport modelling.  The ambient temperature of the repository host rock is a factor influencing the time-development of the temperature distribution within the repository itself.  Many of the processes occurring within the engineered barriers are temperature dependent - for example, bentonite-alteration processes and the interaction of bentonite with groundwater (hence, bentonite porewater composition and sorption constants for near-field transport).  To assure the required properties of the bentonite, it is desirable that a significant thickness of bentonite does not experience temperatures above 100 ˚C.  An ambient rock temperature of 55 ˚C has been assumed in modelling the thermal evolution of the repository.  Results show that the temperature of the bentonite falls to a value close to that of the surrounding rock after about 100 years, with only a small part of the bentonite experiencing temperatures higher than 100 ˚C before that time.

pfep_description_raw:
Estimates for the orientation of regional stress field in the crystalline basement of Northern Switzerland, as derived from seismotectonics and from in-situ measurements, are approximately the same: a NW-SE direction for the horizontal component of the principal stress (sH). There are no direct measurements that give information on the magnitudes of the stress-field components. However, these can be inferred from data from outside the region as follows: |sH| ª  30 - 50 MPa (135˚±10˚); |sh| ª 15 - 25 MPa (45˚±10˚); |sv| ª 30 - 50 MPa.  On a smaller scale, the stress distribution in Northern Switzerland and the surrounding areas is not uniform and individual zones with differing behaviour can be identified. These zones correspond more or less to the individual tectonic units. There is an apparent decoupling of the regional stress field in the basement from that in the sedimentary cover. In the Southern Black Forest and possibly also in Northern Switzerland, young and recent faulting along Hercinian lineaments is indicated both by geomorphology and by seismotectonics and is consistent with the interpretation of the recent stress field.

Data on the regional stress regime are not used directly in post-closure safety-assessment calculations.  However, they provide constraints on the development of long-term scenarios of geological evolution.

host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland

pfep_description_raw:
Colloids, which are present in all groundwaters, may influence the transport of radionuclides through the LPD. Radionuclides, as aqueous species, may sorb, either reversibly or irreversibly, onto natural colloids.  These colloids may be filtered during transport through the LPD, thus reducing radionuclide migration (particularly if sorption of radionuclides on colloids is irreversible).  However, radionuclides associated with colloids may be excluded from matrix pores (e.g. on account of the size of the colloids), and would thus be unretarded by the processes of matrix diffusion (see FEP 5.6) and sorption on matrix pore surfaces (see FEP 5.9), so enhancing radionuclide migration (again, particularly if sorption of radionuclides on colloids is irreversible).  Even where the colloid concentration is low (an upper bound for Area West is 0.1 ppm), these effects may be significant because colloids have a high specific surface area on which sorption can take place.  Whether colloids act predominantly to retard transport (i.e. by sorption of aqueous species and subsequent filtration) or enhance transport (i.e. by sorption of aqueous species and exclusion from matrix pores) is unclear and depends on the properties of the colloids and the water-conducting features.  An additional effect of sorption on colloids in the LPD would be to reduce radionuclide concentration in solution at the bentonite-host rock interface; this would increase the radionuclide-concentration gradient across the bentonite, thus increasing radionuclide releases from the repository near field.

The Reference Model Assumptions for the LPD do not include colloid-facilitated radionuclide transport; the concentration of groundwater colloids is thought to be too low to sorb a significant fraction of dissolved radionuclides.  However, as an alternative model assumption, upper-bound values are assumed for colloid concentration and the distribution coefficients for sorption on colloids and a simple model is employed in which filtration is neglected and all radionuclides sorbed on colloids are excluded from matrix pores.  In this alternative model, reversible sorption on colloids is assumed.  The most pessimistic case would also include irreversible sorption on colloids.  A scenario in which radionuclides are irreversibly sorbed on colloids, and those colloids are unfiltered during transport through the geosphere, could take little credit for the geosphere as a migration barrier. The occurrence of irreversible sorption on groundwater colloids is an open question.  However, this scenario is incorporated within the definition of the Robust Scenario, which assumes the most pessimistic possible representation of the geological barrier.

pfep_description_raw:
The TRU (long-lived intermediate-level waste) silos contain large quantities of cementitious backfill and structural material, as well as small quantities of organic material within the disposed wastes.  Over time, the interactions of groundwater with the silos will lead to a plume of cementitious and organic material, which is expected to alter the mineralogy of the water-conducting features in its path.  It thus has the potential to alter groundwater flow and the solubilities and sorption properties of radionuclides migrating with the groundwater. 

In the Kristallin-I reference design, the TRU silos are sited in a block of LPD, separate from the blocks used for HLW emplacement.  The major fault zone/zones between the silos and HLW emplacement panels may be either water-conducting, in which case they would act as a source of dilution, or non-conducting, in which case they would act as a barrier to groundwater flow.

It is assumed that the TRU silos could be sited such that there would be no hydrological or hydrochemical effect on the migration of radionuclides from the HLW emplacement panels through the LPD.  The relative siting of TRU silos and HLW panels is a subject for future consideration on a site-specific basis.

pfep_description_raw:
The crystalline basement of Areas West (LPD and HPD) and East is intersected to below repository depth by major, sub-vertical regional faults of first and second order.  First-order faults are of lengths > 10 km and have widths in the range 100 m to 1 km (generally in several fault branches).  Second-order faults range in length from a few km to about 10 km and have widths in the range of several m to 100 m.  Some of these faults may be water conducting (major water-conducting faults: MWCF), with a higher hydraulic conductivity than the LPD. However, the proportion of faults which are hydraulically active is uncertain.  As in the case of the LPD (see FEP 5.1), the hydraulic properties of the MWCF are controlled by the properties of the small-scale water-conducting features which dissect them (see FEP 6.2).

The uncertainty concerning the degree to which faults are hydraulically active is treated, in groundwater-flow modelling, by considering two extreme cases: the “Full Model”, in which all first- and second-order faults are  assumed to be active (i.e. all are MWCF) and the “Sparse Model”, in which very few second-order faults are active.  First-order MWCF are modelled as three-dimensional features with a hydraulic conductivity of 10 m y-1. Second-order MWCF are modelled as two-dimensional features with a transmissivity of 200 m2 y-1.  The “Sparse Model” leads to higher flow in the LPD blocks, which flow rate is adopted in radionuclide transport calculations.

pfep_description_raw:
Groundwater flow in the crystalline basement is controlled by the hydrogeological framework, which is the combination of units and structural features of which the MWCF are one type, and the driving forces which are dominated by topographic effects, i.e. recharge in outcropping regions of higher elevation.  The Black Forest is expected to be the principal recharge area for groundwater in the crystalline rocks of Northern Switzerland.  On the basis of local-scale groundwater flow modelling, fluxes in first order MWCF are several orders of magnitude larger than those in the LPD between faults and are predominantly horizontal.

For the modelling of radionuclide transport, where transport within the MWCF is taken into account (see also 6.4), groundwater flow is assumed to be confined to open channels within water-conducting features. The rate of flow within the channels, and hence the advection velocity for radionuclides, is determined from hydrogeological modelling, in which, for outcrop areas of crystalline rocks such as the Southern Black Forest, prescribed constant heads are assigned that approximate the topography and provide the principal driving force for flow.

pfep_description_raw:
Radionuclides would be transported from the bentonite-host rock interface through the crystalline basement to the overlying sediments, along a variety of pathways, depending on their point of release and on the pattern of groundwater flow (see FEP 5.4).  Radionuclides would migrate through the LPD of Area West, or the lower unit of Area East, and would emerge either at the interface with a MWCF or, in the case of Area West, at the interface with the overlying higher-permeability domain (HPD).  Radionuclides entering a MWCF would be transported, in the plane of the fault, through the surrounding LPD and HPD to the overlying sediments.

Transport of radionuclides through the MWCF is not taken into account for a repository located in Area East. For Area West, two possible pathways are considered:
  •  though the LPD directly (upwards) to the HPD and thence to the overlying sediments (the Reference Model Assumption);
  •  through the LPD to a MWCF, upwards the HPD and thence to the overlying sediments (alternative model assumption).

Modelling of transport through a MWCF for the alternative model assumption requires the specification of a flowpath length.  In the current design, the repository would lie at least 100 m below the lower boundary of the HPD.  This gives an indication of the minimum length of a flowpath through a MWCF, before that MWCF enters the HPD.   A pathlength of 200m in the MWCF is assumed in assessment calculations.

Solubility limits appropriate to the groundwater chemistry are not expected to be exceeded (see FEP 6.16) and so radionuclides in the MWCF would exist either in solution in pores within the rock or sorbed onto solid surfaces. In pores through which groundwater flow occurs, predominantly the open channels of the small-scale water-conducting features (see FEP 6.2), radionuclides in solution would be transported by advection.  Interconnections between channels with different properties, and variability in those properties along individual channels, would give rise to mechanical dispersion.  Radionuclides would also diffuse from this flow porosity into adjacent pores where the groundwater is stagnant (see FEP 6.6).  This matrix diffusion would result in a retardation of advective transport.  Radionuclides would sorb onto the surfaces of the channels and the matrix pores, leading to further retardation, and onto groundwater colloids (see FEP 6.15), leading either to enhanced or diminished retardation, depending on the mobility and stability of the colloids.  The degree of sorption is influenced by mineralogy and groundwater chemistry.

The channels within the small-scale water-conducting features are modelled by a conduit of simple geometry (constant cross-section along its length), which follows the one-dimensional representative flow path (see FEP 6.4).  The advection velocity of radionuclides along the conduits is calculated from the flow rate through the water-conducting features (obtained through groundwater-flow modelling) and from the geometry and spacing of the channels within these features.  Hydrodynamic dispersion, the combined effect of mechanical dispersion and molecular diffusion, is modelled as a Fickian diffusion process in the longitudinal (flow) direction.  Transverse dispersion is neglected.  Modelling of sorption and colloid-facilitated transport are discussed in FEPs 6.9, 6.10 and 6.15.

pfep_description_raw:
Radionuclides can migrate from the flow porosity (i.e. the open channels of small-scale water-conducting features) into the static water of the pores of the adjacent wallrock by molecular diffusion.  This process is known as matrix diffusion.  The rate of diffusion through the wallrock pores is a function of pore geometry (constrictivity and tortuosity), the surface properties of the pores (charge) and the size and charge of the diffusing species.  There is uncertainty in the extent of connected porosity in the wallrock, which determines the maximum depth to which radionuclides can diffuse.  A lower limit of 1 cm has been derived on the basis of natural analogue studies. However, it is likely that the entire fracture infill and the altered zone of wallrock immediately adjacent to the channels (see FEP 6.2) is accessible by diffusion, and possibly also the unaltered wallrock at greater distances from the channels.

Diffusion is modelled using a diffusion constant based on a survey of experimental results for comparable crystalline rocks.  The constant is assumed to be nuclide-independent.  “Realistic-conservative” and “conservative” values are defined.  Matrix diffusion is restricted to one spatial dimension, directed normally to the surface of the parallel-walled or tubular conduit.  Matrix diffusion is, in the model, confined to a spatially-limited region of connected porosity surrounding the conduit.  In this region, the transport properties (i.e. diffusion constant, porosity, sorption parameters) are uniform.   The fracture infill, altered wallrock and unaltered wallrock differ in their porosities.  In assigning a single porosity value to the modelled region, which may contain all three rock types, a low (conservative) porosity is used.

pfep_description_raw:
The groundwater chemistry is controlled by a range of factors, including the rock mineralogy, recharge conditions and residence time.  For repository performance, the most important chemical parameters are the ionic strength, the pH and the Eh.  On the basis of a regional synthesis of groundwater chemistry, the predominant groundwater in the crystalline basement of Area West is of the Na-SO4-(Cl-HCO3) type, with about 1 g l-1 total dissolved solids, a pH of 7.66 and an Eh of - 0.18 m volts.  This is taken as a reference water for Area West.  A reference water for Area East has also been define, although on the basis of limited data.  This is of the Na-HCO3-SO4-(Cl) type with 0.5 g l-1 dissolved solids, a pH of 7.68 and an Eh of - 0.03 volts.  The groundwater chemistry determines radionuclide speciation.  This, together with the mineralogy of pore surfaces, influences sorption (see FEP 6.9).

The groundwater chemistry of the MWCF is assumed to be unperturbed by the presence of the repository.  In particular, radionuclides will be released in trace concentrations and bentonite porewater will not influence groundwater composition downstream of the repository.   The groundwater chemistry is taken into account in the
selection of sorption parameter values.

pfep_description_raw:
The interaction of dissolved radionuclides with rock surfaces, excluding precipitation, is termed sorption. Radionuclides can sorb on the surfaces of open channels within water-conducting features and also on the surfaces of pores accessible by matrix diffusion (i.e. pore surfaces within fracture infill and wallrock). The degree to which radionuclides sorb on pore surfaces is dependent on the elemental concentration (i.e. the concentration of the element of which the radionuclide under consideration is an isotope) and on the properties of the rock-water system under consideration - in particular, the mineralogy and the groundwater chemistry. For the crystalline basement, data is available on the mineralogies for the component parts of the different types of water-conducting features (see 6.7) and on the chemical composition, pH and Eh of the groundwaters of Area West and Area East (see 6.8). For a particular rock-water system, radionuclide partitioning between the sorbed phase and the aqueous phase can be determined experimentally. For Kristallin-I, measurements on samples from the crystalline basement are complemented with an appraisal of the wider sorption literature, including measurements on pure minerals. In this case, sorption is determined by adding contributions from the constituent minerals, weighted according to their relative abundances.

The concentration of radionuclides sorbed onto the surfaces of open channels is assumed to be small with respect to that sorbed onto matrix pore surfaces and is neglected in assessment calculations. Sorption on matrix pore surfaces is assumed to be both completely reversible and rapid with respect to the transport times of radionuclides through the MWCF. The assumption that sorption is reversible and rapid is consistent with the sorption database used (data comes mainly from relatively short-term experiments, in which the sorption processes operative are those with rapid kinetics). It is possible that, on longer timescales, other sorption processes, especially irreversible sorption processes, might become important. However, the effect of these would be to further retard radionuclide release and they can, therefore, be conservatively neglected in the modelling of transport. Sorption in the MWCF is represented by a concentration-independent distribution coefficient - i.e., linear sorption is assumed, quantified by a sorption constant Kd, equal to the equilibrium radionuclide concentration in the sorbed phase, divided by the concentration in the aqueous phase. “Realistic-conservative” and “conservative” Kd values are defined for each safety-relevant element. The effect of differences in mineralogy between different rock types (fracture infill, altered and unaltered wallrock within different types of water-conducting features) has been found to be small and Kd values which are independent of rock type are used in assessment calculations. Although the partitioning of many elements in natural rock-water systems between the sorbed and aqueous phases is known to show some concentration dependence, of the elements with safety-relevant isotopes, only caesium has been studied sufficiently to justify sorption also being represented by a non-linear isotherm (see FEP 6.10).

In general, the partitioning of radionuclides between sorbed and aqueous phases is dependent on elemental concentration (i.e. the concentration of the element of which the radionuclide under consideration is an isotope). Where such dependency exists, sorption is said to be non-linear. Sorption is quantified by a relationship termed an isotherm, which may be linear or non-linear. There are several forms on non-linear isotherm, including the Freundlich and Langmuir isotherms.

Although many of the safety-relevant radionuclides may be better characterised by a non-linear isotherm, rather than a linear isotherm (i.e. a Kd value), a suitable database is available only for caesium. Sorption of caesium is described in Kristallin-I by a Freundlich isotherm. In modelling transport through the MWCF, the exponent of the Freundlich isotherm is set to unity (in which case the Freundlich isotherm reduces to a linear isotherm) and a Kd value for the resulting linear isotherm is selected conservatively, such that the amount of sorption calculated using this Kd is always less than with the full Freundlich isotherm. This enables the reference geosphere transport code for Kristallin-I (RANCHMD) to be employed.

pfep_description_raw:
Saline waters are found in the sedimentary units overlying the crystalline basement, in the Permo-Carboniferous Trough and, at a small number of sampling points, in the crystalline basement itself.  Hydrochemical and isotopic evidence suggests that the composition of most groundwater in the crystalline basement is a product of chemical evolution of water entirely within crystalline rock and that the intrusion of saline water from the surrounding sediments is minimal. Most saline waters within the crystalline basement occur in zones of restricted circulation and great age. However, some saline waters, in particular those observed to the north of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough, could have arisen as a result of limited intrusion from the sediments of the Trough. 

Since, on the basis of hydrochemical and isotopic evidence, there is very little intrusion of saline groundwater from the Permo-Carboniferous Trough into the adjacent crystalline basement, the southern boundary of the regional-scale groundwater flow model is assigned a no-flow boundary condition. With regard to groundwater chemistry, reference groundwaters have been defined for both Area West (1 g l-1 total dissolved solids) and Area East (0.5 g l-1) on the basis of a regional synthesis of data. These reference groundwaters form the basis of calculations of sorption parameters for geosphere transport modelling. The occurrence of a small number of samples of higher salinity (5 - 13 g l-1) is neglected. However, it is possible that at least that at least part of a repository in Area West could be affected by small amounts of the more saline waters.

This topic should be considered on a site specific basis.

pfep_description_raw:
The distribution of temperature within the crystalline basement is expected to be correlated with a distribution of groundwater density. Variations in density provide a driving force for groundwater flow.  The geothermal anomaly observed in Central Northern Switzerland (see 6.13) is believed to reflect the overprinting of conductive heat transport by convective heat transport, resulting from the density-driven flow of deep groundwaters along fault systems.  The fault systems in question lie along the northern and southern boundaries of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough; these correlate, as a first approximation, with the two maxima of the anomaly.

Density variations due to temperature (or salinity) are not considered in the domain within which groundwater flow is modelled in Kristallin-I.  However, the density-driven upwelling of groundwater, which is believed to occur in the fault systems lying along the northern margin of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough (the southern boundary of the regional-scale model), is included as a non-zero flux boundary condition along a small part (500 m) of the bottom of the regional-scale model, at its southern limit. The Darcy flux hypothesised to help explain the geothermal anomaly is 2 x 10-10 m s-1, which corresponds (for a hydraulic conductivity within the fault systems of 10-7 m s-1) to a vertical (upward) gradient of 0.002.  However, the results from these simulations predict salinities in the crystalline basement that are much higher than those actually measured.  This indicates the groundwater flow proposed by RYBACH et al. is too high; only model runs with no imposed fluxes gave estimates of salinity consistent with the hydrochemical evidence, which justifies the assumption of the deep Permo-Carboniferous Trough acting as a no-flow boundary for the investigated region.

pfep_description_raw:
The temperature field within the crystalline basement is determined by (i) the large-scale geological and petrophysical properties of the rock (e.g. radiogenic heat production, thermal conductivity) and (ii) by the hydrogeological properties of the rock (in particular, the hydraulic conductivity), which provide a means by which convective heat transport via fluid phases can occur. This can be either free convection (i.e. thermally-driven circulation of deep groundwaters) of forced convection, in areas where groundwater circulation is maintained by marked hydraulic gradients. Temperature data from deep boreholes, together with data on thermal properties of the rock, enable the temperature field, the geothermal gradient and the heat-flux field to be mapped. The vertical geothermal gradient is depth-dependent and has therefore been calculated for two depth intervals:
  •  gradient for the interval 0 - 500 m:40 - 45 ˚C km-1;
  •  gradient for the interval 750 - 1700 m:35 - 40 ˚C km-1.

On this basis, the ambient rock temperature at repository depth (1050 - 1200 m) is expected to be about 55 ˚C. There is a geothermal anomaly in Central Northern Switzerland, with two maxima: one to the north of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough (160 mW m-2)  and the other approximately above its southern margin (170 mW m-2), coinciding with the main overthrust of the folded Jura. This is explained by marked convective heat fluxes in the form of upwelling deep groundwaters.

Temperature gradients may drive groundwater flow; this is neglected in groundwater flow modelling for Kristallin-I: see 5.12. Temperature is also a factor in determining groundwater speciation, and hence the sorption parameters for geosphere transport modelling.
