pfep_description_raw:
Estimates for the orientation of regional stress field in the crystalline basement of Northern Switzerland, as derived from seismotectonics and from in-situ measurements, are approximately the same: a NW-SE direction for the horizontal component of the principal stress (sH). There are no direct measurements that give information on the magnitudes of the stress-field components. However, these can be inferred from data from outside the region as follows: |sH| ª  30 - 50 MPa (135˚±10˚); |sh| ª 15 - 25 MPa (45˚±10˚); |sv| ª 30 - 50 MPa.  On a smaller scale, the stress distribution in Northern Switzerland and the surrounding areas is not uniform and individual zones with differing behaviour can be identified. These zones correspond more or less to the individual tectonic units. There is an apparent decoupling of the regional stress field in the basement from that in the sedimentary cover. In the Southern Black Forest and possibly also in Northern Switzerland, young and recent faulting along Hercinian lineaments is indicated both by geomorphology and by seismotectonics and is consistent with the interpretation of the recent stress field.

Data on the regional stress regime are not used directly in post-closure safety-assessment calculations.  However, they provide constraints on the development of long-term scenarios of geological evolution.

pfep_description_raw:
Colloids, which are present in all groundwaters, may influence the transport of radionuclides through the MWCF. Radionuclides, as aqueous species, may sorb, either reversibly or irreversibly, onto natural colloids. These colloids may be filtered during transport through the MWCF, thus reducing radionuclide migration (particularly if sorption of radionuclides on colloids is irreversible). However, radionuclides associated with colloids may be excluded from matrix pores (e.g. on account of the size of the colloids), and would thus be unretarded by the processes of matrix diffusion (see 6.6) and sorption on matrix pore surfaces (see 6.9), so enhancing radionuclide migration (again, particularly if sorption of radionuclides on colloids is irreversible). Even where the colloid concentration is low (an upper bound for Area West is 0.1 ppm), these effects may be significant because colloids have a high specific surface area on which sorption can take place. Whether colloids act predominantly to retard transport (i.e. by sorption of aqueous species and subsequent filtration) or enhance transport (i.e. by sorption of aqueous species and exclusion from matrix pores) is unclear and depends on the properties of the colloids and the water-conducting features.

In the modelling the Reference Scenario, the effect of colloid-facilitated transport in the MWCF is not considered. However, it is recognised that a scenario in which radionuclides are irreversibly sorbed on colloids, and those colloids are unfiltered during transport through the geosphere, could assume little credit for the geosphere (including the MWCF) as a migration barrier. The occurrence of irreversible sorption on groundwater colloids is an open question. This scenario is incorporated within the definition of the Robust Scenario, which assumes the most pessimistic possible representation of the geological barrier.

pfep_description_raw:
The TRU (long-lived intermediate-level waste) silos contain large quantities of cementitious backfill and structural material, as well as small quantities of organic material within the disposed wastes. Over time, the interactions of groundwater with the silos will lead to a plume of cementitious and organic material, which is expected to alter the mineralogy of the water-conducting features in its path. It thus has the potential to alter groundwater flow and the solubilities and sorption properties of radionuclides migrating with the groundwater.

In the Kristallin-I reference design, the TRU silos are sited in a block of LPD, separate from the blocks used for HLW emplacement. The major fault zone/zones between the silos and HLW emplacement panels may be either water-conducting (MWCF), in which case the MWCF would act as a source of dilution, or non-conducting, in which case they would act as a barrier to groundwater flow.

It is assumed that the TRU silos could be sited such that there would be no hydrological or hydrochemical effect on the migration of radionuclides through the MWCF. The relative siting of TRU silos and HLW panels is a subject for future consideration on a site-specific basis.

The hydraulic properties of the crystalline basement are controlled by the properties of the small-scale water-conducting features which dissect it. In both Area West and Area East, the transmissivity and density of these features, and therefore of the hydraulic conductivity of the rock through which they pass, undergoes an abrupt decrease at depths greater than 400-600 m below the upper surface of the crystalline basement. The upper rock unit in Area West, which overlies the LPD, is termed the higher-permeability domain (HPD). In Area East, given the current limited dataset, it is considered inappropriate to divide the crystalline basement into an LPD and an HPD; although substantially higher transmissivities are measured in both the upper and lower units than in Area West, data are limited to a single borehole and thus may be unrepresentative of Area East as a whole.

For groundwater flow modelling, the HPD is assigned a hydraulic conductivity similar to that of the MWCF: i.e. of 10 m y-1. Radionuclide transport through the HPD is not modelled; radionuclides are assumed to be conveyed instantaneously through the HPD to the overlying sediments and thence to the biosphere (see also FEP 7.6).

pfep_description_raw:
A Mesozoic sedimentary cover overlies, in part, the crystalline basement of Northern Switzerland, as well as the Permo-Carboniferous Trough (PCT) of Northern Switzerland (see 7.3). The Mesozoic cover consists of a heterogeneous sequence of strata, of variable thickness, that are subhorizontal and relatively undisturbed tectonically. The basal unit is the Buntsandstein aquifer, consisting of red conglomerates, sandstones and mudstones. The average thickness of this layer is 15 m and the mean hydraulic conductivity is 10-6 m s-1. This is overlain by a very low-permeability sequence of evaporites and argillaceous marine sediments of Triassic age (Lower and Middle Muschelkalk deposits). These act as a hydraulic barrier that confines groundwater in the underlying Bundsandstein/crystalline-rock aquifer. Some new geochemical analyses suggest minor leakage through the sediments; the consequences of these effects for overall groundwater flow have not been investigated.

For groundwater flow modelling, because of its small thickness and high hydraulic conductivity, the Buntsandstein aquifer is treated as a two-dimensional element characterized by transmissivity. Based on hydrochemical evidence, this is assumed to exchange no groundwater with the overlying sedimentary sequence; the top of the Bundsandstein layer is treated as a no-flow boundary in groundwater flow modelling, and the overlying Mesozoic sediments are not included in the models. Radionuclide transport through the mesozoic sedimentary cover is not modelled. Radionuclides are assumed to be conveyed instantaneously from the crystalline basement to the biosphere (see also 7.6). The Mesozoic sedimentary cover is, however, assumed to isolate the crystalline basement from many of the effects of changes in the surface environment (e.g. climatic changes).

pfep_description_raw:
During the Variscan orogeny, the crystalline basement underwent extensive deformation. A graben structure, the Permo-Carboniferous Trough of Northern Switzerland, formed during the late stage of this orogeny (around 315 - 245 million years ago). The Permo-Carboniferous Trough, which is infilled with sediments of variable but generally low permeabilities and is overlain by the Mesozoic sedimentary cover (see 7.2), represents an important component of the pre-Mesozoically consolidated basement. The presence of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough considerably limits the potential siting areas within Northern Switzerland. Either under, or south of, the Permo-Carboniferous Trough, the crystalline basement is too deep for repository construction, and hence potential sites are restricted to two small areas between the Permo-Carboniferous Trough and the national border (Area West and Area East).

The Permo-Carboniferous Trough forms the southern boundary of the regional-scale groundwater flow model. The greater part of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough is assumed not to contribute to groundwater flow in the crystalline basement, and a no-flow boundary condition is applied at the southern boundary of the regional-scale model. The upper part of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough, filled with Permian deposits, extends as a “shoulder” northwards over the crystalline basement; this is included in the model as a single hydrogeological unit with a hydraulic conductivity of 10-9 m s-1. Radionuclides are not expected to migrate towards the Permo-Carboniferous Trough and radionuclide transport therein is not modelled.

pfep_description_raw:
Groundwater flow in the crystalline basement is controlled by the hydrogeological framework, which is the combination of structural features and units of which the HPD is one, and the driving forces which are dominated by topographic effects (see, however, 5.12): i.e. recharge in outcropping regions of higher elevation. The Black Forest is expected to be the principal recharge area for groundwater in the crystalline rocks of Northern Switzerland. On the basis of local-scale groundwater flow modelling, within the HPD, flow is predominantly horizontal.

Groundwater flow is mainly confined to open channels within the water-conducting features of the HPD and types of water-conducting features are the same as those for the LPD (see 5.2) and MWCF (see 6.2). The rate of flow within the HPD is determined from hydrogeological modelling, in which, for outcrop areas of crystalline rocks such as the Southern Black Forest, prescribed constant heads are assigned that approximate the topography and provide the principal driving force for flow. However, radionuclide transport within the open channels of the HPD is not modelling in the Kristallin-I safety assessment (see also 7.1).

pfep_description_raw:
Groundwater flow in the HPD is driven predominantly by recharge in outcrop areas, such as the southern part of the Black Forest. However,  density-driven flow of deep groundwaters along fault systems may also occur along the northern and southern boundaries of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough (see 5.12 & 5.13), as a result of convective heat transport. Where the crystalline basement is covered by Mesozoic sediments, the Lower and Middle Muschelkalk deposits act as a hydraulic barrier that confines groundwater flow to underlying strata (see 7.2). The Permo-Carboniferous Trough also acts as a barrier to flow (see 7.3).

In modelling groundwater flow, two hydraulic conditions are assumed along the top boundary of the regional-scale model: (i), for outcrop areas, head values (i.e. levels of the groundwater table) are imposed that correspond to approximately to topography, (ii), for areas where the HPD (and Bundsandstein layer) are overlain by a Mesozoic cover, a no-flow boundary is assumed. Two boundary conditions are also assumed along the bottom boundary: (i), a no-flow boundary is assumed as the general condition, on the basis of the probably very low hydraulic conductivity at a depth of 3000 m (the bottom boundary of the regional-scale model), (ii), a non-zero flow boundary condition is assumed along a small part (500 m) of the boundary, at its southern limit, to simulate the density-driven upwelling of groundwater along the northern margin of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough. A no-flow boundary is assigned to the southern model boundary, to simulate the predominantly low-permeability of the sediments within the Permo-Carboniferous Trough.

pfep_description_raw:
Estimates for the orientation of regional stress field in the crystalline basement of Northern Switzerland, as derived from seismotectonics and from in-situ measurements, are approximately the same: a NW-SE direction for the horizontal component of the principal stress (sH). There are no direct measurements that give information on the magnitudes of the stress-field components. However, these can be inferred from data from outside the region as follows: |sH| ª  30 - 50 MPa (135˚±10˚); |sh| ª 15 - 25 MPa (45˚±10˚); |sv| ª 30 - 50 MPa.  On a smaller scale, the stress distribution in Northern Switzerland and the surrounding areas is not uniform and individual zones with differing behaviour can be identified. These zones correspond more or less to the individual tectonic units. There is an apparent decoupling of the regional stress field in the basement from that in the sedimentary cover. In the Southern Black Forest and possibly also in Northern Switzerland, young and recent faulting along Hercinian lineaments is indicated both by geomorphology and by seismotectonics and is consistent with the interpretation of the recent stress field.

Data on the regional stress regime are not used directly in post-closure safety-assessment calculations.  However, they provide constraints on the development of long-term scenarios of geological evolution.

pfep_description_raw:
As a result of continuing action of geological processes, the future surface geology of Northern Switzerland will be different to the present one. The effect of certain erosion processes, such as the removal of the Quaternary gravels or denudation (uniform erosion - max. 100 m), are not expected to be hydraulically relevant for groundwater flow in the HPD. This is because hydrostatic pressure at depth is much greater than any likely variations due to changes in topography and infiltration rate. However, other processes may be more significant and the influence of a range of possible changes, which may occur over the next 106 years, has been investigated using the regional groundwater flow model:
	 •  regional uplift of the Black Forest;
	 •  the resulting displacement of the river network;
	 •  the resulting (linear) erosion of Mesozoic basement cover.
In Area West, with the shift of the regional drainage channel (the river Rhine) to the south and its simultaneous deepening relative to the basement surface, the exfiltration conditions will generally be enhanced: i.e. the upward vertical component of the hydraulic gradient will increase with respect to that of the present day. However, no fundamental changes in the pattern of groundwater flow are expected. In Area East, significant changes in the flow regime could occur. The southward displacement of the Wutach river could bring the area into the catchment of the Wutach, rather than the Rhine river, and into the immediate vicinity of the exfiltration zone. The result would be extremely short flow paths and large hydraulic gradients.

Since radionuclide transport through the LPD is, in any case, assumed to be instantaneous (see 7.1) the estimated changes in hydraulic gradient are unimportant from the point of view of geosphere transport modelling. The possibility of exfiltration to a small valley (e.g. the Wutach) is considered as a variation in the safety-assessment modelling of the biosphere in Area East.

Erosion is considered in the “Continuation of, Alpine Orogeny” scenario, which is covered by parameter variations within the Reference Scenario.  The case of linear erosion leading to exfiltration into, a small valley, in the case of Area East, is treated as a biosphere parameter variation.

pfep_description_raw:
A potentiometric surface (i.e. a contour map of hydraulic head) for the HPD has been derived based on borehole data. The horizontal component of hydraulic gradient generally predominates in the HPD, except beneath areas of recharge (the Black Forest), discharge (the valley of the River Rhine and its tributaries) and groundwater pumping, where vertical components predominate. At Zurzach, thermal wells discharge a long-term (about 30-year) average of approximately 10 l s-1. There is a corresponding minimum in the potentiometric surface. The elevation of the free outflow is about 337 m. The radial extent of the cone of depression is, however, uncertain. East of the investigation area, in the region of Lake Constance, a pronounced potentiometric depression is observed in the deep regional aquifer of Upper Muschelkalk within the sedimentary cover.

In the modelling of groundwater flow, hydraulic-head boundary conditions are imposed in outcrop areas that correspond to approximately to topography (see 7.5). Potentiometric measurements are used in the derivation of further boundary conditions and constraints (e.g. to ensure consistency with the potentiometric depressions in the East of the modelled region and at Zurzach, where a fixed head condition (337 m) is assigned to the model node that represents the thermal wells). A distribution of head is then calculated from a solution of the governing equations for groundwater flow, taking account of the hydraulic properties of the various rock units. Within the modelled region, it is assumed that the magnitude and direction of hydraulic gradient is unaffected by either the amounts or the locations of recharge, discharge (except at Zurzach) and groundwater pumping. Potentiometric measurements are used as a test of the accuracy of the numerical models, and as a basis for the adjustment of those models if necessary.

In assessment models, transport through the HPD is assumed to be instantaneous, so that hydraulic gradient changes are not relevant.

pfep_description_raw:
The distributions of temperature and salinity within the crystalline basement are expected to be correlated with a distribution of groundwater density. Variations in density provide a driving force for groundwater flow. The geothermal anomaly observed in Central Northern Switzerland (see 5.13 / 6.13) is believed to reflect the overprinting of conductive heat transport by convective heat transport, resulting from the density-driven flow of deep groundwaters along fault systems. The fault systems in question lie along the northern and southern boundaries of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough; these correlate, as a first approximation, with the two maxima of the anomaly.

Density variations due to temperature or salinity are not considered in the domain within which groundwater flow is modelled in Kristallin-I. However, the density-driven upwelling of groundwater, which is believed to occur in the fault systems lying along the northern margin of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough (the southern boundary of the regional-scale model), is included as a non-zero flux boundary condition along a small part (500 m) of the bottom of the regional-scale model, at its southern limit. The Darcy flux hypothesised to help explain the geothermal anomaly is 2 x 10-10 m s-1, which corresponds (for a hydraulic conductivity within the fault systems of 10-7 m s-1) to a vertical (upward) gradient of 0.002.

waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel

ebs_concept:

pfep_description_raw:
The actual conditions that will exist in the biosphere at times in the far future are likely to vary in a largely unpredictable manner, due to both natural and anthropogenic events and/or processes. Climate change is predictable in general terms, but the patterns of future human behaviour and local resource use that determine doses received by individuals or populations living in the future are largely unpredictable. 

Bounding scenarios for long-term climatic change in Northern Switzerland over the next one million years can be developed based on analogy with the climate over the last few million years, which is in turn based on an analysis of regional and global indicators, as preserved in the geological record, and on atmospheric and climatic modelling studies. Possible human actions with the potential to perturb the biosphere can also be identified.

Several alternative scenarios are considered quantitatively in Kristallin-I, related to changes in biosphere conditions which may occur in the future. In no case is transition to the changed conditions modelled. Rather, as in the case of the Reference Scenario and present-day conditions, the alternative biospheres are assumed to persist for the entire period under consideration. Three alternative climate-related scenarios are modelled in Kristallin-I:
 •  a periglacial (tundra) climate;
 •  a warm, humid climate;
 •  a warm, dry climate.
In addition, a modified biosphere, in which the gravels currently filling the Rhine valley are removed by erosion, is modelled (see FEP 8.3). Although several scenarios related to future human actions are identified, most are excluded from quantitative treatment in Kristallin-I, for example on the grounds of improbability. One remaining scenario related to future human actions, that  of a deep groundwater well sunk into the HPD of the crystalline basement, is modelled. This scenario, which would be made more likely if, for example, surface waters became polluted, reduces the diluting effect of the biosphere.

A range of future biosphere conditions is considered in alternative climate-related (biosphere) scenarios: Dry Climate State; Humid Climate State; Periglacial Climate State; Rhine Gravels Absent.

pfep_description_raw:
It is considered most likely that radionuclide-contaminated groundwater would be discharged from the HPD in the vicinity of the river Rhine (see FEP 8.1). On discharging from the HPD, groundwater would mix with recent meteoric and river water in local gravel aquifers typical of the upper Rhine valley; these gravels were laid down in the Quaternary period. Alternative scenarios can, however, be envisaged:
 •  The gravel aquifers could be removed. This could occur, for example, in the case of a humid climate which is uninterrupted by ice ages: there would be no alluvial build-up and, if erosion is sufficient to remove the gravels, the Rhine may flow directly over the HPD.
•  For Area East, discharge could occur to the valley of a Rhine tributary. This is possible following down-cutting of the tributary to the basement.

In the Reference Scenario, discharge is assumed to occur to the Quaternary gravels of the Rhine river valley. “Rhine Gravels Assent” is considered as an alternative climate-related (biosphere) scenario; exfiltration to a small valley is considered as a bisophere parameter-variation.

pfep_description_raw:
Exfiltrating contaminated groundwaters may flow directly into surface water systems if the unconsolidated Quaternary gravels of the Rhine river bed are eroded away.  Such a situation is most likely to occur in the long term if a humid climate is established.  The Rhine is expected to shift south due to the uplift of the southern Black Forest, thus leaving its old gravel-filled bed and eroding down to the basement.  In such a climate, erosion dominates over sedimentation and contaminated water can thus exfiltrate directly into the Rhine.

Direct release to surface water may also occur in the case of a glacial climate.  As the ice advances it is expected to scour out the unconsolidated material in the river valleys.  However, the glacial retreat will always be followed by resedimentation, thus this would be a transient phenomenon.

Direct exfiltration to the River Rhine is considered in the “Rhine Gravels Assent” Scenario.

Radon (Rn-222) is the immediate daughter of radium (Ra-226) and is a noble gas with a half-life of about 4 days; it decays through a series of very short-lived radionuclides (half-life 27 minutes or less) to Pb-210 (half-life 21 years).

In the biosphere, if Ra-226 is present in soil, then a fraction of the Rn-222 produced (a few to a few tens of %) would escape to the atmosphere and be rapidly dispersed.  This is neglected in assessment models; this is conservative since this process would lead to a reduction of calculated doses due to Pb-210 and Po-210 through food-chain pathways because of the reduced concentrations of these nuclides remaining in soil.  However, this is a potential for significant doses from Rn-222 and its short-lived daughters in conditions of limited air circulation.  In buildings, Rn-222 emanating from Ra-226 in underlying soil and rocks, or in building materials, may accumulate.

In current assessment models Ra-226 is assumed to decay directly to Pb-210, neglecting any Rn-222 losses and dose factors Ra-226 include the summation of all daughters.  The net bias due to this simplification is thought to be small but deserves attention in future assessment calculations.

Based on the anticipated tectonic evolution in the Kaisten-Böttstein-Leuggern area, it is expected that there will be horizontal movements along faults and that, within the zone of influence of the Jura overthrust, the sedimentary cover which has sheared off from the basement will be transported further northwards.  There have as yet been no measurements of horizontal movements and the assumed values are based on geological considerations.

Two tectonic bounding scenarios are identified.  Scenario A assumes the alpine orogeny is largely complete and that active crustal shortening is no longer expected in Northern Switzerland.  Scenario B assumes that alpine tectonics are continuing with corresponding stresses in the crust in Northern Switzerland.  The extent of regional horizontal movements varies according to the bounding scenario assumed.

Regional horizontal movements in the sedimentary cover (Jura overthrust): 	
< 100 m/My for	Scenario A;	< 500 m/My for Scenario B.
Regional horizontal movements in basement: 	
< 100 m/My for	Scenario A;	< 100 m/My for Scenario B

The horizontal movements in the sedimentary cover are not significant in terms of the repository safety assessment.  The horizontal movements in the basement are largely absorbed by the major faults.

pfep_description_raw:
Movements along faults will occur due to the updoming of the Southern Black Forest and the existing compressive stress field in the crystalline basement resulting from the Alpine orogeny. The relative movement along any fault will lie in the range 0 to 100 m in one million years. The faults are heterogeneous and the properties of the faults are a result of past movements; continuing movement will therefore not change their average range of properties, although previously conductive zones may become less conductive and vice versa.

Movement on major faults that intercept access tunnels connecting the repository panels, or repository shafts, may cause relative displacement of the tunnels in adjacent blocks. This will not be significant if tunnel seals remain intact. Although the movement might adversely affect seals near to such a fault, it is expected that this can be avoided by attention to the choice of seal locations and design.

Seismic activity is low in the potential repository siting areas in Northern Switzerland and the corresponding risk to safety is considered negligible (NTB 93-01). Direct disturbance of a sealed repository by seismic activity can practically be ruled out. In addition, earthquake magnitudes to be expected in Switzerland will never be sufficient to cause serious damage to a deep underground tunnel system during the operational phase (see NTB 84-26; BERGER 1987). 

The possibility of the direct disturbance of the repository zone as a result of an earthquake can thus be excluded.  However, resulting stress changes may be relevant (see FEP 9.6).

waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel
host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:

pfep_description_raw:
During seismic activity, movement occurs along various faults (see 9.3 and 9.4).  This results in stress changes in the intervening rock blocks - eg. a stress relief in the direction parallel to the fault.  The principle effect, in a hard rock, is to change the aperture of various openings in the rock. Thus the transmissivity of the various water-bearing features may change in a direction specific way.  It is assumed that the changes will not be significant compared to the existing range and uncertainty on the characteristics of such features.

It has been observed that stress changes due to fault movement can have a hydrogeological effect, changing the aperture of fractures within a rock mass to cause expulsion or drawing in of water (MUIR-WOOD & WOO 1992). MUIR-WOOD & WOO concluded that the most significant hydrological response is found to accompany major normal fault earthquakes, involving an increase in spring and river discharge to a peak a few days after the earthquake, the excess flow being sustained for periods typically of around 8 months. In contrast, hydrological changes accompanying reverse fault earthquakes are either undetected or else involve falls in well levels and spring flows.

The effect is expected to be small for the crystalline basement and is not evaluated in Kristallin-I.

project_title: Nagra Scenario Development for Kristallin-I
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW) from reprocessing of spent PWR/BWR fuel
host_rock: crystalline basement under sedimentary cover in Northern Switzerland
ebs_concept:
thick steel containers, 
in-tunnel emplacement with bentonite buffer
pfep_description_raw:
Erosion and denudation are processes which cause significant changes in the present-day topography and thus also affect local and regional hydrogeology and the biosphere.  The extent of erosion depends to a large extent on climate and uplift (see FEP 9.2).

The updoming of the Southern Black Forest is expected to be largely balanced by continuing erosion (see Chapter 9 in NTB 93-01). The sedimentary cover of the crystalline basement to the south of the Upper Rhine is currently subject to erosion and denudation processes. In this area, as uplift and erosion continue, the crystalline basement may be exposed on the south side of the present-day course of the Rhine along a strip 100 m to 2 km in extent within the next one million years. The Rhine may also downcut into the uplifting basement. Certain fault zones may thus lose their sedimentary cover, which may modify the hydrogeological regime in the basement. The rates of erosion will depend on rates of uplift and climate.

In the case of an arid climate, surface denudation dominates.  Maximum expected surface denudation is approximately 50m in 1 My.

For humid and glacial climates, linear erosion dominates.  Maximum fluvial downcutting of the Rhine is 200m in 1 My.  Significant lateral erosion of the Rhine towards the south is possible, locally up to 2 km.  In the case of a humid climate, lateral and gully erosion may occur without alluvial build-up of the river bed.  Surface denudation will not be more that 100 m.

Glacial erosion of Quaternary valley fills up to 300 m and locally more (mainly in Alpine Foreland) is estimated.

Possible effects are included in the “Alpine orogeny continues” scenario and biosphere scenarios.

pfep_description_raw: Local removal of the sedimentary cover and the southward shift of the Rhine may result in changes to the hydrogeological regime in the basement, especially in the higher-permeability domain.  The nearer-surface crystalline basement has been progressively altered in the past as a result of stress relief and rock-water interactions, especially hydrothermal alteration, which has been more significant in the higher-permeability domain than in the low-permeability domain (NTB 93-01, Chapter 12).  In future, as the overlying sediment, or the basement itself, is eroded, then the depth of the transition from higher-permeability domain to low-permeability domain might move downwards.  This effect is only expected to be significant in areas where the basement is directly exposed at the surface, for example, near to the river Rhine.  In the areas for potential repository siting, the basement is presently overlain by sediments and alteration of the basement is expected to be negligible within the next one million years.

pfep_description_raw:
Magmatic activity in the repository region could have a major impact on the system. For example, a magma dyke intersecting the repository could force molten rock along the zones of weakness created by the disposal tunnels and associated excavation-disturbed zones; severe alteration and disturbance of the bentonite buffer would result. 

Conditions and consequences of magmatic activity, in the form of intrusions and volcanic activity, have been discussed in detail by DIEBOLD & MÜLLER (NTB 94-26). They have confirmed that a direct intrusion or extrusion of magma is extremely unlikely in Northern Switzerland during the next ten million years. Magmatic activity is not, therefore, considered further.

pfep_description_raw:
A relationship between the increased geothermal gradient in Northern Switzerland and the Permo-Carboniferous Trough has been postulated on several occasions (see, for example, NTB 84-26).  The fault systems at the margin of the trough appear to promote the rise of deep groundwaters.  The thermal waters cause an overprinting of the conductive heat flux by that due to convection. Clear indications of hydrothermal activity are the thermal springs to the north and south of the Permo-Carboniferous Trough (e.g. at Zurzach).  Hydrothermal activity may result in changes in fracture characteristics through hydrothermal neo-mineralisation and, conversely, formation of solution cavities in cataclastic zones (NTB 93-01).

The pattern of hydrothermal activity in the region is not expected to change significantly over the next million years. It is also expected that significant geothermal anomalies can be avoided by repository siting.  Therefore, the process is not included in Kristallin-I assessment calculations, but is identified as a topic for consideration in site investigation studies.

pfep_description_raw:
Palaeo-evidence indicates that climatic conditions in northern Switzerland have varied greatly in the past.  Over the last one million years the climate has cycled between Pleistocene glacials and interglacials with the last glaciation ending around 10,000 years ago.  Climatic change is to be expected over the timescales relevant to repository performance as a result of natural processes and human activities eg. greenhouse effect.

In the Refernece Scenario present-day climate conditions are assumed to prevail in Northern Switzerland.  Future climatic conditions are accounted for in alternative scenarios.  Two bounding scenarios are accounted for.  One assumes that the pattern of Quaternary ice ages will continue over the next million years (cyclic alternation of cold and temperate periods).  The second assumes that the current warm period signals the end of the Quaternary ice ages (either due to greenhouse effects or natural causes).  Three variations in possible climatic conditions have been identified, continuing humid, seasonally humid or arid.

Considered in alternative biosphere scenarios.

pfep_description_raw:
As the climate cools, air temperatures will fall substantially below freezing point for much of the year. If these conditions are sustained, then permafrost (permanently frozen ground) may develop. The depth to which permafrost will penetrate depends on the average surface temperature, geological conditions (thermal conductivity and geothermal flux) and the period of sustained low temperature (DAMES & MOORE 1991). In Arctic and Antarctic regions, permafrost of several kilometres thickness has developed in places. However, modelling and geological evidence suggest that, in currently temperate regions, permafrost of depths up to a maximum of only a few hundred metres is possible over the period of a future glaciation (BOULTON & PAYNE 1993). If summer temperatures remain above freezing point, then a zone of seasonally unfrozen ground will remain above the permafrost layer, which may support migratory animals and nomadic herdsmen. Thus, the biosphere may be partially isolated from the deep groundwater system. However, significant groundwater discharge zones and the courses of major rivers and lakes are liable to remain as open "taliks", free from permafrost due to the heat from discharging groundwater and insulating effect of large water bodies. Thus, while the presence of permafrost may tend to reduce recharge (to high ground), it may focus groundwater discharge to the remaining unfrozen zones (McEWEN & DeMARSILY 1991).

Hydrological effects are not considered, but the Periglacial Biosphere scenario assumes isolation of biosphere from new radionuclide input from geosphere.

pfep_description_raw:
Erosion and sedimentation caused by glacial ice results in overdeepening of valleys, scouring of upland areas, deposition of glacial moraines and modification of stream channel networks.  The net effect is similar to that of fluvial erosion/sedimentation - potential shortening of flow paths and modifications of the biosphere.

Deep erosion by glaciers consists of a combination of grinding (by rock material carried along at the base of the glacier) and planation of uneven surfaces in the underlying rock.  The form of erosion is each case depends on the geology of the underlying rock, the fracturing and roughness of the rocks and on whether the glacier is frozen right down to its base (cold glacier without basal gliding components) or not (warm or temperate glacier).  During the course of the next million years, glacial erosion in Northern Switzerland could lead to further deepening of existing valleys/channels and lowering of potential exfiltration zones for deep groundwaters.

On the basis that most glaciers did not reach the potential repository zone during the Pleistocene, the maximum glacial erosion is estimated at 300m, and locally more (mainly Alpine foreland).

Considered in Alpine Orogeny continues scenario.

Erosion and deposition by glacial meltwaters occurs early in interglacial intervals.  The process potentially results in downcutting of river channels, deposition of alluvium and glacial outwash and formation of stream terraces.  The net effect is similar to other forms of erosion/sedimentation - potential shortening of flow paths and modifications of the biosphere.

The greatest erosive effect of a glacier occurs during its advance.  The river bed, which is filled with sediments, is often completely scoured and surrounding rock eroded away. pfep_name: Ice sheet effects (loading, melt water recharge)
pfep_description_raw:
A scenario that has been postulated in other studies (e.g. see Volume 3 of SUMERLING (Ed.) 1992) is that, as the ice sheet advances then recharge will occur from the meltwater formed under pressure at the base of the ice sheet. In the case of a static or retreating ice sheet, this water may escape as sub-glacial rivers between the ice and ground. However, in the case of an advancing ice sheet a sealed front may be created by the ice sheet advancing over permafrost so that the meltwater is forced downward into the underlying rock. This situation has been modelled for the case of the Fenno-Scandinavian ice sheet during the last glaciation (BOULTON & PAYNE 1993). Assessments of a site in the UK have shown the effects can be significant to radiological performance of a repository (SUMERLING (Ed.) 1992).

In the case of a repository in the crystalline basement of Northern Switzerland, this scenario would only be significant if permafrost were to develop throughout the overlying sediments and higher-permeability domain, so that water flow in the low-permeability domain is increased. However, this is not thought to be possible because of the great depth implied for permafrost formation (500m) and the significant geothermal gradient in the crystalline basement. Studies have indicated a likely depth of permafrost penetration in advance of a glacial advance in Northern Switzerland of only 100 m (ANON 1994).

pfep_description_raw:
Exploratory boreholes may be sunk in the repository region in search of natural resources, eg. minerals, oil, gas, or to identify geothermal sources or geological formations suitable for disposal of liquid wastes by injection.  Boreholes may intersect the repository or pass close by perturbing the groundwater flow paths.  

The only known examples of deep boreholes into the crystalline basement at present are those undertaken as part of the Nagra investigation programme. It is assumed that, if similar investigations for waste disposal are undertaken in future beyond the time at which specific records of the site are lost, then those undertaking the investigation will be aware of the possibility of earlier disposal operations and plan the investigation accordingly.

If deep drilling is undertaken in the crystalline basement in the future, e.g. for scientific or geothermal investigation, then, depending on the target depth and the drilling activity, the repository may or may not be detected.  If the repository is detected, it is assumed that the necessary remedial action will be taken and the borehole will be sealed.  Due to their limited diameter and spacing, inadvertent interception of the emplacement tunnels themselves is less likely than interception of the excavation-disturbed zone (possibly extending up to one tunnel diameter around the tunnels) or water-conducting features that are hydraulically connected to the repository. 

Doses to geological investigators due to examination of core material following a direct hit on a high-level waste or spent-fuel canister have been variously calculated at between 40 mSv (NORDMAN & VIENO 1989) and 20 to 90 Sv (PRIJ et al. 1989), where the probabilities of these events were estimated at 10-8 y-1 (NORDMAN & VIENO 1989) and 2 to 60 x 10-9 y-1 (PRIJ et al. 1989).  This indicates that the doses received may be very high and certainly exceed the regulatory dose criterion. However, the estimated annual probabilities are sufficiently low that the annual risk criterion of 10-6, specified in HSK Protection Objective 2, would not be exceeded regardless of the dose.

In the Reference Scenario, it is assumed no human activities affect the repository system other than those associated with its construction and operation.

pfep_description_raw:
The potential for extraction of geothermal energy in Northern Switzerland has been discussed in RYBACH (1992a) and RYBACH (1992b).   Two categories are considered:
  a)  natural resources (thermal spring and stratiform aquifers)
  b)  resources for artificially aided heat extraction (vertical heat exchanger and Hot Dry Rock systems)

Confined aquifers in the Molasse Basin (to the south of the crystalline basement units considered in Kristallin-I) are considered to be the most likely targets for extraction of natural geothermal waters, especially the Obere Meeresmolasse and Muschelkalk formations at depths of ca. 500 and 3500 m below ground. RYBACH notes the possibility of extraction from the upper weathered parts of the crystalline basement "at greater depth", i.e. lying below the Molasse Basin sediments at depths ca. 4000 m below ground.

Two distinct methods of artificially aided heat extraction are possible: vertical heat exchanger (VHE) and hot dry rock (HDR) systems.  The VHE is a closed circuit device for a fluid to take heat from the first tens/hundreds of metres of the ground and to feed the cold side (evaporator) of a heat pump.  Up to now, over 8000 VHE systems have been installed in Switzerland in a range of geological media.  The depth of such systems is generally rather shallow, only requiring a sufficient temperature to evaporate the pumped fluid, and hence VHE installations will not affect a deep repository.  The hydraulic properties of the crystalline basement of Northern Switzerland (low permeability and porosity) would necessitate heat extraction by HDR technology (i.e. introduction of water from the surface via a borehole with pumped circulation through natural or artificially stimulated fractures (hydrofracturing) in the rock, before return of the steam or steam/hot water to the surface via a second or more boreholes, see RYBACH 1992a; RYBACH 1992b). 

Moderate geothermal gradients are observed in the crystalline basement of Northern Switzerland, in the range 35 to 45 ˚C km-1, and the ambient rock temperature at a depth of 1200 m is expected to be a maximum of 60 ˚C (NTB 93-01).  With existing technology, a viable geothermal energy scheme would require a source temperature of 150 to 200 ˚C;  this could only be found by drilling to depths of about 3 to 5 km, i.e. well below the repository depth.  Thus, an HDR-type geothermal installation at or near repository depth is considered very unlikely.  If, however, a HDR system were installed in a crystalline-basement block housing repository panels, this would provide a direct route for return of radionuclides to the biosphere.  In the longer-term, after abandonment or closure of the thermal project, the higher permeability introduced by stimulated fractures would continue to be a factor leading to enhanced flow of water and possible transport of radionuclides in the affected zone.  A particular feature of this unlikely scenario is that, if an installation were made, the repository may not be detected until after the drilling and hydrofracturing had been conducted and that, if detected afterwards, effective remedial action may not be possible.

It is concluded that, considering both the current technologies for geothermal exploitation and the local geothermal conditions, VHE installations would be too shallow to intercept the crystalline basement rocks and HDR installations would be too deep to affect the performance of a repository.  It is, however, an open issue whether the possible future exploitation of the crystalline basement as a geothermal energy source should be considered as a factor against the siting of a repository in crystalline basement in principle, i.e. conflicting use of natural resources.

Consideration for siting studies.

If, however, a HDR system were installed in a crystalline-basement block housing repository panels, this would provide a direct route for return of radionuclides to the biosphere.  In the longer-term, after abandonment or closure of the thermal project, the higher permeability introduced by stimulated fractures would continue to be a factor leading to enhanced flow of water and possible transport of radionuclides in the affected zone.  A particular feature of this unlikely scenario is that, if an installation were made, the repository may not be detected until after the drilling and hydrofracturing had been conducted and that, if detected afterwards, effective remedial action may not be possible.

It is concluded that, considering both the current technologies for geothermal exploitation and the local geothermal conditions, VHE installations would be too shallow to intercept the crystalline basement rocks and HDR installations would be too deep to affect the performance of a repository.  It is, however, an open issue whether the possible future exploitation of the crystalline basement as a geothermal energy source should be considered as a factor against the siting of a repository in crystalline basement in principle, i.e. conflicting use of natural resources.

Consideration for siting studies.

pfep_name: No Consideration of Future Human Society and Technology
pfep_description_raw:
Over the timescales considered in post-closure radiological assessment it is recognised that human civilisation and technology are likely to change considerably, but it is not possible to estimate other than in very general terms what changes may occur.  Considering that a general principle of radioactive waste disposal assessment is to afford future generations and individuals the same level of protection as current generations and individuals, it is appropriate to assume future human behaviours similar to that observed in the world today.  Impacts to hypothetical critical groups (see S2.6) dwelling in the future and with habits and technologies similar to a group at some location in the world today can then be regarded as indicators of safety.

Phenomena related to futuristic assumptions about human behaviour and technology can be screened out.  In addition, the possibility of cure for cancer is not relevant since the aim of deep underground disposal of radioactive wastes is to ensure environmental and human protection without the need for future human remedial measures.

Over the timescales considered in post-closure radiological assessment it is recognised that human civilisation and technology are likely to change considerably, but it is not possible to estimate other than in very general terms what changes may occur.  Considering that a general principle of radioactive waste disposal assessment is to afford future generations and individuals the same level of protection as current generations and individuals, it is appropriate to assume future human behaviours similar to that observed in the world today.  Impacts to hypothetical critical groups (see S2.6) dwelling in the future and with habits and technologies similar to a group at some location in the world today can then be regarded as indicators of safety.

Phenomena related to futuristic assumptions about human behaviour and technology can be screened out.  In addition, the possibility of cure for cancer is not relevant since the aim of deep underground disposal of radioactive wastes is to ensure environmental and human protection without the need for future human remedial measures.

pfep_name: Basis for consideration of radiological impacts to man
pfep_description_raw:
Doses should be calculated for an average member of a critical group as defined by ICRP, that is a group that is relatively homogeneous in terms of diet and habits, and with location, diet and habits such that the group is maximally exposed.  Considering doses received at long times in the future, i.e. greater than a few hundred years after closure, it is not necessary to base critical group characteristics on behaviour of actual groups at present day in the immediate locality.  Rather, a subsistence community deriving its water supply and dietary needs locally will generally provide a conservative reference case.  ICRP dosimetric parameter values are adopted;  for convenience, dose-per-unit-intake values are taken from NRPB 1987, which, at the time of carrying out the Kristallin-I safety analysis is the most complete and consistent compilation of dose-per-unit-intake values.

Extreme individual human behaviours and details of actual present-day behaviours need not be considered.  Uncertainties in metabolism and dosimetry are not considered.

pfep_description_raw:
Humans, and plant and animal species, may evolve.  Evolution of food plants and domesticated animals, especially, is to be expected through selective breeding and genetic engineering.  Hence metabolism, radionuclide uptake and radiation sensitivity may change.  These changes cannot be anticipated and, following the argument by which changes in human society and technology are neglected (see 2.5, above), should not be accounted for in quantitative assessments.  

Assessments should be carried out assuming metabolic and physiological characteristics and radio-sensitivity of humans, animals and plants similar to that observed today.

Stratigraphic information (thickness and lateral extent) is an important input to the performance assessment (PA).  Stratigraphy-related parameters are input as constants. The PA model represents the three-dimensional physical system in a two-dimensional plane that cuts vertically through the repository and surrounding strata. project_title: Scenario analysis for WIPP CCA
host_rock: bedded salt (Salado Formation, New Mexico, USA)
ebs_concept:
steel pachages, magnesium oxide backfill,
crushed salt, clay, concrete, and asphalt seal components.
pfep_description_raw:
Units of interest to the WIPP project below the Salado are the Bell Canyon and the Castile.  These units have quite different hydrologic characteristics. In part of the area around the WIPP, the Castile has been significantly deformed and there are pressurized brines associated with the deformed areas.  

Where they exist, Castile brine reservoirs in the northern Delaware Basin are believed to be fractured systems, with high-angle fractures spaced widely enough that a borehole can penetrate through a volume of rock containing a brine reservoir without intersecting any fractures and therefore not produce brine.  They occur in the upper portion of the Castile (Popielak et al. 1983).  Appreciable volumes of brine have been produced from several reservoirs in the Delaware Basin, but there is little direct information on the areal extent of the reservoirs or the interconnection between them.  The presence of a pressurized brine pocket is treated in the conceptual model of WIPP.

The presence of a brine reservoir under the repository is speculative, but cannot be ruled out by available information.  A pressurized brine reservoir was encountered at the WIPP-12 borehole within the controlled area to the northwest of the disposal region and other pressurized brine reservoirs have been encountered elsewhere in the Delaware Basin that are associated with regions of deformation in the Castile.  Based on a geostatistical analysis of the distribution of brine encounters in the region, the DOE has estimated that there is a 0.08 probability that any random borehole that penetrates waste in the WIPP will also penetrate an underlying brine reservoir.  Properties are assigned to the hypothetical reservoir consistent with the available information from tests at WIPP-12 and other boreholes.  These properties are also made consistent with the hypothetical reservoir's location under the waste disposal region.

Screening decision:	DP - Accounted for in assessment calculations for disturbed performance.

	Section 2.1.3
	Section 6.4.8
	Section 6.4.12.6

pfep_description_raw:
The tectonic setting and structural features of the area around the WIPP have been characterized (e.g., Powers et al. 1978).  In summary, there is no geological evidence for Quaternary regional tectonics in the Delaware Basin.  The eastward tilting of the region has been dated as mid-Miocene to Pliocene by King (1948, 120-121) and is associated with the uplift of the Guadalupe Mountains to the west.  Fault zones along the eastern margin of the basin, where it flanks the Central Basin Platform, were active during the Late Permian.  Evidence for this includes the displacement of the Rustler Formation (hereafter referred to as the Rustler) observed by Holt and Powers (1988) and the thinning of the Dewey Lake Redbeds (hereafter referred to as the Dewey Lake) reported by Schiel (1994).  There is, however, no surface displacement along the trend of these fault zones, indicating that there has been no significant Quaternary movement.  Other faults identified within the evaporite sequence of the Delaware Basin are inferred by Barrows' figures in Borns et al. (1983, 58-60) to be the result of salt deformation rather than regional tectonic processes.  According to Muehlberger et al. (1978, 338), the nearest faults on which Quaternary movement has been identified lie to the west of the Guadalupe Mountains and are of minor regional significance.  The effects of regional tectonics and changes in regional stress have therefore been eliminated from performance assessment calculations on the basis of low consequence to the performance of the disposal system.

Screening decision:	SO-C - Eliminated from assessment calculations on the basis of consequence.

Relevant CCA Sections for further information:	Appendix SCR, Section SCR.1.1.2
	Section 2.1.5

host_rock: bedded salt (Salado Formation, New Mexico, USA)
ebs_concept:
steel pachages, magnesium oxide backfill,
crushed salt, clay, concrete, and asphalt seal components.
pfep_description_raw:
There are no reported stress measurements from the Delaware Basin, but a low level of regional stress has been inferred from the geological setting of the area.  The eastward tilting of the region has been dated as mid-Miocene to Pliocene by King (1948, 120-121) and is associated with the uplift of the Guadalupe Mountains to the west.  Fault zones along the eastern margin of the basin, where it flanks the Central Basin Platform, were active during the Late Permian.  The inferred low level of regional stress and the lack of Quaternary tectonic activity indicate that regional tectonics and any changes in regional stress will be minor and therefore of low consequence to the performance of the disposal system.   

Sanford et al. (1991, 230) present a figure showing surface uplift in New Mexico during the past 10 million years.  In southeastern New Mexico in the region of the WIPP this map shows an uplift over this period of about 1000 meters, leading to an average rate of 1 meter in 10,000 years.  The DOE assumes that this average rate will continue for the next 10,000 years, based on the geologic stability of the region (FEP No. 1.003).  This amount of uplift or subsidence would not lead to a breach of the Salado because the salt would deform plastically to accommodate this slow rate of movement.  Uniform regional uplift or a small increase in regional dip consistent with this past rate could give rise to downcutting by rivers and streams in the region.  The extent of this downcutting would be little more than the extent of uplift, and reducing the overburden by 1 or 2 meters would have no significant effect on groundwater flow or contaminant transport in units above or below the Salado.  Thus, the effects of regional uplift and subsidence have been eliminated from performance assessment calculations on the basis of low consequence to the performance of the disposal system.

Screening decision:	SO-C - Eliminated from assessment calculations on the basis of consequence.

project_title: Scenario analysis for WIPP CCA
host_rock: bedded salt (Salado Formation, New Mexico, USA)
ebs_concept:
steel pachages, magnesium oxide backfill,
crushed salt, clay, concrete, and asphalt seal components.
pfep_description_raw:
Deformed salt in the lower Salado and upper strata of the Castile has been encountered in a number of boreholes around the WIPP site.

A number of mechanisms may result in salt deformation, including gravity foundering, dissolution, gravity sliding, gypsum dehydration, and depositional processes.  In massive salt deposits, buoyancy effects or diapirism may cause salt to rise through denser, overlying units.  A review of these hypotheses by Borns (Borns, 1987) concluded that gravity foundering of the anhydrite interbeds into the halite was the most probable cause of deformation within the Castile and Salado in the vicinity of the WIPP.

Gravity foundering can arise because of the difference in density between anhydrite (about 2.9 gm/cc) and halite (about 2.15 gm/cc).  Thus, if anhydrite beds overlie halite deposits there is a tendency for the anhydrite to sink and the halite to rise.  Mathematical models for this process suggest a rate of deformation in the order of 0.02 inch per year (0.05 centimeter per year) assuming an evaporite viscosity of 1018 poise and a viscosity of 1019 poise for the Rustler and Dewey Lake (Borns et al, 1983,  133).  These rates can be used to estimate the time required for deformation by scaling the results of accelerated, dynamically similar, experiments conducted in centrifuges.  Through analogy with structures formed in such experiments, the deformation currently encountered in the vicinity of the WIPP would have developed over about 700,000 years (Borns et al., 1983, p. 133).

The timing of deformation in the vicinity of the WIPP has not been unequivocally determined.  Deformation has been postulated as pre-Pliocene (that is, before deposition of the Ogallala about 5 million years ago), but the conditions required for gravity foundering may still be in existence.  Because of the plastic nature of halite, deformation within the Castile has progressively less effect at higher horizons in the Salado.  Thus, even if deformation is still occurring, the time required for an effect to be apparent at the repository horizon would be much greater than the 700,000 years required to establish the present level of deformation.

Thus, natural salt deformation and diapirism severe enough to alter existing patterns of groundwater flow or the behavior of the disposal system over the regulatory period has been eliminated from performance assessment calculations on the basis of low probability of occurrence over the next 10,000 years.

Screening decision:	SO-P - Eliminated from assessment calculations on the basis of low probability.
	(UP - Accounted for near to the repository).

	Section 2.1.6.1

pfep_description_raw:
Faults are present in the Delaware Basin in both the units underlying the Salado and in the Permian evaporite sequence.  According to Powers et al. (1978, 4-57), there is evidence that movement along faults within the pre Permian units affected the thickness of Early Permian strata, but these faults did not exert a structural control on the deposition of the Castile, the Salado, or the Rustler.  Fault zones along the margins of the Delaware Basin were active during the Late Permian Period.  Along the eastern margin, where the Delaware Basin flanks the Central Basin Platform, Holt and Powers (1988, 4 -14) note that there is displacement of the Rustler, and Schiel (1994) notes that there is thinning of the Dewey Lake.  There is, however, no surface displacement along the trend of these fault zones, indicating that there has been no significant Quaternary movement.  Muehlberger et al. (1978, 338) note that the nearest faults on which Quaternary movement has been identified lie to the west of the Guadalupe Mountains.

The absence of Quaternary fault scarps and the stable tectonic setting allows the formation of new faults within the basin over the next 10,000 years to be eliminated from performance assessment calculations on the basis of low probability of occurrence.

Subsidence above natural dissolution features could lead to the formation of, and movement along, local faults.  However, significant dissolution in the region of the waste panels has been eliminated from performance assessment calculations on the basis of low probability of occurrence over 10,000 years (see FEP No. 1.018), so faults arising from dissolution have also been eliminated on the basis of low probability of occurrence.

Screening decision:	SO-P - Eliminated from assessment calculations on the basis of low probability.

This FEP is concerned with the effects of seismic activity away from the immediate source region, and only the effects of groundshaking and earthquakes are discussed.  Other FEPs consider the direct effects of fault movement (FEP No. 1.011), and changes in hydrogeology induced by seismic activity (FEP No. 1.031).  

Causes of Seismic Activity

Seismic activity describes transient ground motion that may be generated by several energy sources.  There are two possible causes of seismic activity that could potentially affect the WIPP site:  natural and human induced.  Natural seismic activity is caused by fault movement (earthquakes) when the buildup of strain in rock is released through sudden rupture or movement.  Human-induced seismic activity may result from a variety of surface and subsurface activities, such as explosions, mining, fluid injection, and fluid withdrawal that are discussed elsewhere.

Groundshaking

Ground vibration and the consequent shaking of buildings and other structures are the most obvious effects of seismic activity.  Once the repository and shafts have been sealed, however, existing surface structures will be dismantled.  Postclosure performance assessments are concerned with the effects of seismic activity on the closed repository.

In regions of low and moderate seismic activity, such as the Delaware Basin, rocks behave elastically in response to the passage of seismic waves, and there are no long-term changes in rock properties, and the effects of earthquakes beyond the DRZ have been eliminated from performance assessment calculations on the basis of low consequence to the performance of the disposal system.  An inelastic response, such as cracking, is only possible where there are free surfaces, as in the roof and walls of the repository prior to closure by creep.  Seismic activity could, therefore, have an effect on the properties of the DRZ.

An assessment of the extent of damage in underground excavations caused by groundshaking largely depends on observations from mines and tunnels.  Because such excavations tend to take place in rock types more brittle than halite, these observations cannot be related directly to the behavior of the WIPP.  According to Wallner (1981, 244), the DRZ in brittle rock types is likely to be more highly fractured and hence more prone to spalling and rockfalls than an equivalent zone in salt.  Relationships between groundshaking and subsequent damage observed in mines will therefore be conservative with respect to the extent of damage induced at the WIPP by seismic activity.

Dowding and Rozen (1978) classified damage in underground structures following seismic activity and found that no damage (cracks, spalling, or rockfalls) occurred at accelerations below 0.2 gravities and that only minor damage occurred at accelerations up to 0.4 gravities.  Lenhardt (1988, 392) showed that a magnitude 3 earthquake would have to be within 0.6 mile (1 kilometer) of a mine to result in falls of loose rock.  The risk of seismic activity in the region of the WIPP reaching these thresholds is discussed below.

Seismic Risk in the Region of the WIPP

Prior to the introduction of a seismic monitoring network in 1960, most recorded earthquakes in New Mexico were associated with the Rio Grande Rift, although small earthquakes were detected in other parts of the region.  In addition to continued activity in the Rio Grande Rift, the instrumental record has shown a significant amount of seismic activity originating from the Central Basin Platform and a number of small earthquakes in the Los Medaños area.  Seismic activity in the Rio Grande Rift is associated with extensional tectonics in that area.  Seismic activity in the Central Basin Platform may be associated with natural earthquakes, but there are also indications that this activity occurs in association with oil-field activities such as fluid injection.  Small earthquakes in the Los Medaños region have not been precisely located, but may be the result of mining activity in the region.  

The instrumental record was used as the basis of a seismic risk study primarily intended for design calculations of surface facilities rather than for postclosure performance assessments.  The use of this study to define probable ground accelerations in the WIPP region over the next 10,000 years is based on the assumptions that hydrocarbon extraction and potash mining will continue in the region and that the regional tectonic setting precludes major changes over the next 10,000 years.

Three source regions were used in calculating seismic risk: the Rio Grande Rift, the Central Basin Platform, and part of the Delaware Basin province (including the Los Medaños).  Using conservative assumptions about the maximum magnitude event in each zone, the study indicated a return period of about 10,000 years (annual probability of occurrence of 10-4) for events producing ground accelerations of 0.1 gravities.  Ground accelerations of 0.2 gravities would have an annual probability of occurrence of about 5x10-6.

The results of the seismic risk study and the observations of damage in mines due to groundshaking, give an estimated annual probability of occurrence of between 10-6 and 10-8 for events that could increase the permeability of the DRZ.  The DRZ is accounted for in performance assessment calculations as a zone of permanently high permeability (FEP No. 2.018); this treatment is considered to account for the effects of any potential seismic activity.

Screening decision:	UP - Accounted for in assessment calculations.

pfep_description_raw:
The Paleozoic and younger stratigraphic sequences within the Delaware Basin are devoid of locally derived volcanic rocks.  Volcanic ashes (dated at 13 million years and 0.6 million year) do occur in the Gatuña Formation, but these are not locally derived.  Within eastern New Mexico and northern, central, and western Texas, the closest Tertiary volcanic rocks with notable areal extent or tectonic significance to the WIPP are approximately 100 miles (160 kilometers) to the south in the Davis Mountains volcanic area.  The closest Quaternary volcanic rocks are 150 miles (250 kilometers) to the northwest in the Sacramento Mountains.  No volcanic rocks are exposed at the surface within the Delaware Basin.

Volcanic activity is associated with particular tectonic settings: constructive and destructive plate margins, regions of intraplate rifting, and isolated hot-spots in intraplate regions.  The tectonic setting of the WIPP site and the Delaware Basin is remote from plate margins, and the absence of past volcanic activity indicates the absence of a major hot spot in the region.  Intraplate rifting has taken place along the Rio Grande some 120 miles (200 kilometers) west of the WIPP site during the Tertiary and Quaternary Periods.  Igneous activity along this rift valley is comprised of sheet lavas intruded on by a host of small-to-large plugs, sills, and other intrusive bodies.  However, the geological setting of the WIPP site within the large and stable Delaware Basin allows volcanic activity in the region of the WIPP repository to be eliminated from performance calculations on the basis of low probability of occurrence over the next 10,000 years.

Screening decision:	SO-P - Eliminated from assessment calculations on the basis of low probability.

Magmatic activity is defined as the subsurface intrusion of igneous rocks into country rock.  Deep intrusive igneous rocks crystallize at depths of several kilometers and have no surface or near-surface expression until considerable erosion has taken place. Aeromagnetic surveys of the Delaware Basin have shown anomalies that lie on a linear southwest -northeast trend that coincides with the surface and subsurface exposures of magmatic rocks. Magmatic activity has taken place in the vicinity of the WIPP site in the past, but the igneous rocks have cooled over a long period.  Any enhanced fracturing or conduits for fluid flow have been sealed by salt creep and mineralization.  Continuing magmatic activity in the Rio Grande Rift is too remote from the WIPP location to be of consequence to the performance of the disposal system.  Thus, the effects of magmatic activity have been eliminated from performance assessment calculations on the basis of low consequence to the performance of the disposal system.

pfep_description_raw:
Shallow dissolution involves percolation of groundwater and mineral dissolution in the Rustler. Dissolution will initially enhance porosities, but continued dissolution may lead to compaction of the affected units with a consequent reduction in porosity.  Compaction may result in fracturing of overlying brittle units and increased permeability.  Extensive dissolution may create cavities (karst) and result in the total collapse of overlying units. 

Flow through fractures is an important contributor to groundwater flow in the Culebra and other units of the Rustler, and the conductivity of fractures is the principal control of this flow.  East of the WIPP site, a significant proportion of the fractures within the Culebra are infilled with secondary gypsum, whereas to the west of the site most fractures are open.  This distribution of infilled fractures closely parallels the spatial variability of lateral transmissivity in the Culebra and is accounted for in performance assessment calculations through the use of geostatistically conditioned transmissivity fields.

Groundwater basin modeling indicates that the Culebra becomes progressively more confined toward the east.  This corresponds to an increase in the overburden towards the east and a decrease in the fracturing associated with dissolution at the Rustler - Salado boundary.  The analysis presented below indicates that the lateral extent of dissolution at the top of the Salado is not expected to reach the edge of the controlled area for some 225,000 years, and the rates of erosion in this region (see FEP Nos. 1.043-1.045) are very low.  The pattern of vertical transmissivity in the Rustler is therefore not expected to change significantly during the next 10,000 years, and neither the degree of confinement of the Culebra nor the pattern of open fractures in this unit will undergo significant change during this period.

Percolating groundwater may result in some dissolution and precipitation of fracture infills.  The present pattern of secondary gypsum in fractures within the Culebra is considered to be the result of changes in precipitation and recharge over many climate cycles and a similar degree of spatial variability is anticipated to persist into the future.  Corbet et al. (1997) have used flow simulations, calculations of gypsum saturation as a function of depth, and calculations of mass transfers along flow paths to show that gypsum is unlikely to have been significantly dissolved from Culebra fractures over the past 600,000 years.  The extent of any changes in lateral transmissivity in the Culebra in the future due to dissolution is expected to be small and will, therefore, be within the degree of uncertainty accounted for by the use of conditioned transmissivity fields.

Thus, the existing features associated with shallow dissolution and changes due to further shallow dissolution are accounted for in performance assessment calculations through the use of multiple transmissivity fields.

Screening decision:	UP - Accounted for in assessment calculations.

Lateral dissolution involves dissolution at the top of the Salado.  Dissolution will initially enhance porosities, but continued dissolution may lead to compaction of the affected units with a consequent reduction in porosity.  Compaction may result in fracturing of overlying brittle units and increased permeability.  Extensive dissolution may create cavities (karst) and result in the total collapse of overlying units.  

Lateral dissolution takes place when percolating groundwater dissolves halite at the top of the Salado, causing collapse of the overlying Rustler with consequent changes in hydrogeological properties.  Nash Draw, some 5 miles (8 kilometers) to the west of the WIPP site, is the most prominent lateral dissolution feature in the region.  An average lateral dissolution rate of from 6 to 8 miles (10 to 13 kilometers) per million years has been calculated by Bachman et al. (1973, 39) for the Salado based on the assumption that the edge of the salt has moved from the Capitan Reef to its present position over the past 7 to 8 million years.  A vertical dissolution rate of 0.06 mile (0.1 kilometer) per million years has similarly been calculated by Bachman (1974, 71; 1980, 97; 1981, 3) using dated ash layers.  Although these are average rates and may be exceeded during particular climate states or by advancing tongues ahead of the main dissolution front, these rates indicate that dissolution of the Salado at the edge of the WIPP site would not take place for some 225,000 years, and an additional 2 to 3 million years would be required for dissolution to reach the repository horizon.

Lateral dissolution may also have affected the Rustler directly.  In the vicinity of Nash Draw, halite is absent from all the units of the Rustler.  Further east, towards the WIPP site, halite progressively appears in younger units.  This has led many investigators to conclude that halite has been dissolved from the Rustler by groundwater (see, for example, Lambert 1983, Bachman 1984, and Lowenstein 1987).  A sedimentological analysis of the Rustler led Holt and Powers (1988) to conclude that halite had either not been formed or had dissolved soon after deposition and, therefore, that only limited lateral dissolution has occurred since Permian times.  This work is summarized in Powers (1997). Even if post-depositional dissolution has taken place, the period over which it occurred is longer than the regulatory period.  Lateral dissolution has therefore been eliminated from performance assessment calculations on the basis of low consequence to the performance of the disposal system.
