FEPs relating to the assessment basis are not included in the WIPP CCA FEP list.  The CCA has been compiled to show compliance with 40 CFR Part 191 and 40 CFR Part 194.  These regulations specify, inter alia, assumptions regarding future human behaviour.

Regulatory screening arguments are used largely to limit speculation concerning future, potentially disruptive, human-initiated EPs.  In particular, the criterion in 40 CFR § 194.25(a), concerned with predictions of the future states of society, requires that compliance assessments and performance assessments "shall assume that characteristics of the future remain what they are at the time the compliance application is prepared."  The scope of compliance assessments and performance assessments, with respect to the consideration of human-initiated EPs, is discussed in the following subsections.

Scope of Compliance Assessments

Compliance assessments need only consider the undisturbed performance of the disposal system (as stated in 40 CFR § 191.15(a) and 40 CFR § 191.24(a)(1)).  "Undisturbed performance" is defined in 40 CFR § 191.12 as "...the predicted behavior of a disposal system, including consideration of the uncertainties in predicted behavior, if the disposal system is not  disrupted by human intrusion or the occurrence of unlikely natural events."  The scope of compliance assessments is clarified further with respect to human-initiated EPs in 40 CFR § 194.54(b), which states that:

Compliance assessments of undisturbed performance shall include the effects on the disposal system of: (1) Existing boreholes in the vicinity of the disposal system, with attention to the pathways they provide for migration of radionuclides from the site; and (2) Any activities that occur in the vicinity of the disposal system prior to or soon after disposal.  Such activities shall include, but shall not be limited to: Existing boreholes and the development of any existing leases that can be reasonably expected to be developed in the near future, including boreholes and leases that may be used for fluid injection activities.

The DOE assumes that "the vicinity of the disposal system" is a region outside and adjacent to the controlled area that extends far enough to include any activities that can affect the disposal system.  Assessments of undisturbed performance must include consideration of human-initiated EPs relating to activities that have taken place or are reasonably expected to take place in the vicinity of the disposal system in the near future.

Scope of Performance Assessments

Assessments of compliance with the Containment Requirements in 40 CFR § 191.13 require consideration of "all significant processes and events," including human-initiated EPs.  The scope of performance assessments is clarified with respect to human-initiated EPs in 40 CFR § 194.32.  At 40 CFR § 194.32(a) the EPA states that

Performance assessments shall consider natural processes and events, mining, deep drilling, and shallow drilling that may affect the disposal system during the regulatory time frame.

Thus, performance assessments must include consideration of human-initiated EPs relating to mining and drilling activities that might take place during the regulatory time frame.  In particular, performance assessments must consider the potential effects of such activities that might take place within the controlled area at a time when institutional controls cannot be assumed to eliminate completely the possibility of human intrusion.

In implementing the Assurance Requirements (40 CFR § 191.14), the EPA has provided criteria relating to the effectiveness of institutional controls.  With respect to active institutional controls, 40 CFR § 194.41(b) states that

Performance assessments shall not consider any contributions from active institutional controls for more than 100 years after disposal.

The DOE assumes credit for active institutional controls, such that no human intrusion will take place within the controlled area for 100 years after disposal.  However, consistent with 40 CFR § 194.41(b), the DOE assumes no credit in performance assessments for active institutional controls for more than 100 years after disposal.

Criteria concerning the credit that can be used for passive institutional controls in reducing the likelihood of future human intrusion are provided in 40 CFR § 194.43(c):

The Administrator may allow the Department to assume passive institutional control credit, in the form of reduced likelihood of human intrusion, if the Department demonstrates in the compliance application that such credit is justified because the passive institutional controls are expected to endure and be understood by potential intruders for the time period approved by the Administrator.  Such credit, or a smaller credit as determined by the Administrator, cannot be used for more than several hundred years and may decrease over time.  In no case, however, shall passive institutional controls be assumed to eliminate the likelihood of human intrusion entirely.

The preamble to 40 CFR Part 194 clarifies that in performance assessments "the likelihood of mining may be decreased by passive institutional controls and active institutional controls, to the extent that can be justified in the compliance application and to a degree identical to that assumed for drilling."  The preamble also limits any credit for passive institutional controls in deterring human intrusion to 700 years after disposal.  For performance assessment calculations, passive institutional controls are assumed to be 99 percent effective for the period of time from 100 years to 700 years after disposal.  Thus, the rates of future drilling and mining for the duration of this 600-year period are assumed to be 1 percent of the predicted rates of drilling and mining after 700 years.

Further criteria concerning the scope of performance assessments are provided at 40 CFR § 194.32(c):

Performance assessments shall include an analysis of the effects on the disposal system of any activities that occur in the vicinity of the disposal system prior to disposal and are expected to occur in the vicinity of the disposal system soon after disposal.  Such activities shall include, but shall not be limited to, existing boreholes and the development of any existing leases that can be reasonably expected to be developed in the near future, including boreholes and leases that may be used for fluid injection activities.

Performance assessments must include consideration of all human-initiated EPs relating to activities that have taken place or are reasonably expected to take place in the vicinity of the disposal system in the near future.

Categorization of Human Activities

In order to implement the criteria in 40 CFR Part 194 relating to the scope of compliance assessments and performance assessments, three categories of human activities have been defined.  Distinctions are made between (1) human activities that are currently taking place and those that took place prior to the time of the compliance application, (2) human activities that might be initiated in the near future after submission of the compliance application, and (3) human activities that might be initiated after repository closure.  The first two categories of EPs are considered under undisturbed performance, and EPs in the third category lead to disturbed performance conditions.

Historical, Current, and Near-Future Human Activities

Historical and current human activities include all types of resource extraction activities that have historically taken place and are currently taking place outside the controlled area.  These activities are of potential significance insofar as they could affect the geological, hydrological, or geochemical characteristics of the disposal system or groundwater flow pathways outside the disposal system.  Current human activities taking place within the controlled area are essentially those associated with development of the WIPP repository.  The observational data obtained as part of WIPP site characterization reflect any effects of historical and current human activities in the vicinity of the WIPP, such as groundwater extraction and oil and gas production.  However, such human activities have resulted only in minor disturbances to the hydrological and geochemical conditions within the controlled area, that will have no significant effects on the long-term performance of the disposal system.

Near-future human activities include resource extraction activities that may be expected to occur outside the controlled area based on existing plans and leases.  Such activities are of potential significance insofar as they could affect the geological, hydrological, or geochemical characteristics of the disposal system or groundwater flow pathways outside the disposal system.  The only human activities that are expected to occur within the controlled area in the near future are those associated with development of the WIPP repository.  In order to bound the analysis of the effects of human activities outside the controlled area, the DOE assumes that any activity that is expected to be initiated in the near future, based on existing plans and leases, will be initiated prior to repository closure.  Activities initiated prior to repository closure are assumed to continue until their completion, potentially at some time after disposal.

Future Human Activities

Future human activities include activities that might be initiated within or outside the controlled area after repository closure.  Performance assessments, but not compliance assessments, must consider the effects of future human activities on the performance of the disposal system.  The EPA has provided criteria relating to future human activities in 40 CFR § 194.32(a), which limit the scope of consideration of future human activities in performance assessments to mining and drilling.  Mining and drilling could occur within the disposal system at a time when institutional controls cannot be assumed to eliminate completely the possibility of such activities.  Thus, mining and drilling may occur within the controlled area after the end of the period of active institutional control (100 years after disposal).  Future human activities could potentially influence the transport of contaminants within and outside the disposal system, by resulting in direct removal of waste from the disposal system or alteration of the geological, hydrological, or geochemical characteristics of the disposal system.  

Criteria Concerning Future Mining

The EPA provides additional criteria concerning the type of future mining that should be considered by the DOE in 40 CFR § 194.32(b):

Assessments of mining effects may be limited to changes in the hydraulic conductivity of the hydrogeologic units of the disposal system from excavation mining for natural resources.  Mining shall be assumed to occur with a one in 100 probability in each century of the regulatory time frame.  Performance assessments shall assume that mineral deposits of those resources, similar in quality and type to those resources currently extracted from the Delaware Basin, will be completely removed from the controlled area during the century in which such mining is randomly calculated to occur.  Complete removal of such mineral resources shall be assumed to occur only once during the regulatory time frame.

Thus, consideration of future mining may be limited to mining within the disposal system at the locations of resources that are similar in quality and type to those currently extracted from the Delaware Basin.

With respect to consideration of future drilling, in the preamble to 40 CFR Part 194, the EPA "reasoned that while the resources drilled for today may not be the same as those drilled for in the future, the present rates at which these boreholes are drilled can nonetheless provide an estimate of the future rate at which boreholes will be drilled." pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE: Acid rain can detrimentally affect aquatic and terrestrial life by interfering with the growth, reproduction and survival of organisms.  It can influence the behaviour and transport of radionuclides in the biosphere, particularly in surface water and soil.  In surface water, it may change the solubility, sedimentation and bioavailability of some radionuclides (Santschi et al. 1986; Schindler and Turner 1982; Wang 1987; Schindler et al. 1980a).  In the soil, acid rain can decrease sorption and thereby increase the mobility of some radionuclides (Sheppard and Sheppard 1988).  Furthermore, it can reduce soil pH and enhance pH degassing of carbon dioxide.  Acid rain might conceivably lead to degradation of the vault concrete.

RESPONSE: Acid precipitation has been shown to modify the behaviour of heavy metals in the environment, and may have a similar effect on many radionuclides.  The most commonly reported acidification effects are the leaching of metal cations from soils and sediments, and inhibition of trace metal and radionuclide sorption to sediment particles (Schindler et al. 1980a, Jackson et al. 1980), resulting in higher trace metal and radionuclide concentrations in surface water.

In the context of the IRUS PSAR, acidification of soils by atmospheric acid inputs associated with NO3- or by SO42-  may have several impacts on the forest ecosystem, or a household inhabited by members of a receptor group.  

The NO3-  anion is typically consumed as a nutrient by plant communities.  Enhanced plant growth will have minimal impact on dose to consumers because the soil-to-plant transfer factor is assumed to be independent of system yield, although in reality, contaminant concentrations in biota are often lower in rapidly growing organisms, a phenomenon known as "growth dilution" or "production dilution" (Hendriks 1995).

The SO42-  anion typically migrates through soils (Hendershot et al. 1991), accompanied by an equivalent flux of cations (either H+ or other exchanged cations).  Cations released in exchange for H+ may be released from cation exchange sites, or result from primary weathering of the soil mineral matrix.  

In the former case, radionuclides deposited on the soil by local atmospheric transport from surface water, or by irrigation, may be leached.  Accelerated leaching of soils would shorten the radionuclide soil residence time, making the model used in SYVAC-NSURE for the IRUS PSAR more likely to overestimate the dose consequence to a receptor group.

Radionuclides leached from the soil surface will either find sorption sites on soil materials deeper in the soil profile, and thus tend to be less accessible to humans, or be leached through the entire soil profile to escape with streamflow.  Although the latter process will tend to increase radionuclide concentrations in surface water, its effect is implicitly accounted for in the SYVAC- NSURE code because the groundwater and surface water compartments are not depleted for any radionuclides diverted from the groundwater flow system to the soil with irrigation water.

Acidification of groundwater in the Lake 233 region is unlikely, although the natural buffering capacity of the groundwater is modest.   Lake 233 serves as the recharge area for most of the groundwater flowing beneath the IRUS site.  As the water seeps through the silty and organic layers of the lake bed, NO3-  and SO42-  are reduced to serve as electron acceptors for the decomposition of organic matter, while generating acid neutralizing capacity in the sediments.  This process will thus act as a natural buffering system for the water flux from the aquifer.

Acidification of surface water may tend to elevate aqueous radionuclide concentrations because mechanisms leading to sedimentation (exchangeable sorption to binding sites on suspended sediments, co-precipitation with Fe- and Mn-oxyhydroxides) are suppressed.

This process may lead to modest increases in the concentration of some radionuclides in the flesh of fish in the pH range 5.6 to 6.5.  More pronounced increases in trace metal, and by implication radionuclide concentrations, are observed in strongly acidified lakes (i.e., pH < 5.6).

These increases are unlikely to be transferred to fish because successful reproduction of most game species is suppressed below pH 5.6 (Schindler et al. 1991).  Thus, under severe acidification, the fish ingestion pathway leading to human exposure will cease to function.

Carbon-14 is a special case, having two phases (gaseous CO2 and water-borne bicarbonate).  The primary chemical form for C-14 is expected to be bicarbonate.  Under strong acid loading, bicarbonate is titrated to base, neutralizing the acid and releasing 14CO2 .  This 14CO2 is highly volatile in comparison with bicarbonate, and will tend to be degassed to the atmosphere (Hesslein et al. 1980; Bower and McCorkle 1980; Bower et al. 1987).  This may occur in the groundwater, in the unlikely event of aquifer acidification, in the soil, or in surface water.  Degassing of 14CO2  to the atmosphere results in its rapid dispersal to trivial concentrations, with minimal dose consequences.

Overall, acid rain will not significantly affect the estimated doses and other impacts examined in the performance assessment.

project_title: Analysis of Safety Issues for IRUS
waste_type: baled and bituminised LLW from Chalk River Laboratories operations
host_rock: large sand ridge, near surface
ebs_concept: waste in reinforced concrete vault above the water table
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Animals might intrude into the vault, promoting the release and spread of contamination in two ways:
   1)	burrowing animals might contact or ingest contaminated soil, and the contaminated animals might be consumed by humans;
   2)	some of the displaced soil might be directly ingested by humans.

Plants growing over or near the covered IRUS vault might draw up and concentrate contaminated water from inside or near the vault through their roots, thus shortening the groundwater pathway to surface soil and humans.

RESPONSE:  With regard to animals, black bears or small animals might intrude into the vault and ingest or inhale soil.  Nuclide concentrations in their tissues would be increased, which might then be consumed by humans.

However, intruding animals are never likely to become an important component of a human's diet.  During the period that the IRUS roof and walls provide a physical barrier, animal intrusion into the vault from above would be prevented.  To enter the vault from below an animal would first need to burrow through the vault cover and down at least eight metres outside the vault.  Only a small amount of contaminated vault material would be transported to the surface, and the impact on humans would be much less than the exposure cases examined in the construction and agricultural intrusion scenarios.

Even in the long term after the vault roof has degraded to rubble, an animal would need to burrow through several metres of IRUS cover and degraded roof material to intrude from above into the topmost vault contents, (which are those most likely to be disturbed by an animal).  Less contaminated waste will be emplaced in the top layer of the vault.  In addition, in the humid local climate infiltrating water will further decrease the contaminant content in the top layers by downward leaching.
Concerning plants, soil ingestion by humans is a potentially important exposure pathway (Hawley 1985) that needs to be considered quantitatively, although individual contributors to this pathway need not necessarily be considered explicitly. 

Contaminants in groundwater may be taken up through the roots of vegetation growing above the flow system.  Root uptake by plants in the human food chain is modelled explicitly in the NSURE and GENII assessment codes.

Several studies have been made at CRL of tree uptake of nuclides from groundwater (Cooper and McHugh 1983, Cooper and Mattie 1990, Cooper and Rahman 1994).  Nuclide uptake by trees growing over a shallow (1 to 2 m deep) aquifer can be spatially heterogeneous, due to variabilities in both the distribution of the nuclides in the soil and the uptake by individual trees (Cooper and Mattie 1990). The chemical speciation of a nuclide also can be important to the uptake into trees.  For instance, while 60Co can be present in water in predominantly anionic, stable, hydrophilic forms, these forms may be less bioavailable than more labile cationic forms (Cooper and McHugh 1983).

Nuclides taken up into a tree are incorporated into the tree's woody and leaf tissue.  Even if the water table is at a depth of the order of 1 m or more, nuclides can still reach the top few cm of earth by autumnal leaf fall and eventual toppling over of the trees after they die (Cooper and Rahman 1994).  As a consequence, it may take many years for the nuclides in the ecosystem to come to an equilibrium distribution. Thus, the paths involved in radionuclide uptake by trees can be complex, and definition of meaningful concentration factors relating content in trees to content in soil can be problematic.

A recent study was made of the rooting depth and water uptake characteristics of trees growing above two tritiated plumes near waste management facilities at CRL (Killey and Uchida 1997).  In cool, humid climates like that at CRL, tree root systems are concentrated in the upper 2 m of soil.  Many trees do extend a small number of roots to greater depths where the unsaturated zone is thicker.  It was concluded in the study that for the soil conditions at CRL, groundwater-transported contaminants will rise no more than about 0.6 m in the  capillary fringe above the water table.  It was further found that 80% of the trees growing 2 to 7 m obtained up to 10% of their moisture requirements from the water table.  There was no evidence of root uptake of groundwater where the unsaturated zone was more than 7 m thick. 

The water table is more than 9 m below the surface at the IRUS site, and the vault roof and earthen cover above it will add more than 4 m to that thickness.  The water table is more than 3 m below the surface for the first 200 m downstream of IRUS.   As a consequence, any trees that might take root above IRUS or within 200 m downstream of the closed vault can be expected to draw up little or no groundwater from the underlying aquifer.

Much of the tritium in the waste in IRUS will have largely decayed away in the period of institutional control.  Many of the long-lived radionuclides in IRUS (e.g. Am, Th, Pu, U, Ra, Nb) sorb well to soil and have relatively low transfer from soil to plants (Davis et al. 1993).

Pathways to humans involving trees (building materials and heating fuel) will result in relatively low doses in comparison to the more direct food chain pathways that were modelled in the assessment, involving direct ingestion of nuclides in groundwater, or in locally grown food.

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Terrestrial animals may become externally contaminated with radionuclides from contact with water, soil or air.  Radionuclides may then be ingested by the animal itself or by another animal through a variety of activities, such as grooming, preening and fighting.  There are two resulting pathways leading to internal doses to humans: 
1) ingestion of the soil by the animal, and ingestion of the animal by humans;
2) transport of the contaminants (in particular, from a pet) to humans in several ways, and human ingestion of the soil.

ebs_concept: waste in reinforced concrete vault above the water table
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Contaminants, such as radionuclides, may adhere to various particles suspended in the water column within water bodies and settle to the bottom.  The processes involved may affect exposure pathways, hence impacts, on humans and non-human biota.  

RESPONSE:  The tendency of radionuclides to attach to particles varies, and some, such as cobalt-60, are much more particle reactive than others and, therefore, settle out more readily (Santschi et al. 1986).  Upon settling, radionuclides become part of the surficial layer of sediments, which is subject to perturbation by wave action and the activity of various organisms.  The latter is referred to as bioturbation.  Beneath the surficial layer, which is not very deep, are the compact sediments, which can be very deep, depending on the age of the water body and the rate of sedimentation.  Occasionally storms can resuspend large quantities of previously deposited sediment into the water column (Bengtsson et al. 1990; Evans 1994).  These sediments tend to re-settle quickly, and so have little impact on annual average contaminant concentrations in the lake, or on the annual average radiological dose to humans or biota exposed to the lake water.  

The presence of some resuspended sediments with associated contaminants is implicitly modelled through the use of a net radionuclide transfer rate from water to sediment.  The transfer of contaminant radionuclides from water to sediment is modelled as a first-order loss process, with the water column compartment being depleted for the sedimentation of radionuclides.  The backwards transfer, or release of contaminants from sediment to water is not explicitly modelled.  

Each chemical element assessed is assigned a unique parameter value representing the best estimate of the mean long-term net transfer rate from water to sediment.  Wherever possible (i.e., in most cases), information about the water-to-sediment transfer rate is based on direct measurements of radionuclide or elemental mass balance budgets for real lakes.  Where information on specific elements is lacking, the environmental behaviour of similar chemical elements is used, or values are based on equilibrium solid-liquid partition coefficients (Kd).  Details of the parameter values used for specific elements can be found in Bird et al. (1992).  A high value (i.e., > 1 a-1) for the water-to-sediment transfer rate is appropriate for elements such as Cs that bind strongly to, and are retained by sediments, whereas a low value (i.e., < 0.1 a-1) reflects geochemically conservative (i.e., weakly sorbing to solids) behaviour exhibited by elements such as Cl.

A radionuclide concentration is calculated for beach sediments using an equilibrium solid-water partition coefficient, or Kd model.  The only pathway leading from beach sediments to humans is assumed to be "groundshine" (see FEP 139).

The uptake of radionuclides from sediments by aquatic biota is modelled implicitly, because most of the data used to calculate bioconcentration factors between lake water and fish flesh are derived from empirical measurements of elemental or radionuclide concentrations in fish tissues and water.  Thus, these data implicitly include the effects of food-chain processes, including sediment ingestion by fish.

 351  Biosphere Model - Oversimplification

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Ash and sewage sludge fertilizers may be contaminated with radionuclides and may be applied to land to increase plant yield.  Radionuclides may then be taken up by plants and enter various food webs.  While in the soil, the radionuclides may expose humans and other organisms to external radiation.  Furthermore, ash may be used in the manufacturing of building materials, which could also result in external radiation exposure.  Similarly, charcoal could be produced from wood contaminated with radionuclides and the charcoal may then be used as a source of heat or as a filter material.  Charcoal production and burning would drive off some radionuclides, whereas others may remain with the ash.

RESPONSE:  All these exposure pathways are related to recycling of radionuclides whereby contaminants that have been released to the biosphere may be reused, or may recycle through different biota or be redistributed before they leave the vicinity of a receptor group or are entirely used up.

There are two aspects to consider:
1) recycling as such, and
2) redistribution of contamination through recycling, e.g., enriching garden soil with animal droppings that are contaminated through sources other than the garden. 

Concerning recycling as such, nuclide source compartments are not depleted in the NSURE environmental transport model when some of the nuclides move to other compartments.  As a consequence, the model overestimates contamination levels and resulting doses.

Redistribution of contamination through recycling is more complex.  The garden manure pathway is probably the most important pathway involved.  In the assessed scenarios, animals can ingest contaminated drinking water, but are assumed to consume only uncontaminated feed, because forage crops are not irrigated.  Therefore, any addition of contaminants to the garden from animal droppings would come from the water ingested by the animals.  Given the relatively small amount of drinking water involved, compared to the much larger amount of irrigation water applied directly to the garden, the additional dose to humans from consuming vegetation absorbing contaminants from the droppings will be relatively small.

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Contaminants may accumulate and concentrate in different organisms, including members of receptor groups, and affect the resulting impacts.

RESPONSE:  Bioaccumulation and biomagnification are related processes, and differ from  bioconcentration (Zach and Sheppard 1992). Bioconcentration refers to the ability of an organism to concentrate a contaminant from its environment, usually from water or soil.  Bioaccumulation refers to the tendency of an organism to continue to bioconcentrate throughout its lifetime.  Finally, biomagnification refers to the occurrence of a contaminant at successively higher concentrations with increasing trophic level in the food web.  All these processes are important in the food-chain transfer of radionuclides and need to be considered quantitatively, although not necessarily separately.

For fish, the three processes are fully included in aquatic concentration ratios.  These ratios are usually based on fish caught in the wild, and so include bioaccumulation with age of fish, and biomagnification for predacious fish near the top of the food chain.  By definition, the ratio accounts for bioconcentration.  Biomagnification through the consumption of fish by aquatic or terrestrial mammals and birds, such as mink, otter, heron, osprey, etc., mainly concerns estimation of doses to non-human biota. 

For domesticated animals, the three processes can be assumed to be fully included in the transfer factors for meat, and poultry and eggs, that have been used in the NSURE code.  However, bioaccumulation and biomagnification cannot be assumed to be included in the transfer factors when humans ingest wild animals, or when doses are being estimated for wild animals.  In principle, food chain models could be modified and used with appropriate transfer factors, but adequate data are not available to establish transfer factors.

Radionuclides, being inorganic contaminants, generally do not bioaccumulate and biomagnify.  For instance, Zach et al. (1989) found that Cs-137 concentration in moose does not change significantly with age.  However, some bioaccumulation from prey species to wolf was found, so that wolves had about a six-times higher concentration than moose.  Cs-137 seems to be a unique radionuclide in this respect.

waste_type: baled and bituminised LLW from Chalk River Laboratories operations

ebs_concept: waste in reinforced concrete vault above the water table
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Animals might intrude into the vault, promoting the release and spread of contamination.  Bioturbation of soil and sediment by plants, and especially by burrowing animals, could physically displace large amounts of soil.  This would promote redistribution and uniform mixing of radionuclides in soil and sediment (Robbins and Edgington 1975, Robbins et al. 1977, Durham and Joshi 1984).  

For agricultural soil, bioturbation has a similar effect as plowing.  This type of mixing is important and thus bioturbation of soil and sediment needs to be quantified, although not necessarily explicitly; for example, it may be adequate to assume that radionuclides are uniformly distributed in soil and sediment.

RESPONSE:  In soil, bioturbation refers mainly to the process whereby the soil is perturbed by animals, e.g., voles, moles, earthworms, etc.  The effect of this is that the soil material and contaminants in it become thoroughly mixed if given enough time.  Within a given layer of soil, bioturbation mainly contributes to the redistribution of contaminants and so has little or no effect.  The action of animals involved in bioturbation could contribute to the transport of more contaminated material from below up to the surface, and this would tend to increase dose predictions.  This is discussed under FEP 4,  Animals (intrusion).   

The soil model in the environmental transport model is based on the assumption of downward leaching of contaminants.  Bioturbation that elevates buried soil to the surface could thus lead to either an increase or decrease in concentration, depending on the specific situation.

Sediments in surface water bodies are modelled as being well-mixed, the mixing being caused by waves, fish, and various invertebrates.  Mixing can lead to the suspension of contaminants to the water column.  Sedimentation is treated through net water-to-sediment transfer rates.  Exposure to sediments is calculated using an equilibrium soil-water distribution coefficient.  This is discussed under FEP 9.  Again, bioturbation could either increase or decrease the estimated nuclide concentrations in sediments.

In summary, it is difficult to judge whether bioturbation will have any significant effect on dose estimates for humans and other biota.

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Explosions or other shocks external to the vault could affect the performance of the vault or of the geosphere.  Explosions, blasting, and vibration after the vault is constructed could alter rock properties, water flow fields, or the integrity of the vault structure.  

RESPONSE:  The types of events to consider include: (i) artillery shells, bombs or missiles from Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Petawawa, (ii) aircraft crashes, (iii) gas line explosions, and (iv) blasting during construction.

(i) Artillery Shells, Bombs or Missiles from CFB Petawawa
 
CRL Protective Services have given verbal assurance that no projectiles from CFB Petawawa have ever landed on the CRL site, nor have there been any aircraft crashes.

The Range Control Officer at CFB Petawawa has written (Slievert 1995) that CFB Petawawa policy allows no artillery impact in the areas adjacent to AECL property, and with the rules and regulations followed by the Military, IRUS is quite safe from any actions by the Military at CFB Petawawa.

(ii) Aircraft Crashes

Under Transport Canada regulations, the Chalk River Laboratories site has been designated as Class F restricted airspace CYR 510.  The applicable Transport Canada operating procedures state that, "No person shall operate an aircraft within the area described [from the surface to an altitude of 3000'] unless the flight has been authorized by the User/Controlling agency" (Transport Canada 1994).  In 1994 September, the Site Licence Holder for the CRL site extended approval previously granted to the Canadian Forces for Department of National Defence helicopters and C-130 Hercules training flights to enter the restricted area at a flight elevation of 1000' above ground level (AGL) and above, but no flights should enter the space above the CRL reactors and other nuclear facilities.  Further, he suggested that military aircraft following the general line of the Ottawa River should overfly the Québec side of the river at least half a mile from CRL.   CRL Protective Services are to be advised of planned major air traffic movements within CRL airspace. (de Verteuil 1994)

If a stray projectile or aircraft did impact directly on the IRUS cover, only minor excavation of cover material would be expected.  If there were any attendant dispersal of contaminated material from the vault, the consequences would be less than those associated with the inadvertent removal and reuse of larger amounts of the vault contents in the agricultural intrusion scenario that is assessed explicitly in the PSAR.

(iii) Gas Line Explosions

There is no natural gas service to CRL.  If a gas line were ever installed during the institutional control period, it is reasonable to assume that the route would be chosen to be well clear of existing structures, including IRUS, to prevent disturbing or damaging them.

(iv) Blasting During Construction

Because IRUS will be located underground in a sand ridge, any vibration due to blasting for any future construction in the area would be attenuated by the sand.  The vibration would be of shorter duration and less magnitude than the vibration associated with an earthquake, against the effects of which the vault is designed.

For the postclosure assessment, no allowance is made for any loss of contaminated groundwater in an IRUS plume into the bedrock.  If blasting caused bedrock fracturing under the aquifer downstream from IRUS, then the groundwater flow path would lengthen and allow more dispersion and sorption than is now assumed.  Hence the resulting doses would be lower than the current estimates of dose.

 100 Seismic Event
 277 Soil Liquification (seismic)
 322 Volcanic Activity

pfep_name: Buffer (plugging by bitumen, slime molds, waste degradation products, etc.)
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  The movement of water and contaminants in the buffer will be affected by properties of the buffer such as porosity, tortuosity, hydraulic conductivity, swelling pressure and sorption.  Plugging of the buffer layers by bitumen, molds, or waste degradation products would compromise the effectiveness and intent of the buffer. 

RESPONSE:  In addition to radionuclide sorption, the buffer layers below IRUS should also permit the vault to drain freely.  The buffer layers have about the same permeability as sand, hence drainage is ensured provided these layers do not become clogged (Sheppard et al. 1995, Woods 1995).  

As discussed in the PSAR (Part III, Secs. 3.4.2 and 5.1), the degradation of bitumen and baled waste in IRUS is expected to be a very slow process - occurring for several hundred to several thousand years.  In contrast to this, the intense degradation of municipal solid waste (MSW) in landfills is a process that occurs for several decades.  Correspondingly, MSW leachate is expected to have much higher levels of dissolved organic carbon and dissolved solids than leachate from the IRUS facility.  

Clogging of the IRUS buffer is unlikely to occur because:
      (i)	The abundance of bacteria in polluted aquifer material below MSW landfills is too scarce to create biofilms (Christensen et al. 1994); therefore it is unlikely that biofilms will form in the IRUS buffer.  
      (ii)	Apart from reported clogging of drain pipe perforations, sand drainage layers above clay liners function well in leachate collection systems of MSW landfills (Ramke 1989).

ISSUE:  The primary function of the buffer layer in the base of IRUS is to sorb material dissolved in waste leachate, and thereby reduce the escape of nuclides from the vault.  The effectiveness of the sorption relies upon the aqueous solution coming into contact with sufficient clinoptilolite or clay to immobilize or retard the contaminants.  Channelling of the buffer as a result of cracking or erosive processes would allow contaminants to pass through the materials with only limited opportunity for ion exchange and sorption.

RESPONSE:  In the earlier design of the IRUS facility (pre-1991) sorption was assumed to occur in the permeable sand/clinoptilolite buffer layer (or floor) and there was no credit taken for sorption in the sand backfill.  The IRUS design now incorporates a sorbing backfill in addition to the sorbing buffer layer.  Many of the buffer layer issues arose because this was the single barrier in which sorption was assumed to occur.  Now, in the new design, the sorptive capacity of the vault system has been increased to include the sand/clinoptilolite backfill, which in turn decreases the reliance on the buffer layer.  FEPs 27, 28a, 28b, 29 and 30 were all based on the earlier design.

In the NSURE vault model, the assumption is made that water will infiltrate uniformly across the buffer.  If channelling were to occur, it would lead to higher local infiltration velocities than if infiltration were uniform, and therefore a shorter residence time of the infiltrating water.  The clinoptilolite or clay could become locally saturated with strongly adsorbed cations sooner than if infiltration were uniform.  However, while total saturation with K+ can reduce the sorption coefficient Kd of clinoptilolite by up to 1.5 orders of magnitude, this will be compensated by the lower ionic strength of the leachate due to the dilution effect of the greater infiltration.  The issue of buffer saturation is discussed further in  FEP 182 - Buffer (chemical saturation).  

The net effect of buffer channelling may thus be expected to be small.

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  The buffer being placed in the base of the IRUS vault will comprise two separate layers.  The upper layer will be a mixture of sand and clinoptilolite (90/10 wt%), and the bottom layer will be composed of a mixture of sand and Dochart clay (90:10wt%).   In both cases the active component represents a relatively small fraction of the total mixture.  Water passing through the bottom buffer layer could wash out the clay, rendering the buffer ineffective.

RESPONSE:  The clinoptilolite particles in the upper layer of the buffer and in the backfill will be coarser than the sand with which they are mixed Woods (1995).  As a consequence, the clinoptilolite will not be subject to washout.

The clay component in the lower layer of the buffer is loosely held because the pore space between the sand particles is only partially filled by the finer particles of clay.  If channelling were to occur and if the clay was washed out and concentrated into a lower stratum, the hydraulic conductivity of the concentrated clay would be expected to be lower than the original sand/clay mix; thus, preferential flow would be around, instead of through the clay.  Tests have been done to measure the hydraulic conductivity of a 50:50 mixture of sand and clay that would be representative of a clay washout and reconcentration condition.  The hydraulic conductivity of the 50:50 mix was only about a factor of 3 lower than that of the 90:10 mix (Woods 1986).  Thus a concentrated clay layer would still provide good drainage.  Further, washout of clay will not decrease its sorptive capacity, and the clay will only be displaced along the downgradient flow path.

As per the discussion in FEP 27, washout of clay from the buffer was an issue of greater concern for the performance of the pre-1991 IRUS design.

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Capillary rise involves the drawing up of soil water above the water table in continuous pores of the soil until the suction gradient upward is balanced by the gravitational pull downward.  Capillary rise of water from the aquifer underlying IRUS might conceivably bathe the lower waste packages and lead to earlier and greater release of contaminants from the packages.
 
RESPONSE:  Fluvial sand generally has a low capillary rise value, generally below 50 cm.  Since the base of the IRUS vault will be located at least 1 meter above the maximum observed water table, capillary rise could not cause sufficient upward movement of aquifer water to reach the base of the IRUS structure (Sheppard et al. 1995). The IRUS backfill and top layer of buffer material contain coarser material than the lower buffer layer, which includes a proportion of fine Dochart clay.  Any water that might perch at the interface between the bottom buffer layer and the coarser native sand below it could not rise sufficiently by capillary action to reach the waste in the vault (Sheppard et al. 1995).  

The IRUS roof will be protected by a several metre-thick multi-layer cover.  The cover includes a capillary break consisting of 70-80 cm layer of cobbles, and a protected 40-60 cm layer of sand.  Even after the roof degrades and allows infiltration, nuclide-bearing water inside the vault could not move upward by capillary rise to the base of the degraded roof through the sand covering the top layer of waste packages.

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  The chemical environment and aqueous chemistry outside the IRUS vault (farfield) will likely differ from those within the vault.  This may affect nuclide migration through the underlying unsaturated layer and the aquifer.  Examples of conceivably important factors are: the nature of and changes in the Eh, pH, and chemical composition of the groundwater; chemical precipitation or dissolution conditions; and chemical kinetics.

Dissolved components in the unsaturated zone under the vault will reflect the chemical conditions established by the vault porewater, i.e., ionic strength (major ions or total dissolved solids (TDS)), and dissolved organic matter (DOM).  The TDS influence the sorption of nuclides on the aquifer substrate particles by competition (both specific and non-specific) for ion exchange sites.

RESPONSE:  The effect of ionic strength was considered in choosing Kd's for the target nuclides in the assessment (Caron 1995).  Ionic strength in the aquifer groundwater will be lower than in the vault because of the leachate dilution that will occur in the aquifer. 

After water infiltrates into the vault, a redox front will form in the unsaturated zone below the vault, between the relatively anoxic vault and the oxygenated soil below.  Redox-sensitive metals such as iron in the vault will be mobilized by corrosion under the anoxic conditions in the vault.  Upon encountering an oxidizing redox front in the far-field, iron will oxidize and likely precipitate as oxyhydroxide in soils, carrying with it and thereby immobilizing some of the nuclides in the groundwater.  These oxyhydroxides will also provide an additional sorption layer and contribute to nuclide retardation.  It is difficult to predict the impact of the redox front because of large uncertainties with respect to its location, the quantities of sorption sites, etc.  Because the main effect is to provide a geochemical sink, nuclide migration may be overpredicted by neglecting it, as has been done in the assessment.

The use of a Kd model will tend to underestimate nuclide sorption because it is based on the assumption of effectively instantaneous sorption/desorption reactions.  The impact of including kinetics would be to delay, lower, and broaden impacts of groundwater transport (Klukas and Moltyaner 1995).

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  A wide variety of climatic factors, such as temperature, precipitation and wind speed, can directly or indirectly influence the behaviour and transport of radionuclides in the environment.  Climate is an important driving force for radionuclide transport through the soil and the atmosphere.  Temperature influences heating fuel needs, which in turn may influence radionuclide concentrations in indoor air and the inhalation dose to humans.  

The current climate may change to become wetter, drier, warmer, or cooler, or to exhibit permafrost conditions.  Related factors include glaciation, the greenhouse effect, and destruction of the ozone layer.  Short-term natural fluctuations in climatic conditions as might occur over the next 500 years need to be considered quantitatively.  

RESPONSE:  There are many uncertainties in evaluating the potential effects of climate change on the behaviour and transport of radionuclides in the environment, and radiation doses to various organisms.

(i) Desertification.
The current levels of meteoric precipitation could decrease substantially, leading to reduced water flow through the geosphere, with accompanying changes to the biosphere.  Large scale desertification could result, inducing extended periods of drought.  Deforestation might occur, and grassland could also disappear.  Exposed soil could erode and dust storms might become a common feature.  Radionuclides might move to the soil surface, which could result in the formation of alkali flats.  Winds could then readily disperse radionuclides.

However, desertification would represent a dramatic step away from current conditions. The area would become uninhabitable for humans and the critical group would be located far away from the vault.  

(ii)  Glaciation
Glaciation may cause activation and creation of bedrock faults; changes in topography, hydraulic heads, groundwater recharge and discharge zones; and isostatic depression.  These effects may significantly change rock and flow characteristics.  During interglacial periods, isostatic rebound could also affect rock and flow characteristics.

Glaciation is not likely to occur within the next 10,000 years and is thus beyond the period of time for which quantitative evaluation is necessary for IRUS. 

(iii)  Greenhouse Effect
The greenhouse effect refers to the presence of carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere that tend to allow solar radiation through to the earth's surface and reflect heat back to it.  Thus, these gases act much as the glass of a greenhouse, with the earth as the greenhouse.

A key concern of a significant human-produced increase in these gases in the atmosphere over the last 150 years is massive climatic change.  This might mean a warmer and drier climate for perhaps hundreds of years.  The duration of the stronger greenhouse effect would depend on further contributions to greenhouse gases, such as from burning fossil fuels, versus the rate of immobilization of the gases into peat, the seas and sedimentary deposits.

The greenhouse effect would likely not influence the overall integrity of the IRUS disposal system, although it would change some characteristics of the biosphere.  However, there are no obvious reasons that these changes would lead to increased radiation exposure of humans and other organisms.

(iv)  Ozone Layer
The ozone layer protects the earth from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun.  This is important because UV radiation can induce skin cancer.  Without an ozone layer, UV could readily penetrate down to the earth's surface, which could constitute an increase in solar radiation.  Certain industrial chemicals may lead to the thinning or destruction of the ozone layer.  The prime culprits are chlorofluorocarbon compounds. 

It is unlikely that failure of the ozone layer would have any direct effect on the overall performance of the IRUS vault, although it could affect sensitive portions of the biosphere and thereby influence the behaviour and transport of contaminants in the environment.  However, the effects are expected to be small, and no new types of exposure pathways are expected.

PRIORITY A

waste_type: baled and bituminised LLW from Chalk River Laboratories operations

ebs_concept: waste in reinforced concrete vault above the water table
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Colloids are particles comprised of contaminants, whereas pseudo-colloids are naturally-occurring particulates (such as clay) to which contaminants have sorbed.  Colloids might be generated within IRUS when infiltration or groundwater enters the vault.  The movement of long-lived and otherwise slow-moving nuclides could be accelerated.

RESPONSE:  The mobility of radionuclides and other contaminants in ground water can be altered by the presence of colloidal material (sometimes referred to as particulates).  Colloids are loosely defined as particles that range in size from 0.001  m to 1  m.  Radiocolloids are colloidal-sized particles containing radionuclides, and can be classified as either true colloids, which are aggregates of the radionuclide itself, or pseudocolloids, which are colloidal material already present in the groundwater onto which the radionuclide has sorbed. Pseudocolloids may be either inorganic, such as oxides of Si and Fe, or organic, such as humic and fulvic acids.

Significant quantities of true colloids are not expected to form from the constituents of LLRW because radionuclide concentrations are very small.  Any radiocolloid migration that arises from LLRW disposal is expected to occur by pseudocolloid migration. In general there is little information available on the abundance, distribution, mobilization mechanisms and mobility of colloids in subsurface environments.  One of the reasons for this lack of information is that it is difficult to avoid sampling artifacts when studying colloids.  Colloids may be generated during sampling by exposing ground water containing readily oxidizable metals  (e.g., Fe2+) to atmospheric conditions, or they may be generated when water is pumped, yielding particles that would otherwise remain immobile.  Experimental procedures for distinguishing between mobile and immobile particulates are not yet well established (Buffle and Leppard 1995). 

Radiocolloid migration is difficult to model because of the complex physical and chemical dynamics of colloids in groundwater.  Colloids can be removed from solution by adsorption onto soil particles, filtration and precipitation.  The stability of colloidal particles is influenced by a wide range of factors, such as: pH, redox potential, particle size distribution and chemical composition of groundwater (e.g., major cations) and surface chemistry of colloidal particles.  For most radionuclides, it is expected that a fraction of contaminant mass transfer will occur by pseudocolloid migration.  This can appear as enhanced radionuclide migration and as enhanced dispersion, in addition to dispersion that occurs by diffusion and mechanical mixing.  Field studies indicate that a very small fraction of the strongly sorbing radionuclide contaminants will experience enhanced migration as a result of colloidal transport (Borkovec et al. 1991, Brey et al. 1994, Bates et al. 1992).  For this reason it is judged that colloid-mediated transport should have little influence on peak dose.

PRIORITY C

ISSUE:  Airborne radionuclides can be directed, diluted and dispersed by convection, turbulence and diffusion.  This in turn can strongly influence dose predictions for various organisms.  Airborne radionuclides may settle on surfaces through wet and dry deposition.  This can lead to contamination of vegetation, soil and surface water.  

RESPONSE:  The importance of wet and dry deposition has long been recognized in contaminant transport, and these processes are well understood.  Soil and other materials contaminated with radionuclides may be exposed and eroded by wind action, and dispersed in the environment.  This would remove radioactivity from the area occupied by receptor groups near the vault, particularly because radionuclides tend to adhere to small clay particles which are more easily carried away than the bulk soil.  

The selection of locations of receptor groups is discussed in the PSAR in Part III, Chapter 2.  The assessed receptor groups inhabit locations where contaminants re-enter the surface environment because they would then be most exposed to all routes and highest concentrations of contamination.  

Wind erosion of soil would tend to reduce radioactivity in the area occupied by receptor groups near the vault, rather than increase it.  Although receptor groups that are further downwind might then have greater airborne exposures, they would less likely be exposed by other routes (such as ingestion of well water or crops grown in an irrigated garden) which are expected to be more significant.  

Estimates of potential doses from releases of vault gases are assessed in Part III, Section 5 of the PSAR.

project_title: Analysis of Safety Issues for IRUS
waste_type: baled and bituminised LLW from Chalk River Laboratories operations
host_rock: large sand ridge, near surface
ebs_concept: waste in reinforced concrete vault above the water table
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  A member of the critical group may be exposed to contaminants through several  exposure scenarios.  One such scenario is the artificial lake exposure scenario in which the individual is affected as a result of their activities associated with an artificial lake (e.g., one created by quarrying or removing sand or gravel) that has filled with water contaminated by material from the IRUS vault.

RESPONSE:  It is possible to construct an almost limitless number of relatively low probability, yet high-consequence scenarios leading to some risk to humans from radionuclides released from the IRUS vault.  One such scenario would be the construction of artificial lakes or ponds fed by groundwater from the IRUS flowpath, and the culture and consumption of fish from those ponds by humans.  Since risk is the product of probability of occurrence and consequence of a given scenario, both need to be considered to make a proper assessment.

(i)  Probability of Occurrence
The groundwater flowing beneath the IRUS site is of sufficient quantity and quality to support the culture of cold-water fish such as rainbow trout.  However, groundwater resources of similar quality and quantity are common in the sandy dune and outwash plains between Petawawa and Deep River.  Thus, the IRUS flowpath is not a unique resource that has a high probability of selection for this purpose.  The construction of artificial ponds or raceways for fish culture need not be assigned a probability of 1, but is much less likely.  

Practical considerations must also be considered in regard to fish culture in the IRUS flowpath.  In order to reach the water table using ponds based on excavations, the critical group would be limited to sites close to Duke Swamp.  Even here, the size of such excavations would be somewhat limited by the topography of the area, and the limitations to the long-term stability of steep sand slopes.  Thus, the most likely scenario for dug ponds involves fish culture in relatively small, shallow ponds near Duke Swamp.

(ii)  Potential consequence
Infiltrating water downgradient of IRUS will tend to depress contaminated groundwater from IRUS beneath several metres of relatively uncontaminated water. Thus, shallow dug ponds are unlikely to be highly contaminated by radionuclides released from IRUS, even when located immediately downgradient.

An alternative scenario for fish culture could involve pumping of contaminated groundwater into raceways.  These raceways would have to be artificially constructed, because ponds excavated into the sandy soils above the water table near IRUS could not retain sufficient water for fish culture.  Assuming that water was pumped into artificial raceways (i.e., constructed of concrete, steel, or wood) implies a serious and sustained effort at fish culture on the part of the critical group.  This in turn implies both forced circulation and aeration of water to provide sufficient oxygen for the fish, and to maintain clean and healthy conditions in the tanks, and the use of artificial diets for the fish.  The major radionuclide having a water-fish-human pathway is 14C.  Vigorous circulation and aeration of the tanks would rapidly release 14C from the culture water, minimizing contamination of the fish.  The use of artificial diets for the fish would further reduce 14C uptake, and the uptake of other radionuclides associated with natural foods.

Although the contaminating 14C pathway is described as water-fish-human, in reality fish obtain most of their carbon through their diet.  This dietary pathway is simply and appropriately modelled in the SYVAC-NSURE code because at steady state, the specific activity of 14C in water, sediments, phytoplankton, and other aquatic biota will all tend towards the same value.  Thus, when 14C release is prolonged and the flux changes only slowly, using a bioconcentration factor to describe the transfer of 14C from water directly to fish is equivalent to modelling a more complex food chain pathway.  When fish are cultured intensively (with artificial diets) in contaminated water, however, these assumptions no longer hold.  The specific activity of 14C in fish would tend towards the much lower specific activity of carbon in the diet.

(iii)  Conclusion
Because of practical limitations on the location and size of dug ponds, and the secondary implications of intensive fish culture in raceways, it is unlikely that the dose consequence to a member of a receptor group who might culture fish in contaminated water would be as serious as a preliminary calculation using a bioconcentration factor and the concentration of radionuclides in the aquifer water might suggest.

In other assessed groundwater pathway scenarios it is already assumed that members of the receptor groups drink contaminated water from the aquifer, use this water for garden crops and livestock on which they depend for food, and consume fish from the nearby lake which also receives the flux of contaminants released from the IRUS vault.  

PRIORITY C

ISSUE:  Dermal sorption of tritium by humans could increase radiation exposure.  Skin absorption of tritiated water vapour can be more important than inhalation (Osborne 1966).  Thus, dermal absorption of tritium should be considered.

A less important issue is dermal sorption by humans through exposure of the skin to various health and beauty products, such as toothpaste, shaving cream, soap, moisturizer, etc.  These products may become contaminated with radionuclides, which could then enter the human body because the skin can be permeable and absorb various substances.  To be of importance, the latter would have to be manufactured locally with contaminated raw materials.

RESPONSE:  Except for tritium, dermal sorption is likely of very minor importance to members of the critical group (or humans in general), compared to the direct ingestion and inhalation of radionuclides.  The water immersion dose conversion factor for tritium has been adjusted to include dermal sorption (Wilkinson 1996a).

The conservatism built into the major pathways described in NSURE for the other nuclides can be considered to include dermal sorption; therefore, no explicit quantitative treatment of dermal sorption is required.  In particular, as concerns animals in the food chain to humans, dermal sorption in fish would be most important and is included in aquatic concentration ratios.

ISSUE:  The IRUS vault has been designed in such a way that the water shed by the roof of the vault will be carried away from the immediate vicinity through a drainage system. Over the course of the centuries following closure, this drainage system could become plugged and inoperative.

waste_type: baled and bituminised LLW from Chalk River Laboratories operations

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  As a result of ecological succession, lakes and swamps may gradually fill in and be transformed into dry land.  The water in the aquifer underlying the IRUS site emerges at the earth's surface at a low-lying area known as Duke Swamp.  If Duke Swamp fills in and becomes dry land, and becomes contaminated with substances released from IRUS, then an individual could be exposed to radiation as a result of activities associated with subsequent use of the land for agricultural purposes.

RESPONSE:  Because portions of Duke Swamp already contain 14C from Waste Management Area "C", radiocarbon dating of its deposits (hence accumulation rate) is problematic.  Indirect methods of estimating accumulation rates of infilling material must therefore be used.  Basal peats in Perch Lake, Perch Lake Swamp and Lake 233 date at about 9000 years before present, based on radiocarbon dating.  If it is assumed that the approximately 3 m of organic sediments overlying glacial material in Duke Swamp have been deposited during the last 9000 years, the average sedimentation rate is about 0.3 mm per year (Rowan 1995).

However, Duke Swamp outlets are bedrock bounded, and it is likely that 0.3 mm per year represents a maximum accumulation rate.  For example, in Perch Lake Swamp, radiocarbon dates of 5500 years before present are obtained within several cm of the surface.  Perch Lake has thus remained static for over 5000 years.  Duke Swamp also receives little or no terrigenous sediments, and if organic debris were to accumulate above the water level it would simply decompose, with the organic deposits remaining at the water level.  Thus if the Duke Swamp outlets remain at their present elevation, the swamp would be expected to remain in its present state for the foreseeable future (Rowan 1995). 

Furthermore, Duke Swamp has been unattractive in the past for agricultural use.  It was not cultivated prior to the expropriation of the site when the AECL Laboratories were established.  The impacts associated with the use of materials from the swamp are assessed separately in the PSAR in Part III, Section 3.13 and in Sheppard et al. (1996).

     (i)	fish (wild or farmed),

   (iii)	fruits, vegetables and cereal crops (garden, field crops, wild),
   (iv)	nuts and sap (e.g. maple syrup),
    (v)	fruits and vegetables raised in a greenhouse, as well as food preparation and inadvertent soil ingestion.

(ii)  Greenhouse Crops.  Plant crops growing in greenhouses could become contaminated with radionuclides through root uptake, water, fertilizers, etc.  This method of food production is much the same as outdoor gardens and field crops.  Therefore greenhouse food production can be considered as part of plant crop production in general, and there is no need for detailed explicit consideration.

Radionuclides in cooking utensils or fuel could also be transferred to food, but this is likely unimportant compared to the other elements of the diet in determining the total dose to humans.  

(iv)  Soil Ingestion.  Ingestion of soil adhering to plants and by direct hand-to-mouth transfer are included in the biosphere model.  Ingestion pathways are discussed in the PSAR in Part III, Section 3.9.2 and in (Wilkinson 1996a).

ISSUE:  Flushing is a very basic feature of water bodies such as lakes, and it is important in determining radionuclide concentrations in water (Cornett and Chant 1988; Cornett and Ophel 1986; Bird et al. 1992).  Flushing usually refers to dilution and dispersion of contaminants.  Flushing rates vary, and water bodies that are stagnant with little or no flushing could have a high potential to accumulate radionuclides.
The flux of radionuclides assumed to be released from IRUS will be progressively diluted as the contaminants migrate through the aquifer, Duke Swamp, Lower Bass Lake and Maskinonge Lake.  As contaminants are diluted, receptor groups are exposed to proportionally less of the contaminants, and are therefore expected to receive a proportionally lower radiological dose.  If incorrect or unrealistic parameters are used to describe the residence time of radionuclides in aquatic environmental compartments, the dose consequence to members of the receptor groups could be systematically biased, leading to incorrect conclusions about the safety of IRUS.

RESPONSE:  The water fluxes used in the performance assessment models to describe radionuclide transport and dilution in the local environment are based on direct measurements made over many years at a number of carefully monitored and calibrated hydrological sampling weirs located at key sites in the Maskinonge Lake drainage basin.  These data have been compared with similar measurements made elsewhere in Ontario and Canada, and are believed to be highly reliable.  The uncertainty associated with these measurements is a very small factor in the overall uncertainty in the IRUS dose estimates.  This uncertainty is incorporated into the model through the use of parameter values that are believed to be realistic (where sufficient data exist), or that will tend to over-estimate consequences where the available data are limited.

Although the model is based on current conditions, long-term climate trends could result in an overall drying of conditions, leading to reduced rates of runoff and contaminant dilution.  If this were the only consequence of a dry climate, then radiological doses could be underestimated using the present rates of dilution and flushing.  Dry climate conditions, however, will also lead to a proportional decrease in the amount of infiltration through the vault and wasteform.  Thus, the rate of radionuclide release from the vault would also be decreased under dry conditions, and the overall radionuclide concentrations in the environment might not be significantly different from those estimated using the measured water fluxes.

Any contaminants in the flow would be diluted by the inflow, decreasing the dose consequences for humans downstream.  If a well were located to the side of the groundwater flow passing under IRUS, less water would be drawn from the flow of potentially contaminated water, again decreasing the consequences compared to the assumed situation.

The aquifer underlying IRUS is driven by the head of water in Lake 233, not the surface topography of the IRUS site.  Changes to the surface topography near IRUS would not be expected to change the path of the flow of aquifer groundwater, which flows in the overburden some 10 m below the ridge surface through much of its path to Duke Swamp.

host_rock: large sand ridge, near surface
ebs_concept: waste in reinforced concrete vault above the water table
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Groundwater underlying the IRUS site is replenished by seepage from Lake 233 and precipitation infiltrating from the surface.  The Lake 233 drainage basin covers about 167 hectares, mainly draining land to the east and to the southeast of the lake.  The nominal surface area of the lake is 11 ha.  However, the surface area of the lake varies widely throughout the year, considerably exceeding this value after snowmelt and drying up entirely during the summer in some years.

Lake 233 has three seasonal inlets, but no surface outlet.  All of the water loss from the lake occurs as a result of surface evaporation and underground seepage beneath the sand ridge to the southwest.  At times when the level of water in the lake is particularly high, water does drain through the north end.  The safety issues related to Lake 233 flooding are an increase in water table elevation under the IRUS vault and the possibility that aquifer flow direction might change.  

RESPONSE: The nominal surface area and elevation of the lake are 11 ha and 161.5 m, respectively.  The lake's water surface elevation and, consequently, its surface area vary over the course of a year, normally with a maximum near the end of the spring melt.  In many years, the lake is almost dry in late summer and early autumn.  Water table records from the vicinity of Lake 233 show that this seasonal cycle is often about 1.5 m, but that there is also some carry-over from year to year, producing longer term cycles in water levels.  From an analysis of water table fluctuations and precipitation data, Wilkinson (1996b) concluded that the return period for a water table elevation at the IRUS site that exceeds the observed average spring peak by more than 2.8 m would be 1000 years.  If this argument is extended back to Lake 233 itself, it might be concluded that the lake level would not exceed the average spring maximum by a proportional amount for a similar return period.  This would provide a maximum lake level of between 164 and 165 m.

There is another limit on the maximum water level in Lake 233.  The lake currently drains solely by recharging the sand aquifer, but there is a topographic sill at the northwest corner of Lake 233 (currently occupied by the road that runs to the Old Mattawa Road) where the ground surface elevation is 164.5 m.  This sill separates the region around Lake 233 from a series of dry depressions and the Twin Lake basin.  There is no evidence of past events of overland flow across this sill, but its presence puts an upper limit on the water level that could exist in Lake 233.   

There is no evidence of major changes in groundwater flow direction in the Lake 233 aquifer (PSAR, Part II Sec. 1.6.2.3).

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  The extent and speed with which radionuclides entering a surface water body are mixed and thereby diluted may have important effects on the dose to receptors.  Incorrect parameter values describing the mixing of radionuclides in surface water bodies might lead to incorrect conclusions about the safety of IRUS.

RESPONSE:  The dose to members of receptor groups is based upon a lifetime of exposure, and exposures are based on annual mean concentrations of radionuclides in the environmental compartments.  Thus, as long as radionuclide mixing in surface water bodies is sufficiently rapid and complete as to appear instantaneous on an annual basis, the relatively simple compartment model used in NSURE is adequate.

Canadian Shield lakes are typically dimictic, undergoing complete mixing events twice each year, in spring and fall.  These mixing events occur when the lake water is at or near a uniform temperature of 4°C, and may last several weeks (in spring) to several months (in fall), depending on weather conditions.  Between these periods of mixing, lake waters are typically stratified.  This stratification is weak in winter, but ice cover protects the lake water from wind shear that could cause continued mixing.  In summer, stratification is stronger because the thermal (and therefore density) gradients in the water column are stronger.  Wind shear stresses mix the surface layers (epilimnion) of most Canadian Shield lakes rapidly (on the time scale of one day) to a depth of between 4 and 10 m (depending on the size and exposure of the water body).  Beneath this depth a zone of rapid temperature and density changes (thermocline) separates the warm, mixed surface waters from the cold bottom waters (hypolimnion).  The hypolimnion is a region of relatively uniform temperature (typically near 4°C) and density.  The lack of shear stresses minimizes vertical mixing of the hypolimnion, but internal circulation tends to result in relatively rapid mixing in the horizontal plane.

The lack of continuous complete mixing of water bodies has little effect on the IRUS safety case for several reasons.  Most importantly, only the long-term mean concentrations of radionuclides in surface water are required.  Since the lakes undergo complete mixing twice each year, short-term incomplete mixing has little effect on the long-term average concentrations.  In reality the radionuclide flux to the lakes is also driven by the two periods of peak groundwater infiltration and runoff.  These occur in spring and fall, during the periods of whole-lake mixing.  Thus, in the real system, most of the annual radionuclide flux will be delivered to the lake while the assumption of rapid, complete mixing is valid.  Radionuclide fluxes to the lake will be lower in the summer because the aquifer approaches base flow conditions at this time, yet even in the summer, the epilimnetic waters of the lake are rapidly mixed.  The lowest radionuclide flux to the lake takes place in winter, when the aquifer is at base flow.  During the winter months, vertical mixing of the lake water is minimal, yet residual currents continue to circulate the lake horizontally at a reasonably rapid (i.e., days to weeks) rate.  Thus, it is unlikely that incomplete mixing will have a significant impact on the mean annual radionuclide concentration in lake water.

ISSUE:  The primary function of the buffer layer at the base of the IRUS vault is to sorb contaminants from waste leachate, thereby reducing the release of radionuclides from the vault.  The effectiveness of the buffer depends upon its ion exchange and sorption properties.  Large quantities of salts, oils, etc. could saturate the active sites rendering the buffer ineffective.

RESPONSE:  This issue was defined before the addition of more sorbing backfill to the IRUS design (i.e., clinoptilolite in backfill), and before the number of waste streams was reduced to three.  Oil, for example, is excluded from the waste streams that will be emplaced in IRUS (PSAR, Part III Sec. 6.2).

To assess buffer stability, experiments were performed with clinoptilolite samples completely converted to the K+ form (i.e., K+ saturated), because K+ is the most strongly sorbing of the major cations present in the vault (Torok et al. 1991).  Measurements of distribution coefficients for Cs, Sr and Co isotopes with as-received clinoptilolite were compared to measurements with clinoptilolite converted to its K+ form.  As expected, the distribution coefficients were lower for the K+ samples, but in no case were they lower by more than one and a half orders of magnitude.

The estimated values of nuclide distribution coefficients (Kd’s) for the vault backfill were reduced to account for the presence of competing ions.  The calculation was based on a reference ionic strength of 0.1 M; the ionic strength of the vault pore water is likely to be considerably lower. Furthermore, as shown in Table III.6-2 of the PSAR, the major competing ion will be Na+, not the more strongly sorbing K+.  Hence, distribution coefficients have been sufficiently reduced to account for the presence of competing ions.

The impact that organic complexing agents will have on radionuclide sorption is assessed in Sections 3.5.2 and 3.5.3 of the PSAR.
