ISSUE:  Meteorite impact could cause changes in topography, changes in the characteristics of the geosphere, and/or exposure or destruction of the IRUS vault. 

RESPONSE:  It has been estimated that more than a thousand iron and stone meteorites fall on Earth every year.  Most fall into the oceans or thinly populated areas.  The average weight is from 10 to 20 kg, but weights range from a fraction of a gram to several hundred kilos and even tens of tons.  Larger meteorites, such as the Tunguska meteorite of 1908, impact the Earth only once in approximately 1000 years (Heide 1964; Krinov 1960;  Krinov 1966).  Meteorites may fall at any hour of the day or night, at any season, and in any part of the globe.  

Meteoric bodies undergo continual deceleration in the atmosphere, and meteorites up to hundreds of kilos in weight come to a near halt at a height of about 12 km.  They then fall to earth under the influence of gravity at their terminal velocity.  As a consequence, meteorites generally impact the earth near vertically (at an angle less than about 30 degrees from the vertical).  

Upon falling to the ground, meteorites with weights of tens or hundreds of kilograms produce pits with a depth normally equal to the meteorite's cross-section.  Only in rare cases do meteorites penetrate to a depth measurable in metres.  The heaviest of all known meteorites, weighing 60 tons, imbedded itself in friable limestone to a depth of only 1.5 m.  Meteorites reaching the Earth are warm, but only occasionally too hot to hold.  This is because they travel through the atmosphere in only a few seconds so that only their surface has time to heat up.  

The effects of meteorite impacts are far less than those of dud shells from a medium-calibre cannon.  The consequences of meteorite-induced damage to the vault roof could be expected to be similar to that due to the onset of roof failure, which is examined in the groundwater release pathway.  The consequences of the impact of a meteorite with sufficient energy to eject and disperse any of the vault contents would be less probable and less severe than the agricultural intrusion scenario, which is also specifically examined in the assessment.  

Meteorite impact that could expose the IRUS vault roof, damage the vault or perturb its contents, or cause significant perturbation to the local overburden topology or underlying bedrock is thus improbable.

As a consequence, meteorites generally impact the earth near vertically (at an angle less than about 30 degrees from the vertical).  

Upon falling to the ground, meteorites with weights of tens or hundreds of kilograms produce pits with a depth normally equal to the meteorite's cross-section.  Only in rare cases do meteorites penetrate to a depth measurable in metres.  The heaviest of all known meteorites, weighing 60 tons, imbedded itself in friable limestone to a depth of only 1.5 m.  Meteorites reaching the Earth are warm, but only occasionally too hot to hold.  This is because they travel through the atmosphere in only a few seconds so that only their surface has time to heat up.  

The effects of meteorite impacts are far less than those of dud shells from a medium-calibre cannon.  The consequences of meteorite-induced damage to the vault roof could be expected to be similar to that due to the onset of roof failure, which is examined in the groundwater release pathway.  The consequences of the impact of a meteorite with sufficient energy to eject and disperse any of the vault contents would be less probable and less severe than the agricultural intrusion scenario, which is also specifically examined in the assessment.  

Meteorite impact that could expose the IRUS vault roof, damage the vault or perturb its contents, or cause significant perturbation to the local overburden topology or underlying bedrock is thus improbable.

ISSUE:  Radiation fields associated with the wastes might lead to physical and chemical changes in waste forms, waste containers, concrete, backfill and buffer.  Similarly, radiolysis might change the chemical environment in the vault, affecting pH and Eh, or leading to the generation of gases. 

RESPONSE:  This issue was described before three specific waste streams were selected for emplacement in IRUS.  The radiation from the relatively low, dilute radionuclides in the baled waste is not expected to significantly affect the chemical or physical properties of the bales and their immediate surroundings.

Internal radiation of bituminized wastes can modify the molecular structure of the bitumen, cause it to release gases by radiolysis, and change its physical properties.  The radiolytic gas can cause bitumen to swell.  Bituminous material hardens with time, and internal irradiation, particularly   radiation, contributes to this hardening (Burnay and Dyson 1986).  Swelling begins to occur at 104 to 105 Gy, changes in physical properties occur at about 106  Gy; leaching may not be affected up to 106 Gy. 

As reported in the PSAR, Part II, Section 3.2, the average on-contact field for drums of bituminized incinerator ash is 0.6 mGyßh-1 or 5 Gyßa-1.  A typical on-contact field for drums of bituminized reverse osmosis concentrate is 30 mGyßh-1, or 250 Gyßa-1.  In neither case would the bitumen in the drums approach an exposure of 106 Gy in 1000 years, even if the radiation fields were not decreasing with time.

The contaminant-free bitumen layer covering the bitumen drums, and the containers in which the drums will be placed, will prevent water (which could undergo radiation-induced radiolysis) from contacting the waste form for hundreds of years, by which time most of the penetrating  , - radiation fields will have decreased to low levels.

Little credit is being taken in the safety case for the protection and isolation the steel drums provide to the bituminized waste sealed in them.   Any physical or chemical changes induced by the radiation in the wasteforms are not expected to affect the containers in which the drums are overpacked, the vault concrete, or the backfill and buffer materials. 

The performance of the IRUS waste forms is discussed in the PSAR in Part III, Section 3.4.

waste_type: baled and bituminised LLW from Chalk River Laboratories operations
host_rock: large sand ridge, near surface
ebs_concept: waste in reinforced concrete vault above the water table
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Precipitation water that falls on ground surfaces can have one of three basic fates.  It can be evaporated or transpired from the land or plant surfaces back into the atmosphere (collectively termed evapotranspiration).  This water has essentially no further interaction with the local environment.  Water that remains at the soil surface may either infiltrate down to the groundwater, or move laterally across the soil surface as surface runoff or overland flow (Bengtsson 1988).  

Overland flow is often predominant on exposed bedrock surfaces, particularly in the granitic terrain of the Canadian Shield, or when soils are frozen.  On sands and for many soils (with the possible exception of heavy clay soils), infiltration may be more important to the water balance than overland flow.  Infiltration is the predominant advective process leading to contaminant leaching from the IRUS vault.  Runoff is also used to calculate the rate at which surface water bodies are flushed, and provides the dilution of the radionuclide flux leaving the aquifer.  

RESPONSE:  For the PSAR, the observed runoff rates measured at hydrological monitoring weirs on Lower Bass Creek, Duke Stream, Bulk Storage Stream, and at the outflow of Lower Bass Lake, were used to estimate dilution rates for radionuclides in the local environment.  These measurements have been integrated into long-term mean values for the PSAR.

Because evapotranspiration and overland flow occur at the expense of infiltration, any changes in the local environment that tend to increase evapotranspiration or overland flow will proportionally reduce infiltration, and reduce the rate of radionuclide leaching from the vault to the groundwater. As discussed under FEP 116 - Flushing of Water Bodies, long-term changes in the precipitation rate and mean annual temperature could change the balance of evapotranspiration to runoff, affecting the rate at which radionuclides are leached from the vault.  These changes, however, would likely be accompanied by proportional changes in the total amount of diluting groundwater flow and surface runoff, and so have little impact on the radionuclide concentrations predicted for the aquatic environmental compartments.

Surface runoff is unlikely in the sandy terrain near the proposed IRUS site, so it has been assumed that all of the precipitation water that is not released back to the atmosphere as evapotranspiration infiltrates into the local aquifer, without any overland flow.  This will tend to lead to overestimates of the radionuclide release rate from IRUS because although both overland flow and infiltration would be available to dilute radionuclides entering surface water bodies, only infiltration can leach radionuclides from the IRUS vault.  Thus, assuming that all runoff infiltrates instead of being allowed to leave as surface runoff will maximize the estimated radionuclide concentrations in groundwater and nearby surface waters.

ISSUE:  Salt used for de-icing purposes on roads near IRUS could have two principal effects: (i) it could impinge upon the IRUS vault, affecting either the chemistry in the vault or the degradation rate of the concrete; (ii) the salts could alter the chemical and physical properties of the geosphere (groundwater, Kds, concentration of chelating agents, colloids, sorption, etc.) through which radionuclides released from IRUS in groundwater will migrate.

RESPONSE:  Information collected on road salt use at CRL and information on road salt use near Toronto suggest that a sodium chloride (NaCl) concentration of 4.95 gßL-1 (i.e., about 0.1 M) is representative of roadside NaCl concentrations in groundwater at CRL, adjacent to the site's main transportation corridor.  Concentrations as high as 23 gßLå1 have been observed in Toronto; this value represents a probable upper limit on salt loading (Killey 1996).  Salt loadings associated with secondary roads are expected to be lower than those associated with highways or other major transport routes.  Current road salt inputs to the IRUS aquifer are limited to runoff from a small section of the CRL plant highway (which is approximately 800 m from the IRUS site), and there is substantial dilution with uncontaminated runoff before the waters recharge the IRUS aquifer.  Current Na+ and Clå concentrations in the Lake 233 aquifer are around 0.001 – 0.002 M (Killey 1996, see also PSAR, Part II Sec. 1.7). 

Ionic strengths of pore water and groundwater equivalent to roadside NaCl concentrations (i.e., about 0.1 M) have been allowed for in the safety case presented in the PSAR—in the event that NaCl from de-icing salts was to impinge upon IRUS and reach roadside concentrations.  Concentrations of this order were used to:
     (i)	Perform ion penetration tests on candidate mixes of IRUS concrete; the selected mix will protect the encased reinforcing steel for over 500 years (PSAR, Part II Section 2.8.2).  
     (ii)	Estimate distribution coefficients in the vault backfill for modelling radionuclide transport; solution ionic strengths were assumed to be 0.1 M (PSAR, Part III Section 3.5.1).  

At current road salt concentrations in the IRUS aquifer, the weakly sorbing Na+ cation will have little if any effect on sorption of cationic contaminants.

waste_type: baled and bituminised LLW from Chalk River Laboratories operations
host_rock: large sand ridge, near surface
ebs_concept: waste in reinforced concrete vault above the water table
pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE:  Surface water bodies are important to the IRUS assessment because several important pathways lead from surface water to humans, and because surface water bodies are valued ecosystem components that implicitly merit protection from environmental impacts.  Long-term changes in the structure, organization, or chemistry of surface water bodies could affect the behaviour and transport of radionuclides in ways that are not accounted for in the NSURE environmental transport model.  Thus, it is necessary to consider the kinds of changes in surface water bodies that are likely to be seen on a time scale of 102 to 104 years, and how these changes might affect the behaviour, transport, and impacts of radionuclides.

RESPONSE:  Canadian Shield lakes are typically water- and sediment-filled bedrock depressions dating from the end of the Wisconsinian glaciation (about 10,000 years before present).  The lakes likely to be most impacted by contaminants discharged from IRUS (Lower Bass Lake and Maskinonge Lake) occupy bedrock controlled basins.  Sediments in these basins can be broadly classified as belonging to erosional zones (sands, gravels and exposed bedrock sites) or depositional zones (having accumulations of soft sediment or gyttja).  Thicknesses of accumulated gyttja in Canadian Shield lakes rarely exceed 5 to 10 m.  In a small lake like Lower Bass Lake, which has nominally cone-shaped basin morphometry (volume of a cone is ("r2h)/3), and a present water depth of about 11 m, an accumulation of 10 m thickness of gyttja in the bottom of the lake (i.e., a conservative estimate) translates into an original cone height of 21 m, with a top surface area ("r2) of 1.1 x 105 m2.  Using the conical model, the soft sediments presently occupy a volume of about 8.3 x 104 m3 on the bottom of the lake.  This volume accumulated over the past 104 years.

Assuming present conditions prevail over the next 104 years, a further accumulation of about 8.3 x 104 m3 will take place, for a total volume of gyttja after 2 x 104 years of lake succession of about 1.66 x 105 m3.  This will occupy the cone to a height of about 12.6 m, leaving the lake with a maximum water depth of about 8.4 m.  This is still a sufficient water depth to support a stratified water column during the summer months, particularly given the relatively sheltered location and small size of Lower Bass Lake.  Because the lake does not presently support cold-water fish species of interest to humans (i.e., salmonids), but is dominated by warm-water Centrarchidae (sunfishes and bass), this progressive filling of the lake will have little impact on contaminant pathways to humans.

Maskinonge Lake is large and deep enough to support cold-water fish species; however, the much greater mean depth of Maskinonge Lake means that progressive infilling over the next 104 years will have much less impact on its physical dimensions and limnology than on those of Lower Bass Lake.  Thus, the effects of physical changes on the Maskinonge Lake system over the next 104 years can be ignored.

Chemical changes to the lake systems considered in the PSAR are unlikely if the present environmental conditions are sustained over the next 104 years.  Occasional forest fires in the local environment may result in short-term increases in runoff and nutrient release rates from forest soils to lakes (Schindler et al. 1980b), but these effects will be temporary.  Human development in the area may result in significantly increased and sustained nutrient loadings to the lakes, leading to eutrophication.  Modest eutrophication would have the effect of increasing system productivity (including fish yield), without necessarily affecting community composition of warm-water assemblages to any great extent.  Extreme eutrophication might eliminate cold-water species from the lakes because of hypolimnetic oxygen depletion.  Under extreme conditions, eutrophication may have a significant impact on community composition in the lake (Schindler and Comita 1972), potentially modifying pathways to humans if fish species are eliminated.  

Extreme eutrophication would probably also reduce the transfer of contaminants to humans through other mechanisms.  For sorbing contaminants, the net transfer from water to sediment might be accelerated by increased rates of particle formation and sedimentation in the epilimnion.  This effect might be partially offset by the subsequent release and recycling of redox-sensitive radionuclides under anoxic conditions in the hypolimnion.  High growth rates in the biological system could also lead to reductions in the water-fish transfer factor, through growth or production dilution (Hendriks, 1995).  For 14C, high nutrient loadings would probably result in the depletion of available CO2 and HCO3- for photosynthesis by algae.  Under these conditions, the lake would absorb as much CO2 as necessary from the atmosphere (Bower et al. 1987), resulting in a dilution of the specific activity of 14C in the system, and a subsequent decrease in the effective water-fish-human pathway radiological dose.

pfep_description_raw:
ISSUE: Present-day topographical features, including outcrops and hills, water-filled depressions, wetlands, recharge areas and discharge areas, sand dunes, river courses, etc. could change due to natural causes over the next 500 to 1000 a.  Such changes could in turn affect doses to receptor groups.

RESPONSE:  The topography at the Chalk River site is dominated by bedrock surfaces, glacial tills, and fluvial/aeolian deposits of sand.

For the purposes of the postclosure assessment in the PSAR, the underlying bedrock structure can be viewed as permanent, at least until the next onset of continental glaciation.

The future stability of the glacial till and sand deposits on the Chalk River site can be assessed on the basis of their historical stability.  It appears that the major dune ridges, including the ridge that is the site of the IRUS vault, were deposited shortly after the most recent glacial retreat, about 104 years before present (King and Killey 1994, Brookfield 1996).  Because the sand grain sizes are too large to permit large scale dune formation under present meteorological conditions (wind speeds are generally too low), it has been hypothesized that the driving force for the dune formation was cold adiabatic winds sweeping down from the retreating ice sheet.

Since the formation of the ridges within a few hundred years of deglaciation, they have remained stable, with a vegetative cover.  Thus, as long as vegetative cover is maintained on the ridges, major topographic changes and new erosion are unlikely.

The present vegetative cover on dune deposits at CRL is a young (<100 years) mixed hardwood forest, typical of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence biome.  The forest is young because of wide-scale logging and land clearing in the 19th and early 20th century.  Since that time, the land has been allowed to revert to forest because it is too poor to make farming an economical venture, and because of the establishment of the CRL site.  If logging were  renewed on the CRL property, it would be unlikely to result in widespread soil erosion.

In areas where surface vegetation has been removed and the sand is exposed, natural succession rapidly results in re-vegetation by grasses, small shrubs, and trees.  Thus, the present vegetative cover forms a self-sustaining anchor for the sand, that has effectively stabilized the dunes for the past 104 a.

Two other components of the CRL landscape are important to the postclosure assessment of IRUS.  These are the wetlands (Duke Swamp) and lakes (Lower Bass Lake and Maskinonge Lake).  The effects of successional processes on the lakes are discussed under FEP 292, Surface Water Bodies (physical/chemical changes).  Discussed here are the effects of successional processes on wetlands.  For additional information on ecological succession of Duke Swamp in particular, see FEP 102, Ecological Successions.  

As discussed by Reid et al. (1994), wetlands are constantly subject to change in response to climatic, physiognomic and biological factors.  In addition to short-term changes in response to cycles of drought and flood, long-term evolution, or succession, of wetlands may result in progressive change in the wetland habitat.

The classical view of wetland evolution was developed in Europe, and focused on the conversion of open water to dry land, or terrestrialization of shallow water bodies.  In this model (as applied to North American habitats), ingrowth of emergent vegetation (giant reed grass or cattail) from the margins is followed by alder, tamarack, black spruce, cedar, and birch, resulting in the deposition of reed and then wood peats over the lake sediments.  Subsequent invasion and dominance by Sphagnum mosses results in the waterlogging of the site, and eventual loss of trees, culminating in a continuous Sphagnum-dominated carpet.

This classical view is largely an oversimplification.  Walker (1970) examined the stratigraphic sequences (i.e., lake mud, swamp mud, fen peat, wood peat, bog peat) of a large number of wetland sites, and concluded that there is no single "forward" direction of wetland evolution.  Although most pathways appear to be directed towards a final ombrotrophic (i.e. deriving water and nutrients primarily from precipitation) bog stage, as the proliferation of peat deposits increasingly isolates the surface of the wetland from groundwater influence, the full sequence of stages is most likely to be observed in large inland lake basins.  In small kettle-type basins, invasion by sphagnum may occur at an early stage, giving rise to floating mats of vegetation surrounding a central pool.  Walker (1970) also identified examples of "reverse" succession.

Wetland evolution may also be marked by prolonged periods of relative stability.  Jackson et al. (1988) cored a wetland set in sand dune topography adjacent to Lake Michigan.  They concluded that the wetland originated as a pond about 3000 years before present (b.p.) as the water level of Lake Michigan progressively declined.  The fossil record of pond vegetation was remarkably stable, and characterized by submersed and floating-leaved macrophytes between 3000 and about 150 years b.p., when the pond was invaded by cattail (Typha).  This invasion coincided with the disturbance of European settlement, land clearing, and railway construction.

Thus, although wetlands are perceived as a successional stage leading to terrestrialization of aquatic habitat, they may persist for long periods of time as stable ecosystems.  The effects of human disturbance on wetlands are not readily predictable.

The wetland located in the IRUS hydrological flowpath, Duke Swamp, appears to be in a relatively stable successional state.  Much of the wetland is well supplied with groundwater seepage, passing through the dune ridge from Lake 233.  The south end of the Duke Swamp is treed; however, the north end (receiving seepage from the IRUS site) tends to be more fen-like, with few trees.  Central portions of Duke Swamp may be more or less ombrotrophic.  In the absence of human intervention, Duke Swamp is likely to persist in something much like its present condition for the foreseeable future.  Long-term trends will probably be towards an increasingly ombrotrophic condition in central areas, as peat accumulates and forms a water table mound.  This may in turn force more groundwater flow into the margin of the wetland, increasing the extent and importance of channelling of the water flow, already observed in the northern end of the wetland.

While greater channelling could have the effect of increasing radionuclide export rates from the wetland to Lower Bass Lake, no credit is presently taken for contaminant attenuation in the wetland, so this change would not affect the safety case.

Meteorite impact has already been studied by d'Alessandro and Bonne /1981/. The probability of a meteoritic impact can be reasonably estimated from existing statistical information about such  occurrences. Hartmann /1965/ gives the following empirical relationship to estimate the frequency of meteoritic impacts:

          ND = K . D -2.4

where ND is the number of meteorites having a diameter larger than D (km) and K is equal to about 10-13 impacts/km2.year. From available data it is known that craters of a few hundreds meters in depth can be formed by meteorites having a diameter approximately three times the crater depth /Hartmann 1965/.

However, the effect of an impact may propagate to greater depths. Smaller meteorites that create craters with a depth of about 100 m are assumed to cause at least temporarily permeable fractures in clays. The frequency of having a crater with a diameter of 300 m in a 4 km2 rectangle is estimated to be about 7.2 10-12 per year.

A meteoritic crater of a 600 m diameter can destruct a repository located at a depth of 200 m and radioactive materials can be thrown in the atmosphere. The frequency of a 600 m meteoritic crater hitting a 1 km2 repository however is estimated to be about 1.4 10-12 per year (the crater may occur in a 4 km2 rectangle).

Meteorite impacts have not to be considered because the estimated annual occurrence probability is a few orders of magnitude lower than 10-8 per year.

Status: Rejected - low probability

pfep_description_raw:
Magma is a naturally occurring mobile rock material generated within the earth and capable of intrusion into other rocks and extrusion at the earth's surface. These processes lead to the formation of igneous rocks through solidification and related processes. The movement of magma is called the  magmatic activity.  An intrusion (or plutonic rock) is a body of rock that forced itself into pre-existing rocks, either along some structural features (e.g. cleavages) or by deformation and cross cutting the invaded rock (e.g. dykes). The term extrusive is synonymous with volcanic and is applied to igneous rocks that have flowed out at the surface of the earth.

Magmatic activity is related to tectonics, which means that a higher activity occurs near the borders of tectonic plates (cf. § 1.2.01) /Pannekoek 1973/. Plutonic and volcanic activity is found in Belgium only in rocks of Primary (Palaeozoic) age, between the Cambrian and Devonian period, i.e. 570 350 million years BP /Robaszynsky and Dupuis 1983, Goossens 1984/. There are no traces of more 
recent magmatic activities in Belgium.

The nearest volcanic region of recent age is situated 150 to 200 km to the east in the German Eiffel massif. All volcanos are extinct for more than 20,000 years.

The area of Mol is not located in a critical zone and the known activity in Belgium is quite old. Hence it can be concluded that the probability of disturbance of a repository by magmatic activity is extremely low and 
has not to be included in the performance assessment.

pfep_description_raw:
Those processes (chemical, physical, biological, ..) affecting a sediment after its initial deposition, while it is at or near the earth surface, i.e. under conditions of pressure and temperature that are normal to the surficial or outer part of the earth's crust, are called diagenesis. Metamorphism dealing with higher temperatures and pressures (cf. § 1.2.04) is excluded by definition.

Diagenesis will result in the creation of a hard rock, starting from loose sediments. Two important processes are compaction (consolidation) and cementation. Compaction or consolidation of sediment deals with the reduction in bulk volume, in response to the increasing weight of overlying material being deposited, or pressures resulting from ground movement. Cementation is the process by which individual particles of a sediment are held together by a secondary developed material.

The Boom clay at Mol has undergone diagenesis since the deposition of the sediments. Actual activity or activity in the near future (1 million years), is to be considered as late burial changes. The following processes may take place or can be important :

 -  changes in geochemical conditions (pH and Eh); 
 -  changes of mineralogical composition, e.g. formation of autogenic micas and chlorites ;
 -  completion of development of concretions and cementation processes.

It is not evident if important changes can occur during the next million years, since they depend on many other factors e.g. denudation. A further reduction of the permeability or a higher micro-fissuration could result of diagenesis. Since both phenomena determine the ground water movement within the host formation, the process of diagenesis is important enough to study its influences on the final disposal conditions.

For sand layers the permeability and porosity may decrease due to cementation. However this process is extremely slow and it can be neglected in the safety analysis.

Comment:  Diagenesis is a slow process and it will not change drastically the behaviour of the repository system; its possible influence might be taken into account by considering larger uncertainties for the related model parameters. Diagenesis can be treated in the normal evolution scenario.

Status:  Kept, relevant to the clay layer

pfep_description_raw:
Uplift and subsidence are gradual vertical movements of a part of the earth's crust, without horizontal displacement. Both are closely related to fault zones (cf. § 1.2.09).  These zones occur in the regions where orogenesis, epeirogenesis or isostatic forces are active.

Orogenesis is a period of mountain building, leading to the formation of intensively formed belts that constitute mountain ranges. An  orogeny extends in time for some tens of millions of years. There appears to be an average interval of 200 300 million years between orogenesis, although there is little evidence for a marked period in their occurrence. In Belgium we can find two orogenetic periods, the Caledonian (500 million years BP) and the Hercynian one (300 million years BP). A third period in Europe is the Alpine orogeny, that started about 55 million years ago and is still active /Fourmarier 1954/. Actual fault and volcanic activities found on the European continent are related to this Alpine orogenesis. Orogenesis itself is not a problem for a disposal site, but the creation of faults and earthquakes through the forces induced can be important (cf. § 1.2.08 and 1.2.09).

Epeirogenesis is a vertical, either upward or downward, movement of continental or subcontinental land masses as a result of widespread adjustment of level. The movements are generally even in character, producing little more than tilting, slight warping, and minor faulting of rocks.

From the palaeographic evolution of marine and continental deposits in north west Europe, a future tendency can be depicted / Vandenberghe et al 1980/. By carefully examining existing data on land levels, it has been shown that for the northern part of Belgium a slight subsidence of 0.5 to 1 mm/year for 100 km away from an hinge axe is to be taken into account. The Mol site is situated at less then 50 km to the north of this uplift subsidence axis.  If the present tendency is constant a total subsidence for the Mol region is estimated at 50 to 100 m over the coming 200,000 years /Vandenberghe et al 1980/.

Although nothing is known upon the continuity of this epeiro-genetic movement, what makes forecasts of the future situation extremely difficult, the mentioned activities can have an influence on the relative position of the land surface compared to the sea level. Consequently uplift and subsidence should be considered in the safety study.

Comment:  The uplift and subsidence rates can be estimated and the possible consequences can be evaluated in the normal evolution scenario.

A diapir is an intrusion that domes the overlying cover after having pierced the lower layers. Generally, it develops a narrow neck at greater depth and results in a balloon like shape. Diapiric structures originate from differences in the geostatic load in sedimentary strata, as it is the case for salt domes. 

Small diapir like structures have been observed in the Boom clay under and along the River Scheldt / Schittekat et al 1983/ at depths not exceeding 20 m. No diapirs have been observed in the numerous clay pits that were dug in the Boom clay.

For this reason and because no driving force, i.e. a differential geostatic load can be foreseen, diapirism has not be considered in the performance assessment.

The term seismicity is synonym for earthquakes. Strong earthquakes are produced by sudden movements along fault planes. The shocks can be measured on more or less arbitrary scales, e.g. the scale of Mercalli. Of the many thousands of earthquakes which occur worldwide each year, only a few are destructive or even noticed by man. The present earthquake regions are associated with younger-fold mountain regions, and present activity is a phase of the end of the Alpine orogeny.

The seismic activity in Belgium is also related to this orogeny, and with uplift and subsidence  (cf. § 1.2.06), but the seismicity index (the number of shocks/year/100,000 km^2 over a period of 50 year) is very low : 0.02. Nevertheless, earthquakes are to be considered in the scenario study : a plastic clay, like the Boom clay, will not deform much by the forces of an earthquake, but the underground structure of the repository might be damaged by the induced forces.

Comment:  Seismicity has the potential to perturb the performance of the near field barriers; it should be considered in the altered evolution scenarios.

Faults are fractures in rocks where one side of the fracture has moved with respect to the other side. The relative displacement of the two sides can range from a few centimetres to hundreds of meters. Faults are rarely single planar units : normally they tend to occur as parallel to sub parallel sets of planes along which movement has taken place to a greater or lesser extent. Such sets are called fault or fracture zones.

Around the area of Mol several fault zones are observed / d’Alessandro and Bonne 1981, Marivoet and Bonne 1988 / and probably some zones may not be detected at present. Although it is unlikely that new faults are created by tectonic activity, it is always possible that some of the existing faults are reactivated again, for example during an earthquake. Depending on which fault is reactivated, the impact on the disposal facility itself can be important. The reactivation of fault zones can create new flow paths for the ground water and thus influence the migration of radionuclides.

Hence, faulting is a potentially important phenomenon in the evaluation of the safety of the geological repository.

Comment:  A Fault activation cannot be forecasted and since it has the potential to perturb the performance of the clay barrier, it should be considered in the altered evolution scenarios.

Faults are rarely single planar units : normally they tend to occur as parallel to sub parallel sets of planes along which movement has taken place to a greater or lesser extent. Such sets are called fault or fracture zones.

Around the area of Mol several fault zones are observed / d’Alessandro and Bonne 1981, Marivoet and Bonne 1988 / and probably some zones may not be detected at present. Although it is unlikely that new faults are created by tectonic activity, it is always possible that some of the existing faults are reactivated again, for example during an earthquake. Depending on which fault is reactivated, the impact on the disposal facility itself can be important. The reactivation of fault zones can create new flow paths for the ground water and thus influence the migration of radionuclides.

Hence, faulting is a potentially important phenomenon in the evaluation of the safety of the geological repository.

Comment:  A Fault activation cannot be forecasted and since it has the potential to perturb the performance of the clay barrier, it should be considered in the altered evolution scenarios.

pfep_description_raw:
Rock heterogeneity can be important because of the differences that may exist in permeability and chemical composition. Heterogeneities can have a decisive influence on the migration of radionuclides.

Heterogeneities can in the first place determine the water flow. More permeable layers represent preferential pathways for the radionuclide migration and they can influence the repository performance in a negative way (cf. § 1.5.05).

Mineralogical heterogeneities produce different sorption characteristics and consequently they influence theradionuclide migration pattern and migration velocity (cf. § 1.6.07).

The studied part of the Boom clay, i.e. the clay around the underground gallery, looks rather homogeneous in composition. It has not been proven at this moment that the clay formation is homogeneous on a larger scale and over the whole thickness of the clay layer, and geophysical loggings suggest the occurrence of tiny silty layers.

The occurrence of those heterogeneities in the host formation are to be included within in the safety study, while further research on homogeneity and characteristics of the Boom clay layer is also recommended.

The Neogene aquifer consists of a series of different sand layers. The multi-layer structure of the Neogene sands can strongly influence the water movement and the resulting migration of radionuclides in the aquifer. The potential influence of the multi-layer aquifer system should be evaluated in the aquifer modelling.

Comment:  Rock heterogeneities should be characterized and they can be taken into account in the normal evolution scenario.

pfep_description_raw:
Various undetected geological features can be mentioned : faults, shear zones, breccia pipes, lava tubes, intrusive dykes and gas or brine pockets.

Undetected faults are likely present at the Mol area and further investigations on this subject have to be carried out (cf. § 1.2.09).

Shear zones are undergoing forces tending to deform, by the displacement of one part of a rock body relative to another part. These forces are rather weak for sedimentary strata as clay formations.

Breccia pipes are rocks consisting of angular fragments cemented together in a finer matrix. In the southern part of Belgium some breccia pipes are found but none have been found in the northern part of Belgium. Neither are they expected to appear in the region in the next million years, as there is a close relationship between their formation and magmatic activity. Lava tubes and intrusive dykes are also rare in Belgium : a well known lava tube is the one of Quenast / Fourmarier 1954 /.  All registered activities in Belgium (see also § 1.2.03) are much older then 100 million years, and it is not expected that new activities will appear within in the next million years.

No gas or brine pockets have been observed in North Belgium.

If some undetected features are to be considered, we should conclude that only the existence of undetected faults should be included in the safety study. All other features have such low probability of occurrence that they can be excluded.

pfep_description_raw:
A rise of the sea level as high as 100 m can be expected in the case that all the ice from the glaciers of the world should melt /Vandenberghe et al 1980/. In this case large parts of Belgium should be recovered by the sea, including the Mol area. The deposition of new sedimentary layers and the absence of man above the repository site will reduce the radiological consequences of the disposal. Sea flows may give rise to deep erosions (about 100 m), but they are not expected to affect the Boom clay in the Mol region as this clay layer begins at a depth of 180 m.

A less dramatic sea-level rise (20 m) will have strong influences onto the geo-hydrological system, but it is not expected to alter the confining capability of the clay system /Patyn 1987/, neither to influence the repository itself.

A new glaciation period could result in a fall of the sea level of about 100 m /Vandenberghe et al 1980/.  At the same time a subsidence estimated between 50 to 100 m for the region of Mol (cf. § 1.2.06) should strongly reduce this phenomenon and only an effective fall of the sea-level less then 50 m may be expected, resulting in a reactivation of the river erosion /Patyn 1987/. However the time required for rivers to come to equilibrium are much longer than the duration of a glaciation. The most relevant consequence of a fall of the sea level will be the deepening of the river valleys in the region. This deepening changes the regional hydrological system, and may also create new   or shorter   pathways for the released nuclides /Patyn 1987/.

Extensive river erosion, sea-level lowering and whatever climatic change are to be considered in the scenario analysis.

Another sea-level rise of about ten meters is also expected to occur in the next 250 years because of the greenhouse warming / Wildenborg et al 1990, Goodess and Palutikof 1991 /. This phenomenon will be discussed in § 2.4.09.

Comment:  Changes at the future sea-level can be estimated with climatological models based on the Milankovitch astronomical theory. Sea-level change should be considered in the normal evolution scenario.

waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW), spent fuel (SF) and medium level wastes (ILW)
host_rock: plastic clay, the Boom Clay at Mol
ebs_concept: emplacement in concrete lined galleries
pfep_description_raw:
Several glaciations have occurred during the Quaternary. The Milankovitch astronomical theory, which is based on a combination of three characteristics of the earth's orbit (eccentricity, obliquity and  precession), tries to explain the frequency of the  glaciations. New calculations carried out by Berger /Berger 1981/ indicate a tendency to a new but moderate glaciation : the first  moderately cold period should reach its minimum in about 5,000 years AP and two more severe glaciation periods might be expected after 23,000 and 54,000 years AP. An important development of ice-sheet over the north hemisphere can be expected with a high probability of occurrence between 50,000 and 100,000 years AP /Wildenborg et al 1990/. In addition to the drastic temperature lowering and sea-level fall, periglacial effects as permafrost formation, erosion and "subglacial" erosion are to be taken in account.

Permafrost can be defined as a "permanently frozen ground" /Whitten and Brooks 1978/ but it may contain some unfrozen patches and some near surface parts that can melt in summer. Permafrost can be classified as continuous and discontinuous permafrost. The development of this phenomenon can be very important for the hydrogeological system by the fact that a frozen ground behave as an impervious layer.

Erosion following the sea-level fall by fluvial action has to be considered because it affects the drainage of the aquifers (cf. § 1.3.04).

"Subglacial" erosion or erosion below the ice can occur by circulation of melting waters underneath the ice-sheet. Depressions of several hundreds of meters have been observed in Northwest Europe; some of them located near to Gorleben (Germany) reach depths of 400 m and they are attributed to subglacial erosion during the Elsterian glaciation /Wildenborg et al 1990/. We may not exclude completely the occurrence of this periglacial effect but it will depend of the extension of the ice-sheets during future glaciations.   

Belgium is located at the margins of the area that were affected by the quaternary glaciations. Because of the absence of ice-caps, subglacial erosion has not occurred. The depth of observed periglacial effects in Belgium never exceeds a depth of about 10 m /Paepe and Vanhoorne 1967/. For these reasons the probability of drastic glaciation effects such as a destruction of the repository by glaciers or a loss of the clay plasticity because of glacial overburden are believed to be very low. On the basis of observed intensities and frequencies of geological phenomena in the past, the same conclusion has been drawn by Vandenberghe, Bonne and Heremans /Vandenberghe et al 1980/, even in the very worse case in which a new glaciation should be combined with a continental uplift.

On the other hand the occurrence of secondary glaciation effects such as shallow glacial erosion and permafrost cannot be excluded and should be considered in the performance assessment.

Comment:  Moderate glaciations and its associated effects, such as permafrost, should be considered in the normal evolution scenario. Severe glaciations, which are not certain to occur, can change drastically the repository system and they should be considered as altered evolution scenario's.

project_title: SCK-CEN FEP Catalogue for disposal in the Boom Clay, 1994
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW), spent fuel (SF) and medium level wastes (ILW)
host_rock: plastic clay, the Boom Clay at Mol
ebs_concept: emplacement in concrete lined galleries
pfep_description_raw:
Recharge to ground water is not easy to estimate since many parameters determine the recharge process. Conditions of the soil, vegetation, topography, aquifers or impervious areas are mostly not known enough in detail to calculate a correct recharge value. 

Two methods are used to get an idea of the recharge. The net rainfall can be estimated by subtracting the evapo-transpiration from the total rainfall. In a second approach the annual river discharge is measured to calculate the recharge in the catchment. The base flow of a river originates from the ground water reservoir. This means that the yearly discharge of the river minus the run off, which is to be estimated from the hydrograph, indicate the amount of water that has been added to that aquifer in that catchment area.

For the region of Mol, situated in the basin of the River Nete, the annual rainfall is about 750 mm. About 65% of this amount evaporates : a net rainfall of 250 mm per year reaches the aquifer. Roughly the same result is obtained by using the discharge data from the rivers /Patyn 1987, Poesen 1978, Deboosere and Platteeuw 1980/.

These data are valid for the actual conditions, and may stay for periods in the order of thousand years or less. The value of the recharge is depending on the amount of rainfall and the conditions of the soil and vegetation, and they may change quite fast compared to radioactive waste disposal times.

Since changes in the ground water recharge influence directly the regional hydrological system, and since ground and surficial water bodies are the main vectors for the released nuclides, ground water recharge cannot be discarded from the safety assessment.

Comment:  Variations of the ground water recharge rate should be considered in the normal evolution scenario (cf. § 1.3.01).

project_title: SCK-CEN FEP Catalogue for disposal in the Boom Clay, 1994
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW), spent fuel (SF) and medium level wastes (ILW)
host_rock: plastic clay, the Boom Clay at Mol
ebs_concept: emplacement in concrete lined galleries
pfep_description_raw:
The discharge of ground water towards the biosphere can occur via different paths : surface water (drainage), springs, wells and discharge to the sea. The volume of water drained equals the yearly amount of recharge, and represents hence vast volumes.

The water directly drained is mainly younger ground water that infiltrated recently, and stayed in the upper zone of the water bearing formation. Only water abstraction by deep wells characterized by a convergent flow pattern, is an obvious pathway to bring the deeper ground water directly to the biosphere.

Near Mol most surface waters remain permanently in hydraulic and effluent contact with the phreatic aquifer. Springs can only originate when at a particular place the ground water potential is higher than the topographical level. In case of a water table aquifer this release is mainly composed of recently infiltrated water. 

Hydrological simulations and piezometric levelling have shown that the ground water flow for the region concerned is in all aquifers directed to the west. In the present conditions the Neogene aquifer in the Mol region discharges into the Rivers Nete /Patyn 1987/.

The flux through the semi pervious Boom clay at the Mol site, is directed downwards. This means that the released radionuclides can also be transported to the underlying sands of Berg. This aquifer is not extensively exploited in the areas where it is confined (like at Mol), but it is used as a water resource in the zones where it outcrops. Hydrodynamic simulations have shown that the flow in this aquifer is also directed to the west, discharging into the Rivers Rupel and Scheldt. Leakage fluxes west of Herentals are directed upwards /Patyn 1987/.

Since for all aquifers concerned the ground water flow is directed to the west some discharges to the Scheldt estuary occur. In the case of a decrease of the net precipitation the resulting lowering of the ground water table should make that this pathway becomes the most important one.

Comment:  The ground water discharge is simulated with the aquifer model in the normal evolution scenario.

project_title: SCK-CEN FEP Catalogue for disposal in the Boom Clay, 1994
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW), spent fuel (SF) and medium level wastes (ILW)
host_rock: plastic clay, the Boom Clay at Mol
ebs_concept: emplacement in concrete lined galleries
pfep_description_raw:
Ground water flow follows the law of Darcy, that states that the flux through a given section equals the product of the hydraulic conductivity (K) and the hydraulic gradient (i) along the flow path. Ground water flow will cause the transport of released radionuclides. The K value of an aquifer cannot change dramatically in the period considered since geological phenomena involved take much longer times (see § 1.2.5). On the other hand the hydraulic gradient depends on many factors, such as effective rainfall, surface water levels, pumping rates, and hence it might change relatively fast.

As ground water is the most important vector for the released nuclides, the flow in the aquifers remains a very important topic in the safety analysis of the geological repository.

The water flow in the clay formation itself is extremely slow, because of the very low K value. Whether the water flow in the Boom clay is Darcyan (i.e. a linear relationship exists between the gradient and the flux, without a threshold gradient) or not needs further research.

Channelling and preferential pathways are characterized by a higher velocity, than the one that would be expected on the basis of the general characteristics of the water bearing formation. The existence of such pathways depend upon the lithology and the sediment structure of the aquifers. In sandy aquifers they surely exist, e.g. thin layers with coarser sediments or silty sand bands. The potential influence of the layered structure of Neogene aquifer should be examined (cf. § 1.2.11).

The possible existence of preferential pathways in the Boom clay is extremely important because the waste is disposed in this clay layer especially for its impervious character, and the existence of preferential pathways (by sedimentological characteristics, microfissures, ...) might cause an advective velocity which is several magnitudes higher /Marsily 1981/ than the velocity calculated on the basis of the permeability of the formation. Therefore the permeability of the clay layer on a macroscopic scale should be carefully examined experimentally as it might influence strongly the performance of the repository system (cf. § 1.2.11).

Comment:  Ground water flow is simulated with the aquifer model in the normal evolution scenario.

project_title: SCK-CEN FEP Catalogue for disposal in the Boom Clay, 1994
waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW), spent fuel (SF) and medium level wastes (ILW)
host_rock: plastic clay, the Boom Clay at Mol
ebs_concept: emplacement in concrete lined galleries
pfep_description_raw:
In the ground layers an unsaturated and a saturated zone can be distinguished. The unsaturated zone is that part of the aquifer where not all pore spaces are filled with water. The pressure in the saturated zone, below the ground water table, is equal to the hydraulic pressure.

In the Campine area the thickness of the unsaturated zone varies from 1 to 5 meters. This zone will be important only in the area where the radionuclides transported by the ground water have reached the top of the water table.

The saturated zone of the Diestian aquifer above the Boom clay is  more than 100 m thick. The aquifer situated under the clay, i.e. the Berg sands, is about 30 m thick. Only those two aquifers can have an important impact on the transport of radionuclides.

Comment:  The ground water conditions are considered in the normal evolution scenario.

pfep_description_raw:
In general fresh water overlies salt water, as a result of density differences. Near the coast brackish water intrudes from the sea and pushes the fresh water aside in a wedge-shaped salt water tongue. The position of the transition zone between the fresh and the brackish water depends on the ground water recharge in higher areas, and it can be influenced by intensive pumping from the aquifers. 

For the Mol site, which is located about one hundred kilometres from the sea, the regional aquifers are not endangered by a seawater intrusion.

waste_type: vitrified high-level waste (HLW), spent fuel (SF) and medium level wastes (ILW)
host_rock: plastic clay, the Boom Clay at Mol
ebs_concept: emplacement in concrete lined galleries
pfep_description_raw:
Natural thermal effects are found in areas where magmatic activity is or was located. This magmatic activity yields geothermal water or, more general, warm (or hot) ground water. The repository at Mol is located at a depth of about 220 m. At this depth the temperature differs slightly from the air temperature due to the general geothermal gradient (approximately 2.5°C / 100 m), but no geothermal activity is found at that depth.

As no magmatic activity has been recorded nor is expected to occur within the time scales considered in the radioactive waste safety studies, the natural thermal effects will not have to be considered in the study.

On the other hand, geothermal water is being used at Turnhout, approximately 20 km north of Mol, from the carboniferous strata, at depths of about 800 m. Although the same geological circumstances do not exist in the Mol area, prospecting and reconnaissance cannot be ruled out completely. Such events are considered as intrusion scenarios (see section 2.3).

Status: Rejected - administrative reason

At present ground water is the only resource in the Mol area which is exploited. Also for the near future there seems not to be any other resource in the underground for which an exploitation drilling should be carried out.

The Neogene aquifer, which overlies the Boom clay layer, is an important water resource for the region and many pumping wells are in operation. Because of its very high probability of occurrence, this event has been analyzed in the earlier performance assessments as a pathway to the biosphere within the normal or altered evolution scenario's.

At present the Rupelian aquifer, which underlies the Boom clay layer, is not used for water abstraction in the Mol area. However the sinking of a water well in the Rupelian aquifer cannot be excluded.

This FEP is considered as relevant.

An exploitation drilling sunk in the Rupelian aquifer should be considered for the identification of the altered evolution scenarios.

pfep_description_raw:
Various hydrological and transport parameters such as density, viscosity and diffusivity are temperature dependent. However migration of radionuclides is not expected during the thermal period, because the design lifetime of the overpacks is assumed to be at least 500 years.

Possible thermal convection effects around a H.L.W. repository have been evaluated by Ecole de Mines de Paris /Goblet and Cordier 1987/. The study shows that the appearance of thermal convection cells in the Boom clay is not expected because of the low permeability of the Boom clay.

The same study /Goblet and Cordier 1987/ shows also that the occurrence of thermal convection phenomena, e.g. convection cells, in the Neogene aquifer will depend of the repository geometry and of the induced temperature increases at the top of the Boom clay layer.

At the moment it is not possible to decide upon the relevance of the induced hydrological changes in the aquifer because these phenomena depend of the repository configuration and dimensions.

Comment:  The induced hydrological changes can be evaluated and they should be considered in the normal evolution scenario.

pfep_name: Alteration and weathering along flow paths
pfep_description_raw:
Short description: 
Chemical (water-rock) reactions between flowing groundwater and the rock and any fracture minerals will lead to progressive changes to the solid phases along the flow path and to its hydraulic properties. These water-rock reactions can impede or enhance radionuclide transport depending on their nature. 

Technical description: 
Groundwater can react with the adjacent rock, and any fracture-coating and infilling minerals causing alteration and weathering of the groundwater flow paths. This can occur both in the near and far-fields. Rock-water reactions generally occur when the system is out of chemical equilibrium and this situation could arise from perturbations caused by the presence of a repository or by the rapid influx of chemically different waters from the surface. 

Under natural geological conditions, alteration and weathering processes at depth are generally slow at ambient temperatures and require geological timescales for significant changes to the physical and chemical properties of the rocks to take place. However, severe and more rapid alteration to the rock might be experienced around a repository because the local groundwater chemistry will be significantly altered by reaction with the waste and the engineered barrier system materials. These altered groundwaters, when they flow out of the engineered barriers, may be far from chemical equilibrium with the host rock and will react with them. This will be particularly the case for the SFR where the large volumes of cement will cause the groundwater to become very alkaline (see SFR-23 "Groundwater chemistry in the near-field rock"). Also, in the spent fuel repository, the higher temperatures and temperature gradients occurring after repository closure will impact on the equilibrium between the groundwater and the rock, where maximum temperatures are reached a few hundred years after closure (see SFL-46 "Temperature of the near-field"). 

In the upper part of the host rock (near surface), infiltrating groundwater is usually out of chemical equilibrium with the rock. Changes to the groundwater recharge system, such as variations in recharge rates, volumes, locations and depths, can be brought about by climate change. If recharge increases (e.g. as a consequence of glaciation), it is possible that fresh, oxidising waters would be able to penetrate deeper into the far-field rock than they do at the present time. These waters would then be out of chemical equilibrium with the far-field rock and would react with them. Scenarios such as these are considered in a number of performance assessments. 

Many water-rock reactions will involve the replacement of thermodynamically unstable minerals by hydrous minerals stable at low temperature and pressure. This alteration may liberate radionuclides already sorbed on the existing minerals, which would be a nonconservative process. However, the newly formed minerals may themselves incorporate radionuclides in their mineral structure making them inaccessible to the flowing groundwater. In addition, the neoformed hydrous alteration products generally are more efficient at sorbing radionuclides to their surfaces than the minerals they replace. However, they may be efficient sorbents for only a limited time as they are gradually transformed to more stable crystalline phases. 

Other water-rock reactions will involve dissolution and precipitation if the solubility of fracture filling mineral phases changes due to variations in the groundwater temperature or chemistry (Eh, pH and concentrations of dissolved species). For example, an increase in temperature in the near-field of the spent fuel repository due to the early thermal peak may cause increased dissolution of silicate minerals and a subsequent precipitation of silica (potentially as colloids) downstream from the repository. Calcite, on the other hand, which has a lower solubility at higher temperatures, may precipitate closer to the repository. Likewise, the introduction and mixing of chemically distinct groundwaters from the near-surface along fast pathways (see GEN-35 "Fast transport pathways") may cause more rapid dissolution and precipitation of minerals in the fractures. 

Both mineralogical transformation and dissolution-precipitation reactions will result in changes to the hydraulic properties of both the accessible bulk rock and any fractures present. Changes in rock porosity will be linked to the groundwater flux through the rock and to volumetric changes associated with dissolution and precipitation reactions. Changes in hydraulic conductivity and fracture transmissivity will be linked to changes in porosity. Relatively minor changes in porosity may cause large changes in hydraulic conductivity. Consequently, alteration of fracture surfaces may have an effect on the fraction of rock available for flow, sorption and matrix diffusion. The impact on repository safety may thus be positive or negative depending on whether the water-rock reactions enhance or impede groundwater flow. 

Rock deformation due to stress changes (e.g. caused by the thermal load or glaciation) may also affect porosity. These changes will be most marked in lithologies which contain higher proportions of minerals thermodynamically unstable at low temperatures and pressures. Neoformed minerals will be most abundant in zones of enhanced water flow. Thus alteration and weathering of rock minerals has the potential to heal existing and newly formed fractures. 

Water-rock reactions will be controlled by groundwater residence time, the rate of mineralwater reaction and temperature. In some cases, groundwaters never reach chemical equilibrium due to slow reaction rates and the inherent thermodynamic instability of the mineralogy concerned. Silicate mineral dissolution reactions are generally slow (in the range 10-1 to 10-7 mol m-2/yr at 25°C) and silicates are poorly soluble (of the order of 10-3 to 10-5 g/l). Some minerals may never reach equilibrium and will exist only due to their slow kinetics and limited contact with the water. 

Dissolution and precipitation reactions are driven by departure from thermodynamic equilibrium. In water-rock systems, departure from chemical equilibrium is governed by groundwater flow and changes in temperature. Flow of groundwater will redistribute solutes and thus potentially perturb chemical equilibria between minerals and aqueous solutions. A thermodynamic description of a water-rock system only defines whether a solid will tend to dissolve or precipitate. The rate at which a solid reacts with a fluid may be more relevant. Rate limiting mechanisms are of two types (Berner, 1978): ‘transport-controlled’ kinetics where dissolution is limited by the rate of transport of solutes away from the dissolving crystal and ‘surface reaction-controlled’ kinetics where dissolution is limited by the rate of detachment of ions from the surface of the crystal. 

The applicable rate limiting mechanism can be estimated from the solubility of the mineral concerned. Below a solubility of about 10-4 moles/l, surface reaction control dominates. This would include all silicates and carbonates in systems where pH > 4 (Lasaga, 1984). The dissolution behaviour of evaporite minerals such as halite, gypsum, anhydrite etc. should be transport-controlled. In contrast, the rate of dissolution of silicates should be dominated by the intrinsic dissolution rate constant and should be relatively unaffected by the groundwater flow rate. Using solubility data from Berner (1978) one volume of calcite would require approximately 105 volumes of freshwater for complete dissolution and one volume of feldspar would require approximately 107 volumes of freshwater for complete dissolution. 

Alteration and weathering along groundwater flow paths can be predicted using thermodynamic equilibrium models and databases. However, these models are limited in their ability to treat kinetics and solid-solution mineral series. 

Origin in the repository system: 
The alteration of groundwater flowpaths will occur in the near-field rock by repository-induced processes such as the early thermal pulse causing chemical disequilibrium between the groundwater and by changes to the near-field groundwater composition due to reaction with the engineered barrier system materials. Alteration and weathering along groundwater flow paths will occur in the far-field rock by natural, time-dependent processes, such as climate change driven variations in the volume and composition of recharge groundwaters. 

Impact on the repository system: 
Rock-water interactions may change the radionuclide transport properties of the near-field and far-field rock by potentially changing the hydraulic properties (groundwater flow system) of the bulk rock mass and any fractures that may be present. 

In addition, rock-water interactions can fix radionuclides into (or liberate radionuclides from) the mineral lattice and surface sorption sites. In general the neoformed alteration minerals have better sorptive properties than the minerals they replace. 

Bibliographic references: 
Berner RA (1978) Rate control of mineral dissolution under earth surface conditions. American Journal of Science, 278, 1235-1252. 
Lasaga AC (1984) Chemical kinetics of water-rock interactions. Journal of Geophysical Research, 89, 4009-4025.

pfep_description_raw:
Short description: 
Anion exclusion is an electrostatic phenomenon whereby anionic species in solution are repelled from mineral surfaces by their negative electrical charge. In fine grained materials, such as a clay-rich buffer, anion exclusion can be an effective retardation process. 

Technical description: 
Due to the atomic structures of many silicate minerals, their surfaces are generally negatively electrically charged. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced for the flat, ‘sheet-like’ phyllosilicate minerals such as clays and micas. As a consequence, negatively charged anionic species and negatively charged complexes in solution in ground and porewaters (and suspended colloids also with negatively charged mineral surfaces) are electrically repelled from solid mineral surfaces in rock or in mineral-based materials, such as compacted bentonite. This electrostatic repulsion phenomena is known as ‘anion exclusion’. 

This repulsion force arises because cations may be released from interlayer sites in the mineral structure, resulting in a negatively charged silicate framework, surrounded by a diffuse cloud of cations. This charged surface and cloud of ions is called a double layer. The double layer consists of ions attached to the mineral surface (the ‘fixed’ or ‘Stern’ layer), whereas outside that lies the ‘diffuse’ or ‘Gouy layer’ in which ions are free to move. In smectite clays, the surface charge results from substitutions in the silicate framework, so the charge is effectively independent of pH. In a compacted clay such as bentonite, the Gouy layers on adjacent particles overlap, so that anions will be effectively excluded from the pores. 

If a pressure gradient is applied to the system, water molecules are able to move through the pores, but negatively charged dissolved species cannot. The clay can thus act as a semipermeable membrane allowing the passage of water but not dissolved anionic species. This process is also known as ‘membrane filtration’ (Hanshaw and Coplen, 1973). 

Anion exclusion is thus dependent on the characteristics of the pores in the solid material (e.g. clay-rich rock or bentonite), the ionic strength of the solution and the charge of the diffusing species. Experiments examining the diffusion of anionic species through compacted bentonite have shown that the diffusion flux is dependent on the density of the bentonite, the electrolyte concentration in the porewater and the charge of the anionic species. At high bentonite densities and low electrolyte concentrations, the pore volume accessible to anionic species, the effective porosity, is smaller than at lower densities and higher electrolyte concentrations. 

Anion exclusion can affect the diffusive mass transport of species in solution. When anion exclusion does occur, its likely impact will be to lower the diffusion flux (retard) anionic species, with respect to the flux of cationic species. Consequently anion exclusion should be considered when assigning diffusivity values to diffusing anionic species. 

In the repository environment, anion exclusion theoretically can cause retardation of radionuclides in anionic form in solution (or bound to negatively charged colloids). However, since the electrical repulsion forces act over very small distances, anion exclusion is only likely to cause retardation in clay-rich materials with small pore spaces. The most likely parts of a repository where this may occur are (i) a clay-rich buffer or backfill, (ii) a clay-rich host sedimentary rock, or (iii) in small aperture microfractures in crystalline rock that are filled or lined with clay minerals due to alteration of the rock matrix (see GEN-1 "Alteration and weathering along flow paths").

Short description: 
Cave-in or collapse of deposition holes, caverns, tunnels or access shafts in a repository could take place under certain circumstances. This, in turn, might change the properties of the surrounding rock and the engineered barriers leading to earlier or faster radionuclide release. Cave-in is, therefore, of potential significance in performance assessment. 

Technical description: 
Cave-in of the excavated parts of the repository is possible if the rock is not self-supporting and if the buffer, backfill and any engineering-supports are not sufficiently strong to hold-up the rock mass. It represents an extreme example of loss of mechanical strength of the rock mass and is only possible under certain circumstances, such as when fracturing of the rock mass is sufficient to allow movement of blocks of rock to take place or when this movement is made possible by some change in the properties or continuity of the near-field materials and supports. 

There is a complete spectrum of possible damage to the rock mass, from minor adjustments on a single fracture to total collapse of an underground structure. Small movements of the rock can occur in the engineered damaged zone and can be caused by creeping of the rock mass (see GEN-5 "Creeping of the rock mass"). This FEP is concerned with extensive, but not necessarily total collapse, of a part of an underground opening anywhere in the repository. 

Unless sufficient space is available in the repository near-field, significant cave-in could not take place, since a prerequisite for such a process to occur is the dilation of the rock mass. If space is available, cave-in will be exacerbated by an increase in the number or size of fractures, and displacements along them. This could be caused by repeated cycles of glacial loading (e.g. Hansson et al., 1995), by thermally-induced stresses, by the swelling of materials in the near-field (e.g. bentonite) or by time-dependent decreases in the strength of the rock mass due to chemical processes. 

Fracturing will also tend to be increased where a high contrast exists in the value of the deformation modulus between the rock mass and the backfill. In places where rock support has been required during repository construction, e.g. when a tunnel intersects a fault zone, the support (which is likely to consist of rock bolts, mesh, shotcrete etc.) will degrade over time and this could allow movement to take place on fractures that had previously been held securely. Chemical changes to the engineered barriers and reinforcements could alter the support provided by these materials to the rock mass. 

Thus, in order for a cave-in to occur, it would be necessary for substantial changes to have taken place in the support provided to the rock surrounding a part of the repository and for sufficient space to have been made available. A reduction in rock support on its own, e.g. if rock bolts were to lose their effectiveness, would be insufficient to allow a cave-in to occur. In this case, fractures could suffer some displacement and may show some dilation but insufficient additional space would not allow the rock mass to collapse. 

In the spent fuel repository, the buffer within the deposition hole will, under the majority of chemical and hydrogeological conditions expected in the repository, provide considerable support to the wall of the deposition hole, and the thickness of bentonite between the rock and the canister and the strength of the canister itself will prevent the possibilities for cave-in. Unless a significant proportion of this bentonite is removed from a deposition hole, or unless the canister degrades to such an extent that its volume is sufficiently reduced, it seems unlikely that a reduction in the swelling capacity of the bentonite on its own would allow cavein of the hole to occur. 

A tunnel or an access shaft has an increased possibility of suffering a cave-in, since these parts of the repository are more likely to intersect fracture zones with substantially higher transmissivities than the deposition holes, which will be selected so as to minimise fracture intersections. There is also a chance of movement on these larger fracture zones. Thus, there is an increased likelihood of damage, either to the backfill, to the rock support systems or to the rock mass adjacent to the deposition area. Nevertheless, cave-in will, again, only occur if sufficient space is available and this seems likely to occur only when a sufficient volume of the backfill has been removed by erosion (see SFL-17 "Erosion of the buffer and backfill") or when movement on a fault or fracture zone has resulted in considerable dilation of the rock mass (see GEN-17 "Faulting"). 

In the SFR, cave-in of the silo is unlikely because the reinforced silo structure and the cementitious backfill will act to support the rock. Cave-in of the rock vaults is possible because they will be backfilled only loosely with sand and crushed rock with no swelling pressure. However, the radiological impact of cave-in of the rock vaults would be limited because the majority of the activity in the SFR is located in the silo. 

The implications of a cave-in are dependent on where it takes place. The closer it is to the waste the more significant it is likely to be. The potential effects of a cave-in on the performance of a repository are an increase in the hydraulic conductivity of the rock mass in the vicinity of the cave-in, increased channelling of groundwater flow that could result in there being further damage to the backfill or, in an extreme case, damage to a waste packages, although this is considered unlikely. 

Origin in the repository system: 
Cave-in of all or a part of the repository excavations might occur if the rock mass is fractured and sufficient void space is available to allow movement of the individual rock blocks. Given that most void spaces will be filled by a buffer or a backfill during normal repository closure operations, this void space can only occur by extensive degradation, collapse and removal of the engineered barrier materials.

Impact on the repository system: 
Extreme cave-in occurring close to the waste might impact on the mechanical stability of the engineered barriers and may lead to early failure of the waste packages, resulting in early or enhanced radionuclide release, although this is considered unlikely. 

Cave-in is most likely to affect the hydraulic characteristics of the rock mass at the site of the collapse. Hydraulic conductivity and the extent of channelled groundwater flow are both likely to be enhanced by cave-in. 

Bibliographic references: 
Hansson U, Shen B, Stephansson O and Jing L (1995) Rock mechanics modelling for the stability and safety of a nuclear waste repository. SKI Technical Report, 95:41. 
Shen B and Stephansson O (1990) Modelling of rock mass response to repository excavation, thermal loading from radioactive waste and swelling pressure of bentonite. SKI Technical Report, 90:12. 
SKI (1996) SITE-94: deep repository performance assessment project. SKI Technical Report, 96:36, Two Volumes.

2.1.07 (Mechanical processes and conditions in wastes and EBS), and 
2.2.06 (Mechanical processes and conditions in geosphere)
